title: Describe the API contract as a machine-readable manifest
description:
## What changes for the user
Nothing visible. Today the only description of what the screens expect from a backend is TypeScript that a Go program cannot read, so a real backend that misspells or forgets a field would show up as a blank on screen, or as a total that is silently missing a part. After this lands that description also exists as a file both sides read, and the gate can catch the mismatch before anyone sees it.

## Outcome
Every method of the interface's API contract is classified, and one generated, versioned file describes the whole contract for a non-TypeScript reader: each method's route, class, argument schemas and result schema, plus the error envelope. The gate fails when that file is stale.

## Context
The interface talks to its backend through one TypeScript interface, `FinwiseApi` in `web/src/api/types.ts`, with 13 domains and 82 methods declared in `web/src/api/contract/`. Today an in-memory stand-in (`web/src/api/fake/`) implements it. A Go backend is being built to implement the same contract; it will be read-only at first: reads answer, every write is refused with one error.

**Why a classification.** Nothing in the types says which methods change state. The server needs that to refuse writes without a handler per write, and tests need it to prove none was forgotten. Four classes:
- `session`: the PIN gate itself, `session.status`, `session.unlock` and `session.lock`.
- `read`: returns data and changes nothing.
- `evaluate`: takes a draft, computes a result and stores nothing (`budget.evaluateScenario`).
- `write`: changes state. `session.changePin` and `changes.undo` are writes.

The classification lives beside the contract as a constant checked by a mapped type over `FinwiseApi`, so a method that is added, removed or renamed without being classified is a type error, not a runtime surprise.

**Why an error type.** The contract has none: failures are `null`, a result union for the PIN, or prose comments saying "Refused". A backend that refuses writes needs one representation. Kinds: `locked` (no valid session), `read_only` (a write or an evaluation was refused), `ledger_unavailable` (the bank data cannot be read), `bad_request`, `unknown_method`, `internal`, and `network` (client side only: the request never got an answer). On the wire an error is `{"error":{"kind":"<kind>"}}`.

**The wire, decided.** One route per method, `POST /api/<domain>/<method>`, whose body is the JSON array of the method's arguments in declaration order and whose answer is the method's result as JSON (`null` for a method that returns nothing). An optional trailing argument may be omitted or `null`. Rejected: resource-style REST, which needs 82 hand-written mappings on each side for no other consumer.

**The manifest.** A script under `web/scripts/` writes `internal/contract/contract.json` with: a format version; for every method its domain, name, route, class, an array schema for its arguments and a schema for its result; the shared definitions; and the schema of the error envelope. Object schemas forbid properties the contract does not declare. The file is versioned and never edited by hand, like `web/src/styles/tokens.css`; the freshness check compares the generated output with the file on disk, not with git, because a built but uncommitted change must not fail the gate that runs before the commit.

**The generator and its risk.** `ts-json-schema-generator` 2.10.0 (MIT, supports TypeScript from 5.9 below 7; the repository is on 6.0.3) is the first choice. It may not resolve a mapped or conditional type that extracts arguments and results from `FinwiseApi`. Settle that first: if it cannot, walk the methods with the TypeScript compiler API, which is already a dependency, and use the generator only for named types. Either way no schema may come out as the empty schema.

**Proving the schema can fail.** The stand-in is type-checked against the contract, so every answer it gives must validate. A test calls every `read` method of the stand-in over the prototype dataset and validates each answer against its result schema with `ajv`. If an answer does not validate the schema is wrong. The same test mutates one answer (a number turned into a string, a required field removed, an unknown field added) and expects each mutation to be rejected.

Dependencies are pinned to exact versions, as everywhere in `web/package.json`.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Removing one method's entry from the classification makes `npm --prefix web run typecheck` fail, and so does adding an entry for a method that does not exist.
- [ ] `internal/contract/contract.json` lists every method of `FinwiseApi` exactly once, each with a route of the form `/api/<domain>/<method>`, a class, an arguments schema and a result schema.
- [ ] `session.status`, `session.unlock` and `session.lock` are `session`; `session.changePin` and `changes.undo` are `write`; `budget.evaluateScenario` is `evaluate`.
- [ ] No arguments schema and no result schema in the manifest is the empty schema or accepts any value.
- [ ] Every answer of every `read` method of the stand-in, over the prototype dataset, validates against its result schema.
- [ ] A number turned into a string, a required field removed and an unknown field added are each rejected by validation.
- [ ] `bin/ci` fails with a message naming the manifest when `contract.json` on disk differs from what the script generates, and passes after the script is run.
- [ ] `ApiError` and its kinds are exported from the contract, and the error envelope's schema is in the manifest.
- [ ] `npm --prefix web run parity` still reports every state at or under 0.05%.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and editing any contract type without regenerating the manifest makes it fail.

## Tests
- Unit: the manifest covers the classification one to one; route format; no empty schema.
- Conformance: every stand-in answer against its schema, and the three mutations rejected.
- Unit: the freshness check fails on a stale file and passes on a fresh one.
- The type-level guard is broken once on purpose and the compiler error quoted in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `web/src/api/contract/classification.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/errors.ts`, `web/src/api/types.ts`, `web/scripts/contract-manifest.mjs`, `web/src/api/contract/manifest.test.ts`, `web/package.json`, `web/package-lock.json`, `internal/contract/contract.json`, `bin/ci`, `AGENTS.md`
**Reads only:** `web/src/api/fake/`, `web/src/api/contract/`

Two new contract files, one script with its test, one generated file, and one new step in the gate. No screen, no store and no stand-in rule changes; `web/src/api/types.ts` only gains exports.
close_reason: Every method of FinwiseApi is classified under a mapped type (removing or inventing an entry fails typecheck with TS2741 / TS2353). internal/contract/contract.json lists 82 methods (3 session, 23 read, 1 evaluate, 55 write) with route, class, argument and result schemas and the error envelope; contract:check exits 1 on a stale file and bin/ci names the manifest. Every read answer of the stand-in validates with ajv and the three mutations are rejected. bin/ci: CI green. Parity: 174 checked, 0 over 0.05%.

title: Work out the card's bills and each pot's balance and yield
description:
## What changes for the user
The card page has to answer three questions: when does the bill close, which bill is this purchase on, and how much of what was already spent this month will only be charged next month and has to be set aside. The pots page has to say how much each pot holds and how much it yielded this month. Today those answers come from invented constants. After this lands they can be worked out from the bank's own records, and where the records cannot support an answer the app says it does not know instead of showing a zero.

## Outcome
Two Go packages of pure functions: `internal/cardrules` (the closing date, the bill a purchase falls on, the amount that falls on the next bill) and `internal/potrules` (a pot's identity over time, its latest balance, its yield for a month with the daily rows behind it), plus the ledger query for a pot's yield.

## Context
finwise is a personal finance app over a SQLite ledger collected from the person's banks. `internal/ledger` already reads that ledger read-only and returns typed rows with amounts in integer cents; `internal/brday` gives a day and a month in Brazil time. This bead adds interpretation for the card and for savings pots. Apart from the one query it adds to the reader, it does no SQL and no I/O.

**The closing date is predicted from a table, never read from a forecast.** The provider's `creditCardMetadata.billForecastDate` carries only a month on the card in use and must not be read. For that card (C6) the closing date depends only on the weekday of the nominal due date, with no exception across the bills examined:

| the due date falls on | days from closing to due |
| --- | --- |
| Monday to Thursday | 6 |
| Friday | 7 |
| Saturday | 7 |
| Sunday | 8 |

Which table applies to a card is the caller's choice: the rules take the table as a parameter and export the one above; this package does not work out which bank an account belongs to. The ledger keeps the nominal due date. The bank moves a due date on a non-business day to the next business day for payment, and that does not change the closing date. The due day itself is read from the ledger, never written in code. A card of a bank with no such table (the Itaú cards show no single offset per weekday) has an unknown closing date: return unknown, do not guess.

**`bills.closing_date` is the first day of the next cycle.** A purchase dated, in Brazil time, on or after a bill's `closing_date` belongs to the next bill; the day before belongs to that bill.

**The bill of a purchase.** `creditCardMetadata.billId`, when present, joins `bills.id` and is the answer. When absent, the purchase belongs to the first bill whose closing date is after the purchase day; with no such bill yet, to the predicted next one.

**The amount that falls on the next bill.** The purchases of the month dated on or after the predicted closing date, plus those of the two days before it that have not received the closed bill's `billId` (a purchase made right before closing sometimes slips to the following bill).

**A manual closing day** is a setting the person can choose later; the rules take it as an optional parameter, and it moves the closing date while the due date stays fixed.

**Pots.** `reserved_balance_history` has one row per reserve entry of an account's latest sighting of a day. A pot is identified by `reserve_id`, valid only when `stable_identity = 1`; names repeat, so two pots with one name are two pots. A pot whose identity is not stable cannot be followed across days and is reported for its latest day only. The latest balance comes from the reader's existing query. A pot absent from the latest sighting of its account is closed.

**Yield is not the change in balance.** A deposit raises the balance and yields nothing. The collector's README has a query for it, `caixinha_yield` (near lines 339-555 at the time of writing): copy it into the reader with a citation and honour its `reason` column, which says when the yield of a day cannot be computed. When it cannot, the yield is unknown, not zero. Decided with the user: yield is shown per month and opens to its daily rows.

**Two bases.** Nubank reports yield net of tax and Mercado Pago gross. Whether to convert to one base is open; until then every yield figure carries its base, and two bases are never added together.

**Attributing a movement to a pot.** A deposit or withdrawal row sits on the account and does not name the pot. This package receives such movements as plain values (account, day, amount) and attributes one to a pot when the account has exactly one pot, or when exactly one pot's balance changed by that amount on that day; otherwise the movement stays on the account as unattributed and is counted.

**What the sources leave open.** For each, write the smallest safe rule, state it in a comment, and report how many rows it matched on a real ledger, as a count only: the bill of a purchase with no `billId`; movement attribution; one base for yield.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] For a due date of 2026-01-12 (Monday) the closing date is 2026-01-06; 2026-03-12 (Thursday) gives 2026-03-06; 2026-06-12 (Friday) gives 2026-06-05; 2026-09-12 (Saturday) gives 2026-09-05; 2026-04-12 (Sunday) gives 2026-04-04.
- [ ] A card of a bank with no table returns an unknown closing date.
- [ ] A purchase on a bill's `closing_date` belongs to the next bill, and one the day before belongs to that bill.
- [ ] A purchase with a `billId` belongs to that bill even when its date says otherwise.
- [ ] A fixture carrying a `billForecastDate` that contradicts the table changes no result.
- [ ] The amount for the next bill includes a purchase on the predicted closing date, includes one made the day before without the closed bill's `billId`, and excludes one made the day before that carries it.
- [ ] A manual closing day moves the closing date and leaves the due date unchanged.
- [ ] Two pots with the same name on one account are two pots with separate balances.
- [ ] A pot with `stable_identity = 0` is reported for its latest day and has no history.
- [ ] A day with a deposit and no yield reports a yield of zero for that day, not the deposit.
- [ ] A day the query marks as not computable makes the month's yield unknown.
- [ ] Yields of a net pot and a gross pot are never summed into one figure: the function that totals yields returns one total per base.
- [ ] A movement on an account with one pot is attributed to it; on an account with two pots it is attributed only when exactly one pot's balance changed by that amount that day; otherwise it is returned as unattributed.
- [ ] The yield query is prepared against the collector's real schema by the existing schema test.
- [ ] A test skipped unless `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set runs the rules over a real snapshot and logs only counts: bills, purchases per bill source (`billId` or date), pots, months with known and unknown yield, movements attributed and unattributed.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and the opt-in run completes with counts and no error.

## Tests
- Unit: the closing table for each weekday and for year and month ends; bill assignment on both sides of a closing date; the next-bill amount.
- Unit: pot identity, closed pots, yield against deposits, unknown yield, the two bases, movement attribution.
- Golden: the yield query against the real schema file.
- Integration, opt-in: a real snapshot, counts only.
- Each rule is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/cardrules/`, `internal/potrules/`, `internal/ledger/pot_yield.go`, `internal/ledger/pot_yield_test.go`, `internal/ledger/queries.go`
**Reads only:** `internal/ledger/`, `internal/money/`, `internal/brday/`, `web/src/api/contract/card.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/savings-pots.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/card-rules.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/savings-rules.ts`, `bin/ci`

Two new packages of pure functions with their tests, and one new query in the reader: its statement joins the registry in `queries.go`, where a test requires every statement of the reader to live, and its code is a new file. No other reader file changes.
close_reason: internal/cardrules predicts a card's closing date from a weekday table passed in by the caller, places a purchase on its bill (the bill id wins; otherwise the first bill closing after the purchase day; unknown beyond the window or without a table), and sums what the month's spending puts on the next bill. internal/potrules follows a pot by its stable reserve id, reports a pot without one for its latest day only, gives a month's yield with its daily rows and its base, never adds two bases, and attributes a movement only when exactly one pot can claim it. The reader gains the collector's yield query, run as three statements over the same CTEs because the single statement does not prepare in this module's SQLite. bin/ci: CI green; the opt-in runs over a real snapshot completed with counts only. Review added a test for the closing day itself. Left for the reads: the yield query is slow when called once per pair of sightings, and a sighting with no pot returns no row.

title: Dispatch writes through the recorder with their arguments checked against the manifest, answer refusals with a reason, and serve undo
description:
## What changes for the user
Today every button that changes something answers "Somente leitura por enquanto. Nada foi alterado." No
button starts working with this piece alone: it is the machinery every one of them will run on, and the
actions themselves (the budget, the categories, the tags, the settings) arrive one group at a time after
it. What it settles is how a change behaves once it exists. A change is saved whole or not at all. A
change can be taken back, and when it can no longer be taken back because something was edited after it,
the app says so instead of quietly overwriting the newer edit. When the app has to say no (the month is
closed, the item no longer exists) the server gives the reason instead of a generic failure. A person
who starts the app without telling it where to keep their entries sees exactly what they see today. If
this piece were wrong the person would find a change half saved, a request the app should have turned
away accepted, or an undo that destroyed something they did later.

## Outcome
The router runs a handler for a write or an evaluation when the server has its own database and the
method has a handler, and refuses with `read_only` otherwise, still before the body is read. A write's
arguments are checked against the method's schema from the manifest before its handler runs; the handler
works inside one transaction through a recorder that the router commits, and any failure keeps nothing.
A handler's refusal is answered as `{"error":{"kind":"refused","reason":"..."}}` with status 409.
`changes.undo` is the first write with a handler. A walk over the manifest replaces the test that
expected all 56 writes and evaluations to be refused.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is the SQLite snapshot a
separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app only reads it. *The app's database* is
`finwise.db`, owned by the package `internal/authored`; the server has one only when started with `--db`
/ `FINWISE_DB`, and without it runs as today's read-only server. *The contract* is the TypeScript
interface `FinwiseApi` under `web/src/api/contract/`; *the manifest* is `internal/contract/contract.json`,
generated from it and never edited by hand, which lists 82 methods: 3 of class `session`, 23 `read`, 1
`evaluate` (`budget.evaluateScenario`) and 55 `write`. *The stand-in* is the in-memory fake backend under
`web/src/api/fake/` that the design prototype runs on; it is the only existing statement of how writes
behave.

Four pieces this slice stands on, each described in plain words because it is another slice's:

- *The recorder and the undo engine* ({{F2}}): the layer of `internal/authored` through which every
  change to the app's database is written and journaled, and the engine that reverses a recorded change.
  *The journal* is the pair of tables `changes(id, at, day, author, method, extended, undone_at)` and
  `change_effects(change_id, seq, tbl, key, col, before, after)`. The recorder works from a closed
  registry of journaled tables of two shapes: an *attribute table* holds one row of independent facts
  per key, and an effect on it is one column changing; a *set table* holds rows that are facts by
  existing, and an effect on it is one row appearing or disappearing.
- *The per-request views* ({{F3b}}): a handler's third parameter is one value carrying a view of each
  store, opened for the request: the ledger's (one handle, one read-only transaction on the snapshot)
  and the app's database's (one read-only transaction, or an empty view when there is no database). The
  same slice made the clock a required part of the API's configuration.
- *The contract's side of refusals and the schemas* ({{F4a}}): the kind `refused` and a closed list of
  nine reasons in the TypeScript contract and in the manifest, and `internal/contract` handing out each
  method's argument schema with its definitions and the list of reasons.
- *The parsers* ({{F4b}}): `ParseReais` and `Reais.UnmarshalJSON`, which read an amount from its decimal
  text into integer cents and refuse anything beyond one billion reais, and `ParseWholeNumber`.

**What the code is today in the files this slice changes (each point checked in the file named, as it
is before those four pieces land).**

- `internal/api/router.go`: `serve` checks, in order, the verb, the session, the method's class, the
  content type and the body. A `write` or `evaluate` method is answered `read_only` after the session
  check and before `readArguments`, so its body is never read. `readArguments` requires
  `application/json`, at most 1 MiB, a JSON array, and a length between the method's `MinArguments` and
  `MaxArguments`; nothing else about the arguments is checked. `checkRegistered` refuses a handler for
  any name that is not a `read` method.
- `internal/api/reads.go`: one `Registry`; `Register` panics on a second handler for a method;
  `NewReadRegistry` runs the twelve functions of `domainRegistrations`.
- `internal/api/errors.go`: six kinds with their statuses (`locked` 401, `read_only` 403,
  `ledger_unavailable` 503, `bad_request` 400, `unknown_method` 404, `internal` 500); `errorEnvelope`
  holds only a kind; `kindOfReadError` maps a handler's error by its class (`badArgumentsError`,
  `readOnlyError`, the ledger's errors, anything else `internal`) and never looks at its text.
- `internal/api/conformance_test.go` compiles every method's result schema with
  `github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6` (a direct requirement in `go.mod`), draft 7, and validates
  an answer decoded by the library's own `UnmarshalJSON`. No non-test file imports that library today.
- `internal/api/router_test.go`: `TestEveryWriteAndEvaluationIsRefusedWithASession` requires exactly 56
  write and evaluate methods and `read_only` for each over four bodies (`[]`, `not json`, empty,
  `{"a":1}`); `TestAWriteIsRefusedBeforeItsBodyIsRead` proves with a counting body, for
  `transactions.setLine` only, that the body is read zero times;
  `TestAHandlerCannotBeRegisteredForAWrite` expects `NewHandler` to refuse a handler for
  `transactions.setLine`, `budget.evaluateScenario`, `session.unlock` and `no.such`.
- `internal/api/budget.go`: `readBudgetView` answers `read_only` whenever it is given a draft, even a
  malformed one, and `TestTheBudgetViewRefusesAnyDraftAsAWriteIsRefused` (`budget_test.go`) pins that
  for the drafts `[]`, a one-group document, `0` and `"x"`.
- `internal/api/session_routes.go`: `sessionService.dispatch` knows `status`, `unlock` and `lock`.
  `session.changePin` is of class `write` in the manifest, and a test in `session_routes_test.go` expects
  it to answer `read_only` without the PIN comparison running.
- `web/src/api/fake/changes.ts`: the stand-in's `undo` restores a whole-state snapshot and throws a plain
  error for a change it does not know or has already undone (`writes.test.ts`, "refuses a change it does
  not know, or one already undone", which calls `undo('nope')`).

**1. The registry.** It takes handlers of every class except `session`. `checkRegistered` becomes: a
registered name must exist in the manifest and must not be of class `session`. `Registry.Register` and
`domainRegistrations` keep their names (the repository's `AGENTS.md` documents them); `changes.undo` is
registered by a new `registerChanges`, in a file of its own, listed there.

**2. The argument schemas, compiled and applied.** At start the router compiles each method's argument
schema, as `internal/contract` hands it out, so a manifest whose schema does not compile stops the
program at start instead of being half-honoured. The compiled schema is applied to the arguments of
every write and evaluation that has a handler, before the handler runs; a mismatch is `bad_request`.
The arguments are validated from the bytes that arrived, with the schema library's own decoder, so no
number passes through a float on the way. Reads are not validated this way: they keep their own strict
decoding (`decodeArgument` in `arguments.go`). `budget.view`'s draft is validated only from the slice
that makes it real, the budget's arithmetic on the server ({{B3}}); until then it keeps refusing any
draft with `read_only`, as its test says, including drafts that are not a document at all. Handlers
still parse what a schema cannot say: months and days (`YYYY-MM` and `YYYY-MM-DD` in Brazil time,
through `internal/brday`, `bad_request` for `2026-13`, as `monthArgument` in `fresh_install.go` does for
reads), money, whole numbers, and whether the thing named exists.

**3. The `write`/`evaluate` branch of `serve`.** The order of checks stays verb, session, class,
arguments. In the class branch: no authored store, or no handler for the method, answers `read_only`,
still before the body is read. Otherwise the router reads the arguments, validates them against the
method's schema, runs the handler, commits and answers.

- *A write* receives a recorder that already holds one immediate transaction and the facts of a change:
  its author, the method, the instant and the Brazil day. The author of a change made over HTTP is
  `person`; the other two authors of the journal are `rule` (the rules that classify new transactions
  when a new snapshot is brought in) and `model` (reserved for a later nightly call), and neither is
  written here. The method is the qualified name (`transactions.setLine`); the instant is the request's
  clock and the day is `brday.DayOf` of it. The journal is never trimmed.
- *The change's row is written lazily.* It is written with the change's first effect, or when the
  handler asks for the id because it must answer one; a handler that does neither leaves no trace in
  the journal. The handler performs its recorded writes and returns; the router commits. The change id
  is the handle the contract returns (`ChangeResult.changeId`, a decimal string). What a write handler
  reads of the app's database it reads inside that same transaction. It also receives the request's
  ledger view.
- *An evaluation* (`budget.evaluateScenario`, whose handler arrives with the budget's arithmetic on the
  server, {{B3}}) receives the same read-only views as a read and stores nothing.
- *Null and empty changes.* Where the contract's result type allows null (16 of the writes do), "nothing
  to do" and "no such target" both answer null and record nothing: the handler records no effect and
  asks for no id, so no row is added to `changes` or `change_effects`. Where it does not, a write that
  changes nothing records an empty change (it asks for the id it must answer) and answers that id, whose
  undo is a no-op.
- *Extending a change.* One later write extends an existing change instead of opening its own ("all
  purchases here", `transactions.applyLineToEstablishment`): it appends its effects to the change that
  set the line, marks it extended and answers the same id, so one undo takes back both. With the row
  written lazily nothing here stands in its way: such a handler never asks for a new id. It is not
  built here.
- *Failure.* Any failure rolls the whole thing back: a handler's error, a panic (which `logging.go`
  already answers as `internal`), a refusal, a result that cannot be encoded, a commit that fails. A
  write that fails at run time answers `internal`, including when the five-second wait for the write
  lock (`busy_timeout(5000)`, set by the database's connection settings) runs out. A failed write never
  leaves the write lock held. The answer is written only after the commit.
- *The ledger.* `ledger_unavailable` is answered by a write exactly as by a read, through the same
  classifier, when the snapshot it needs is missing; nothing is recorded. A write that needs no snapshot
  (`changes.undo`) works while the snapshot is missing.
- Handlers stay plain functions of the context, the raw arguments and the request's stores, with no
  `net/http` type in their signature: a later command-line client is expected to call them outside HTTP.

**4. The `refused` answer in Go.** The envelope is a closed union: every kind but `refused` has no other
field; `refused` always carries one reason of a closed list.

```
{"error": {"kind": "refused", "reason": "<one of the list>"}}      HTTP 409
```

| reason | when | what the person reads (the interface's text; the server sends none) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `month_closed` | saving or applying a budget for a closed month; closing a month already closed | "Esse mês já está fechado." |
| `future_month` | closing a month after the current one | "Esse mês ainda não chegou." |
| `pending_reviews` | closing a month while a transaction of that month or an earlier one waits for review | "Resolva as pendências do mês antes de fechar." |
| `stale_change` | undoing or extending a change that is unknown, already undone, already extended, or overwritten since | "Isso já foi alterado depois e não pode mais ser desfeito." |
| `not_found` | a write whose result cannot be null names a transaction, pot, subscription or establishment that the ledger does not list or `finwise.db` does not have | "Esse item não existe mais." |
| `unknown_line` | a write names a budget line that the budget of the month it is resolved in does not have | "Essa linha não existe no budget desse mês." |
| `invalid_budget` | saving a budget with a duplicate or empty line name, an unknown or repeated line id, an unknown group | "O budget tem linha sem nome ou repetida." |
| `unstable_pot` | a write to a pot whose identity the bank does not keep stable | "O banco não identifica esse cofrinho de forma estável." |
| `split_with_reimbursement` | splitting a purchase that has a linked reimbursement, or linking one to a split purchase | "Uma compra dividida não pode ter reembolso ligado." |

In `errors.go`: the kind with status 409; the nine reasons as constants, held equal by a test to the
list `internal/contract` hands out from the manifest; an error a handler returns that carries only a
reason (no text: an argument may be a row id, as `badArgumentsError` already says of itself); and the
one classifier, which reads and writes share, answering it. The envelope of every other kind is byte for
byte what it is today. Only `stale_change` has a producer when this lands; each other reason is first
produced by the slice that owns its rule. The sentences are the interface's and the server sends none.

The other kinds keep their meaning. `bad_request`: the arguments do not match the method's schema or
cannot be parsed (a month, a day, an amount), which is a bug in a client. `read_only`: a server without
`--db`, and a write method that has no handler yet. The request log is unchanged (verb, route, status,
duration, error kind): the reason is not added to it, and no argument, body or key ever is. New files in
`internal/api` log nothing; `handler_silence_test.go` allows only `logging.go` and `router.go` to name a
logging package.

**5. `changes.undo(changeId)`.** The engine is the recorder's ({{F2}}); this slice is the method. Its
contract: in one immediate transaction with foreign keys deferred to the commit,

1. collapse the change's effects per unit (a table, a key and, for an attribute table, a column): the
   first `before`, the last `after`;
2. if the change is unknown or already undone, or a later change that is still in force has an effect
   on any of those units, refuse with `refused` / `stale_change` and change nothing. The journal's order
   decides, not the value: a unit set from A to B, then to C, then back to B by later changes is not the
   first change's to take back. As a guard against a write that escaped the journal, a unit whose
   current content differs from that `after` is refused the same way;
3. otherwise restore every `before`, in reverse order of `seq`, and mark the change undone.

Two rules of the attribute shape belong to the engine and show through the method: creating a row is
itself a unit, so a later change to any column of that row makes the change that created it stale; and
a restore is computed for the whole row and written once, never column by column. Undo returns nothing
(the method answers `null`) and is not itself undoable: it is not a recorded change. It is an ordinary
write handler all the same: it records no effect of its own and asks for no id, so it adds no row to
`changes`. A string that is not the id of a change the journal holds, whatever it looks like (`"999"`,
`"nope"`, `""`), is an unknown change and is `stale_change`; `bad_request` is only for an argument that
is not a string. Undoing a change that was extended takes back both, as the contract's own comment on
`undo` says.

**6. The manifest walk.** It replaces the "all 56 are refused" test. Every write or evaluation of the
manifest has exactly one implementation, a registered handler or, for `session.changePin` alone, the
session service; or it is in an explicit `writesWithoutHandler` list in a test file. Never two of the
three, never none. `session.changePin` is of class `write` and so passes `checkRegistered`, but it is
not a generic write handler: it needs what only the session service has (the caller's token, the
lockout, the session store), so the router will hand it to `sessionService` together with the authored
store in the slice that changes the PIN ({{P1}}). Until that slice it stays in `writesWithoutHandler`
and answers `read_only` like any write without a handler, with no PIN compared; the walk fails if the
registry ever holds a handler for it. The list only shrinks: each slice that implements a method removes
its name, and it is empty when every write of the contract is implemented. When this lands the only
implementation is the handler of `changes.undo`, and the list holds the other 55 names,
`budget.evaluateScenario` and `session.changePin` among them. With no authored store, every one of the
56 is refused before its body is read; with one, a listed method still is. The count stays pinned at 56.

**No table of the real schema is journaled when this lands.** The first journaled tables arrive with the
budget's own tables, its lines, versions and scenarios ({{B2}}), so the proofs of this slice run
handlers registered only in tests, on scratch tables, as the recorder's own property test does. Find how
that test gives a database a scratch journaled table; if that is not reachable from the tests of
`internal/api`, exposing it for tests is part of this slice, in a new file under `internal/authored`.

**Tests this slice must adapt because the registry now holds a write.**
`TestEveryRegisteredReadHasAConformanceCase` (`conformance_test.go`) and `TestEveryReadMethodHasAHandler`
(`reads_coverage_test.go`) walk every registered name and would report `changes.undo` as a read with no
case, or as a handler that is not a read. Both must look at read methods only.
`TestAHandlerCannotBeRegisteredForAWrite` is rewritten for the new rule.

**Decisions, with what lost.**

- The server runs read-only when no `--db` is given, and a write method without a handler answers
  `read_only`: slices land one domain at a time and the app is never half-broken, and the interface
  already handles `read_only`. Lost: a switch that flips all 56 methods at once.
- Where a result type allows null, an unknown target answers null, as the contract's comments say;
  `not_found` is for results that cannot be null: the screens already treat null as "nothing happened".
  Lost: refusing every unknown id.
- Undo is the inverse of recorded effects, refused when what it would overwrite has changed since: the
  stand-in's snapshot restore silently destroys later changes, and with money, refusing is the safe
  failure. Lost: snapshot restore; last writer wins.

**Where the server departs from the stand-in on purpose.** Typed refusals instead of thrown errors; the
envelope carries a reason; unknown targets of non-null results are refused. The stand-in throws a plain
error for an unknown or already undone change; the server answers `refused` / `stale_change`. Each
departure is pinned by a test, and the final report names it.

**Failure paths this slice owns.**

| what goes wrong | what happens |
| --- | --- |
| the snapshot is missing while writing | the write answers `ledger_unavailable`; nothing is recorded |
| a write fails halfway, or waits out the lock | one transaction: nothing of it is kept; `internal` |
| an undo meets a later change | `stale_change`; nothing is restored |
| the process stops between a write's commit and its answer | the change is stored; that the interface then says the result could not be confirmed and refetches is the interface's part ({{F6}}: what a failed write shows on screen) |
| two tabs, or a tab and the job that brings a new snapshot into the app's database, write at once | writes queue; each is its own change; an undo that lost the race is refused |

**Privacy.** The repository is public and a real ledger is a person's whole financial history. Nothing
in this slice needs a real ledger: every fixture is invented, no `.db` file is opened by hand, and no
value from a real snapshot (amount, description, name, document, id) is ever printed, logged, copied
into a file, a commit, a bead or a pull request. An argument of a write can be a row id or a document
number, which is why a refusal and a bad argument carry no text.

**Conventions.** Work happens in a git worktree of its own and ends at local commits: atomic,
Conventional Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a plan in a commit
message. Money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path. Every SQL statement over the
app's database is a registered constant, so this slice executes none of its own outside
`internal/authored`. Interface text is Brazilian Portuguese and everything else is English; a design
value in a component comes from a token (this slice touches no component).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `NewHandler` compiles the argument schema of each of the 82 methods and returns an error when one
of them does not compile (a test feeds it one).
- [ ] With no authored store, each of the 56 write and evaluate methods answers 403 `read_only` for the
bodies `[]`, `not json`, empty and `{"a":1}`, and for each of the 56 a counting body is read 0 times.
- [ ] With an authored store, a write with no handler answers 403 `read_only` with its body read 0
times, and `session.changePin` still answers `read_only` with the PIN comparison called 0 times.
- [ ] The manifest walk fails when a write or evaluation is neither implemented nor in
`writesWithoutHandler`, when it is both, and when the registry holds a handler for `session.changePin`;
the list holds 55 names, `session.changePin` among them, and the registry one, `changes.undo`; the test
still requires 56 in all.
- [ ] `NewHandler` refuses a handler registered for a name the manifest does not have and for
`session.status`, `session.unlock` and `session.lock`, and accepts one for `transactions.setLine` and
for `budget.evaluateScenario`.
- [ ] For a test handler registered on `budget.save` that decodes the document's amounts as `Reais`: an
amount sent as a string, `lines` sent as an object, a group key outside the editable five, a line
without `amount`, a line with an extra field, and an argument array of the wrong length each answer 400
`bad_request` with the handler called 0 times and no row added to `changes`; `"amount":1e400` and
`"amount":1000000000.01` answer 400 `bad_request` with no row added; and the well-formed document
`["2026-03",[{"key":"rec","name":"Receita","lines":[{"name":"Salário","amount":8000}]}]]` reaches the
handler, which reads 800000 cents.
- [ ] `budget.view` answers `read_only` for the four drafts of
`TestTheBudgetViewRefusesAnyDraftAsAWriteIsRefused`, which passes unchanged.
- [ ] A test write handler that records one effect on a scratch table answers 200 with a change id, and
`changes` has one new row whose author is `person`, whose method is the qualified name, whose instant is
the test clock's and whose day is that instant's Brazil day.
- [ ] A test write handler that records nothing, asks for no id and answers null adds 0 rows to
`changes` and to `change_effects`; one that records nothing and answers the change id adds 1 row to
`changes` and 0 to `change_effects`, and undoing that id answers 200 `null`.
- [ ] A test write handler that returns an error, one that panics, one that returns a refusal and one
whose result cannot be encoded, each after recording an effect, leave `changes`, `change_effects` and
the scratch table as they were, and a write made right after does not wait for a lock.
- [ ] A write that cannot take the write lock because another connection holds it answers 500 `internal`
and records nothing; how the test avoids waiting five seconds is the implementer's.
- [ ] A test write handler that asks the ledger something while the snapshot file is missing answers 503
`ledger_unavailable` and records nothing; `changes.undo` succeeds while the snapshot file is missing.
- [ ] Two writes sent at the same time both answer 200 with two different change ids.
- [ ] A test evaluation handler runs with its arguments validated and leaves every table as it was.
- [ ] A refusal answers 409 with the body exactly `{"error":{"kind":"refused","reason":"stale_change"}}`;
every other kind's body has no `reason`; Go's reasons are the nine of the table above and a test holds
them equal to the list `internal/contract` hands out.
- [ ] `changes.undo` of a recorded change puts the scratch table back and answers 200 `null`, adding no
row to `changes`; a second undo of the same id answers `stale_change`; `"999"`, `"nope"` and `""` answer
`stale_change`; `[7]` answers `bad_request`.
- [ ] After a later change to the same unit, undo of the first answers `stale_change` and the table
keeps the later content; the same when later changes took the unit from B to C and back to B, although
the value now equals what the first change left; once the later change is itself undone, the first can
be undone.
- [ ] After a write to the scratch table that went around the recorder, undo of the change that last set
that unit answers `stale_change` and restores nothing.
- [ ] The request log of a refused write holds the kind `refused` and no reason, argument or id;
`TestOnlyTheRequestLogWritesAnything` and `TestNoSourceFileOfTheHTTPLayerTouchesAFloat` pass unchanged.
- [ ] No file under `web/` and no file of `internal/contract` is changed.
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, each against its own deliberate break, named in the final
report: the walk against a name removed from the list; validation against a router that skips it; each
rollback case against a router that commits before checking the handler's error; the null case against
a router that asks the recorder for the change's id before the handler runs; the journal-order case
against a call of the engine made to compare values only; the envelope test against a `reason` written
for every kind.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, the manifest walk passes with `changes.undo` as the only
implementation and 55 names listed, and every row of the failure-path table above has a test that
produces it, except the process stopping between commit and answer, which is argued from the order of
commit and answer in the code.

## Tests
- Integration with `httptest`, no authored store: the 56 refusals over four bodies, and the counting
  body for each of the 56.
- Integration with `httptest`, over a scratch `finwise.db` in the test's temporary directory and
  handlers registered only in the test: argument validation (nested, extra field, missing field, length,
  huge number); a recorded write and its `changes` row; null and empty changes; error, panic, refusal and
  unencodable result; the lock that is not released in time; a missing snapshot; two writes at once; an
  evaluation.
- Integration with `httptest`: `changes.undo`, its success and each `stale_change` case (unknown, undone
  twice, a later change in force, a value put back by later changes, a later change itself undone, a
  write around the recorder), over scratch tables of both shapes.
- Unit: Go's reasons equal the list `internal/contract` hands out; the envelope's JSON for `refused` and
  for each other kind.
- Unit: the manifest walk, with a test of the walk (a name in no place, a name in two, a handler on
  `session.changePin`).
- Unit: `NewHandler` on a schema that does not compile, and on the registrations it must refuse.
- Unit: the request log of a refused write.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/api/router.go`, `internal/api/reads.go`, `internal/api/errors.go`,
`internal/api/changes.go`, `internal/api/router_test.go`, `internal/api/reads_coverage_test.go`,
`internal/api/conformance_test.go`, `internal/api/helpers_test.go`
**Reads only:** `internal/authored/`, `internal/contract/`, `internal/api/reais.go`,
`internal/api/budget.go`, `internal/api/budget_test.go`, `internal/api/session_routes.go`,
`internal/api/session_routes_test.go`, `internal/api/logging.go`, `internal/api/handler_silence_test.go`,
`internal/api/arguments.go`, `web/src/api/contract/classification.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/changes.ts`,
`go.mod`, `AGENTS.md`, `bin/ci`

One package. Three existing source files change (the router's class branch and its start, the registry's
check, the error kinds), one is new (`changes.go`, with `registerChanges` and the handler of undo), and
the tests follow: four existing test files and new ones for the dispatch, for undo and for the manifest
walk with its list. No read handler is touched, `budget.go` keeps refusing drafts, the session service is
not changed, and nothing under `web/` or `internal/contract` is edited. `internal/authored` is used as
delivered and no file it already has is edited; if no scratch journaled table is reachable from the
tests of `internal/api`, the one addition is a new test-support file there. `conformance_test.go` and
`reads_coverage_test.go` change only to look at read methods. `go.mod` gains no requirement: the schema
library is already there, now imported by production code too. `AGENTS.md` is not edited here.

title: Save a transaction's tags and note and an establishment's nickname, default line and fixed tags, and show the nickname wherever a name is shown
description:
## What changes for the user
Today the transaction panel offers a field for tags, a note, a nickname for the establishment or the
person, a default budget line and fixed tags for the establishment, and the list offers "add a tag" for a
selection; every one of them answers that the app is read-only. The person cannot call an establishment
by a name they recognise instead of the bank's wording, cannot mark the purchases of a trip to find them
later, and cannot leave themselves a reminder on a purchase. After this lands each of those is kept and
is still there after a restart: a tag typed in the panel shows on the row and in the tag filter, a tag
added to a selection can be taken back from its toast, the note stays where it was written, a nickname
given once renames every purchase at that establishment (or every PIX with that person) in the lists, in
the panel and on the card's page, and the default line and the fixed tags chosen for an establishment are
remembered.

## Outcome
Eight methods of the API stop answering `read_only` when the server runs with its own database and are
answered by handlers: `transactions.addTag`, `removeTag`, `addTagToMany`, `setNote`, `setNickname`,
`setDefaultLine`, `addFixedTag` and `removeFixedTag`. Each is one recorded change that `changes.undo`
takes back exactly. Tags enter through one normalisation whichever method brings them. A nickname is
shown wherever the name of a transaction or of an establishment is shown today (the transaction list,
the panel, the card's purchases and bill items), through one function that later screens call too. The
nickname and the default line are stored by establishment key through store functions that take a key,
so the settings screen's two writes can share them. For each of the five fields (own tags, note,
nickname, default line, fixed tags) there is a golden file of the write's effects, a read that shows the
value, and an undo that restores the state before.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is a SQLite snapshot that a
separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app only reads it, and the file may be swapped
under it at any time. *The app's database* is `finwise.db`, owned by the Go package `internal/authored`,
where everything the person authors is kept; the server has one only when started with `--db`, and
without it every write answers `read_only`, as today. *The stand-in* is the in-memory fake backend under
`web/src/api/fake/` that the design prototype runs on; it is the only existing statement of how writes
behave, and its behaviour is the rule here except where this text says the server departs from it. *The
manifest* is `internal/contract/contract.json`, the generated description of every API method (route,
class, argument and result schemas, error envelope). *The recorder* is the layer of `internal/authored`
through which every change to the app's database is written, and *the journal* is what it writes: one
*change* per write (author, method, instant, Brazil day) and its *effects*; `changes.undo(changeId)`
applies the inverse of a change's effects and is refused with `refused` / `stale_change` when something
it would overwrite was changed since. *The index* is the pair of tables `tx_index` and `tx_ids` in which
the app's database remembers the transactions it has seen: the bank's id of a transaction can change (a
pending row is replaced by a posted one), so the database mints a key of its own, `tx_key`, and maps
every provider id seen to it; everything authored about a transaction hangs on `tx_key`, never on the
provider's id. An *establishment key* is the identity of an establishment or a person, a text with the
prefix `doc:`, `name:` or `text:` computed by `internal/txrules/counterpart.go` (`counterpartOf`); under
`doc:` it is a document number, and a document of eleven digits marks a person. A *budget line* has an
integer id minted by the app's database and a name that belongs to a budget version; the budget *in
force for a month* is the latest version starting at or before that month. The built-in *fees line* is
in no group, has a fixed id and the fixed name `Tarifas e juros`, and can be named in a write in any
month whose budget has at least one line. A *golden file* is the exact, committed answer of one call
over an invented fixture.

**What this builds on, delivered by earlier work.**

- The recorder, the journal and the undo engine ({{F2}}). A journaled table has one of two shapes. An
  *attribute table* holds one row of independent facts per key; an effect is one column changing, a row
  whose columns are all at their defaults is the same as no row, and a restore is computed for the whole
  row and written once. A *set table* holds rows that are facts by existing; an effect is one row
  appearing or disappearing. No statement may insert, update or delete in an authored table outside the
  recorder; a test fails if one does.
- A handler receives one value carrying a view of each store for the request ({{F3b}}): the ledger view
  is one handle and one read-only transaction, so every ledger query of a request sees the same
  snapshot; the clock comes from the request's context and is never the host's.
- Write dispatch ({{F4c}}): the registry takes handlers of class `write`; the router validates the
  arguments against the method's schemas from the manifest before the handler runs (a mismatch is
  `bad_request`), hands the handler a recorder that already holds one immediate transaction and the
  facts of the change (author `person`, the method, the instant, the Brazil day), commits when the
  handler returns, and rolls everything back on any failure. A handler refuses with the kind `refused`
  and one reason of a closed list (HTTP 409); the two this slice uses are `not_found` and
  `unknown_line`. The change's id, a decimal string, is the `changeId` every one of these methods
  answers. A test file keeps an explicit list of the writes that still have no handler,
  `writesWithoutHandler`; a method leaves it when its handler lands.
- The write conformance harness and `internal/authored/authoredtest` ({{F5}}): every write has cases in
  a mode. For a *recorded change* the answer validates against the manifest, the change's effects match
  a golden file under `internal/api/testdata/golden/writes/`, and undoing it returns a canonical dump of
  every journaled table to the dump taken before. A *refusal* case expects 409, its reason, and no table
  changed at all. Reads over the full invented ledger with an invented authored state have their own
  list of cases, `authoredReadCases`, and golden files under `testdata/golden/full-authored/`. The test
  that proves no handler logs what it reads runs every write case. A list names the refusal reasons that
  have no producer yet; the slice that first produces a reason removes it and adds its case.
- The budget's tables and the line menu ({{B2}}): lines with stable ids, budget versions per month, the
  fees line, and the lookup that resolves a line's name in the budget in force for a given month to its
  id, or says the month's budget does not have it.
- The transactions' tables, the index and the merged reads ({{T1}}): the migration `0003_transactions`
  with, among others, `tx_state(tx_key, …, note, …)` (an attribute table, one row per transaction),
  `tx_tags(tx_key, tag, position)`, `establishments(key, nickname, default_line_id)` and
  `establishment_tags(key, tag, position)`; the index; and the reads of the transaction list, the
  transaction detail and the filter options answering from those tables. No migration is added here: if
  a column proves missing, say so in the report instead of adding a migration file.

**What the code is today (each point checked in the file named).**

- `web/src/api/contract/classification.ts` classes the eight methods as `write`;
  `web/src/api/contract/transaction-detail.ts` and `transactions.ts` give their signatures. All eight
  answer `Promise<ChangeResult>`: the result cannot be null.
- `internal/api/router.go` refuses every `write` with `read_only`.
- `internal/api/transactions_wire.go`, `transactionFrom`: `Name` and `OriginalName` are both the
  ledger's name and `Tags` is always `[]`.
- `internal/api/transaction_detail.go`: `detailFrom` answers `OwnTags` and `SuggestedTags` empty and
  `Note` as `""`; `counterpartOf` answers the key with a null nickname, a null default line and no fixed
  tags, and nil when the transaction is a movement (neither the establishment section nor the person
  section applies, by `sectionsOf`).
- `internal/api/transactions.go`, `readTransactionFilterOptions`: `Tags` is always `[]`.
- `internal/api/card.go`: `purchaseWireOf` (the pay-ahead purchases and the purchases that may fall on
  the next bill) and `itemsOf` (the items of a past bill) copy `transaction.Name` from the interpreted
  ledger row. `closingCardBillOf` in `internal/api/review_closing.go` copies its names from the card
  overview's pay-ahead purchases, so it follows `purchaseWireOf` without being edited.
- `internal/api/subscriptions.go` answers `subscriptions.candidates` with an empty list
  (`readNothingListed`) and `internal/api/budget.go` answers `budget.establishments` with `[]`
  (`readBudgetEstablishments`): two places where a name will be shown do not exist yet.
- The interface already sends these writes. In `web/src/components/transaction-panel/`: `TagsSection.vue`
  sends `addTag` with the typed text, trimmed, on Enter (never an empty one) or with a suggestion
  clicked, and `removeTag` with the chip's text; `NoteSection.vue` sends `setNote` with the textarea's
  value as it is; `EstablishmentSection.vue` starts the nickname field from the shown name and sends
  `setNickname` on "Salvar", sends `setDefaultLine` with a name picked from the line menu, sends
  `removeFixedTag` from a chip, and opens a menu titled `Tag fixa para <nome>` of the known tags the
  establishment lacks, each sending `addFixedTag`; `PersonSection.vue` sends `setNickname` with the
  field's value and says `Vale para todo PIX com <nome original>.`. The tags and note sections are shown
  for every transaction, movements included (`TransactionPanel.vue`). After each of these the panel only
  bumps the revision so every screen fetches again (`panelActions.ts`); it shows no toast, so the change
  id is not used there. `web/src/components/transactions/useTransactionActions.ts` sends `addTagToMany`
  for the selection with a tag picked from the known tags, then toasts `Tag <tag> adicionada a <n>
  transações.` with an undo action that calls `changes.undo` with the answered id. No file under `web/`
  changes in this slice.

**The rules common to the eight writes.**

1. *The target.* A write resolves the transaction it names through the same interpreted ledger read the
   API lists transactions with (the one `transactions.detail` uses for its target: `readTransactionDetail`
   in `transaction_detail.go`), in the request's ledger snapshot, so it has the row's current facts: its
   establishment key, whether the other side is a person, whether it is a movement. An id that read does
   not list (an unknown id, a tax row folded into its purchase, a pot movement) is unknown: the write is
   refused with `refused` / `not_found` and nothing is recorded. This is a departure from the stand-in,
   whose `change()` in `transaction-edits.ts` answers a change id for a transaction that does not exist.
   The write then creates or refreshes the transaction's row in the index (`tx_index` and `tx_ids`
   record observations, are not journaled and are not undone). The function that does this resolution
   for a write arrives with the index ({{T1}}); the other groups of transaction writes land in parallel
   with this one and need the same function, so if the tree holds none when this work starts, write it
   once beside the index and use it, never a second copy in a handler file.
2. *One change.* Each call is one change by `person`. A write that leaves everything as it was (a tag
   the transaction already has, a note equal to the stored one, a nickname equal to the stored one)
   records an *empty change*: it answers the change's id, the change has no effect, and its undo is a
   no-op. None of the eight writes a history step (the stand-in records none for them).
3. *The snapshot.* When the ledger snapshot is missing the write answers `ledger_unavailable`, through
   the same classifier a read uses, and nothing is recorded. A write that fails halfway, or waits out
   the database's five-second lock, keeps nothing and answers `internal`.
4. *No month is closed to these.* Closing a month freezes its budget, not its transactions: none of
   these writes is refused because the transaction's month is closed.
5. *Bulk is all or nothing.* `addTagToMany` validates the whole list before changing anything: a
   repeated id counts once, and one unknown id refuses the call (`not_found`) with nothing recorded and
   no table changed. The stand-in instead skips the ids it does not find.

**Tags.** One normalisation for every way a tag enters (`addTag`, `addTagToMany`, `addFixedTag`): trim;
drop the leading `#` characters; trim again; turn each run of white space into one hyphen; put one `#`
in front. A tag that normalises to nothing is ignored (an empty change). The stand-in normalises only in
`addTag` (`normalizeTag` in `transaction-edits.ts`) and without the second trim, so `"# a b"` becomes
`#-a-b` there and `#a-b` here; `addTagToMany` and `addFixedTag` store the text as it arrives there.

- `addTag(id, tag)`: adds the normalised tag to the transaction's own tags unless it is already among
  them. Only the own tags are compared: a tag the establishment has as fixed can also be an own tag.
- `removeTag(id, tag)`: removes that own tag; a tag the transaction does not have is an empty change. A
  removal names a tag as it is stored; whether the argument is normalised before the comparison is the
  implementer's, as long as removing `#trabalho` removes the stored `#trabalho`.
- `addTagToMany(ids, tag)`: for each transaction of the list that lacks the tag among its own, adds it.
  An empty list, or a list where every transaction already has it, is an empty change. Its undo removes
  exactly the rows this call added: a transaction that already had the tag keeps it.
- `addFixedTag(id, tag)` and `removeFixedTag(id, tag)`: the same for the fixed tags of the transaction's
  establishment key (`establishment_tags`); adding one the key already has is an empty change.
- A tag's `position` is the order it was added in and is never renumbered: removing a tag leaves the
  others where they were, and a tag added later goes after every tag the transaction (or the key) has.
  How a position is numbered is the implementer's, under that rule and under this vector: add `#a`,
  `#b`, `#c`, remove `#b`, undo the removal, and the own tags read `#a`, `#b`, `#c` again.

**The note.** `setNote(id, note)` stores the text as sent, without trimming, in `tx_state.note`. An
empty text is the default, so a transaction whose only authored fact was a note that is now empty has no
row left.

**The nickname.** `setNickname(id, nickname)` acts on the establishment key of the transaction: the
nickname is trimmed, and a blank one clears it. It works for an establishment and for a person (one
nickname for every PIX with them). A row of `establishments` whose nickname and default line are both
unset is the same as no row. Vectors from the stand-in's `panel-writes.test.ts`: `"  Pão  "` on one
purchase names every purchase of that key `Pão` and the detail answers `counterparty.nickname: "Pão"`;
`"   "` afterwards brings the ledger's name back and `counterparty.nickname: null`.

**The default line.** `setDefaultLine(id, line)` stores the line for the transaction's establishment
key. Only an establishment has a default line: when the other side is a person, or the transaction is a
movement, the write is refused with `not_found`. A default line belongs to no month, so the name is
resolved in the budget in force for the *current* month (the Brazil month of the request's instant),
not the transaction's own; a name that budget does not have is refused with `unknown_line`. The line is
stored by id. The write is not retroactive: it touches no transaction (the stand-in's vector: after
`setDefaultLine` the detail answers the new `counterparty.defaultLine` and the transaction's own `line`
is unchanged); it acts on transactions that arrive later, through the rules that classify new
transactions, which are later work. A default line is never cleared by a budget save, because a save
for a later month must not touch the current one; it is resolved where it is used, so a read shows it
only while the current month's budget has the line, and answers null otherwise while the stored id
stays.

**What the plan of this work leaves open, and what constrains it** (this is why the bead is `spec:open`).

- *`setNickname`, `addFixedTag` and `removeFixedTag` aimed at a movement.* The refusal for a movement is
  stated for `setDefaultLine` only. The interface never sends the other three for a movement (the detail
  answers no `counterparty`, so neither section is shown), and the stand-in stores them under the
  movement's key. The implementer chooses between refusing with `not_found` and storing as the stand-in
  does; one test pins the choice and the pull request says which.
- *The collation of the known tags.* They are listed "alphabetically" and nothing more is fixed. The
  comparison must be deterministic and pinned by a test that includes an accented tag and an upper-case
  one.
- *File and function names*, and how positions are numbered (above).

**What the reads answer.** The reads of the list, the detail and the filter options are delivered merged
with the authored tables by {{T1}}. The rules for the fields this slice writes are stated here in full
so each can be checked after its write; where one of them is not yet answered from the tables, this
slice completes it.

- `Transaction.name` is the nickname when the establishment key has one, otherwise the ledger's name;
  `originalName` is always the ledger's name, kept so a search still finds it.
- `Transaction.tags` is the transaction's own tags in the order they were added, followed by the fixed
  tags of its establishment key in the order they were added, without repeats. This is what the
  contract's comment says; the stand-in's `allTags` in `rules.ts` lists the fixed ones first, and the
  server departs from it on purpose.
- `TransactionDetail.ownTags` is the own tags alone, in order; `note` is the stored note;
  `counterparty` is `{key, nickname, defaultLine, fixedTags}` with the default line's name as the
  current month's budget names it.
- The *known tags* are every tag in use, on a transaction or fixed on an establishment, alphabetically;
  they are `transactions.filterOptions(month).tags`. `TransactionDetail.suggestedTags` is the known tags
  the transaction lacks among its own. The stand-in answers a seeded list with no rule behind it
  (`state.tags` in `transactions.ts` and `transaction-detail.ts`); on a database where nobody has typed
  a tag the known list is empty, so the selection's tag menu and the fixed-tag menu offer nothing until
  a first tag is typed in a panel. That follows from the rule and is not a defect.
- *A nickname shows wherever the name of a transaction or of an establishment is shown.* One function
  answers the name to show for an establishment key (the nickname, or the name the ledger gives), and
  every read uses it. This slice brings under it the places that show a name today: the list and the
  panel (`transactionFrom`), and the card (`purchaseWireOf` and `itemsOf` in `card.go`, and through
  them the closing view's card bill). The other places the rule names do not exist yet and must call
  the same function when they are built: the subscription candidates ({{SB1}}: subscriptions created by
  hand), the establishments of a budget line ({{B3}}: the budget's view and `budget.establishments`),
  the name in the toast of a line change and in the history text of "all purchases here" ({{T2}}: the
  line writes), the reimbursement's link and candidates ({{T5}}), and the settings overview ({{S3}}).
- Without `--db` the authored view is empty and every one of these reads answers exactly as today.

**The settings screen shares the store.** `settings.setNickname(key, nickname)` and
`settings.setDefaultLine(key, line)` take an establishment key instead of a transaction; their handlers
arrive with the settings overview of establishments and people ({{S3}}) and must share the store
functions of this slice. So the functions that write a nickname and a default line take a key, and the
handlers here only find the key of the transaction they were given.

**Identity and what follows from it.** If the bank later words a row differently, its establishment key
changes: the row is then a new establishment, visibly, and the nickname, default line and fixed tags
stored under the old key stay where they are; nothing authored is deleted or moved. A transaction the
ledger stops listing keeps its tags and its note; nothing is deleted. Grouping keys that differ is
deferred work.

**Privacy.** The repository is public and a real ledger is a person's whole financial history. An
establishment key under `doc:` is a document number: it is never logged, and it appears in a golden file
only because the fixture it comes from is invented. The rule in full: a real snapshot may be opened
read-only; no value from it (amount, description, name, document, id) is ever printed, logged, copied
into a file, a commit, a bead or a pull request; a count may be shown to the person running a test and
goes into no file; a test that touches a real ledger runs only when `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` names a
file. Nothing in this slice needs a real ledger. Every fixture is invented, and `-update` of the golden
files refuses to run while `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set. New files in `internal/api` log nothing;
the no-leak test's list of strings must cover what the new write cases carry (a tag, a note, a nickname,
a line's name, an establishment key).

**Conventions.** Work happens in a git worktree of its own and ends at local commits: atomic,
Conventional Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a plan in a commit
message. Money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path (this slice moves no amount).
Every SQL statement over the app's database is a registered constant, prepared against the migrated
schema by a test. Interface text is Brazilian Portuguese and everything else is English; a design value
in a component comes from a token (this slice touches no component). Register the handlers in a
registration function of this slice's own files, the way write dispatch registers a write handler,
instead of adding lines to `registerTransactions` in `transactions.go`, which the sibling slices landing
in parallel would edit too. Each departure from the stand-in named above (unknown targets refused, bulk
all or nothing, one normalisation, own tags before fixed ones, known tags derived) is pinned by a test,
and the final report names the test beside the departure.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] With `--db`, each of `transactions.addTag`, `removeTag`, `addTagToMany`, `setNote`, `setNickname`,
`setDefaultLine`, `addFixedTag` and `removeFixedTag` answers 200 with `{"changeId": "<decimal id>"}`
that validates against the manifest; none of the eight remains in `writesWithoutHandler`; without `--db`
each still answers `read_only` before its body is read.
- [ ] Each of the eight has a write-conformance case in the recorded-change mode whose effects equal its
golden file under `internal/api/testdata/golden/writes/` and whose undo returns the canonical dump to
the one taken before; together the cases cover the five fields: own tags, note, nickname, default line,
fixed tags.
- [ ] A table test of the normalisation passes these rows through `addTag`, `addTagToMany` and
`addFixedTag` alike: `" viagem de trabalho "` gives `#viagem-de-trabalho`; `"#viagem-de-trabalho"` gives
the same and is stored once; `"#"` and `"   "` store nothing; `"##a"` gives `#a`; `"# a b"` gives
`#a-b`; `"a  b"` gives `#a-b`.
- [ ] After `addTag` of `#a`, `#b`, `#c`, `removeTag` of `#b` and `changes.undo` of that removal,
`transactions.detail` answers `ownTags: ["#a","#b","#c"]`.
- [ ] A transaction with own tags `#b`, `#a` (added in that order) whose establishment has fixed tags
`#a`, `#c` answers `tags: ["#b","#a","#c"]` in the list and in the detail, and `ownTags: ["#b","#a"]`.
- [ ] `transactions.filterOptions` answers the known tags, every tag in use once, in the pinned
alphabetical order; `suggestedTags` of a transaction is that list without its own tags; after
`removeTag` of the last use of a tag it is no longer known.
- [ ] `addTagToMany(["x","y","x"], tag)` adds the tag once to each of the two transactions;
`addTagToMany(["x","no-such-transaction"], tag)` answers 409 `refused` / `not_found` and the canonical
dump and the index are unchanged; after `addTagToMany` over one transaction that had the tag and one
that had not, `changes.undo` leaves the first with the tag and the second without.
- [ ] `setNote` stores `"abastecer na sexta"` and the detail answers it; an empty note afterwards leaves
no row for a transaction with nothing else authored.
- [ ] `setNickname(id, "  Pão  ")` makes `name` read `Pão` for every listed transaction of that
establishment key in `transactions.list` and `transactions.detail`, leaves `originalName` as the
ledger's name, and answers `counterparty.nickname: "Pão"`; `setNickname(id, "   ")` restores the
ledger's name, answers `counterparty.nickname: null` and leaves no row in `establishments` for a key
with nothing else set; the same works for a transaction whose other side is a person.
- [ ] On a ledger built for the test with card purchases on a past bill, in the pay-ahead and in the two
days before a closing, a nickname on their establishment is the `name` in `card.overview`'s
`bills[].items[]`, `payAhead.purchases[]` and `mayFallOnNextBill[]`, and in `review.closing`'s card bill
purchases.
- [ ] `setDefaultLine` stores the line by id; the detail answers `counterparty.defaultLine` with its
name and the transaction's own `line`, `classifiedBy` and `pending` are unchanged; no row of any
transaction is among the change's effects.
- [ ] `setDefaultLine` is refused with `not_found` for a transaction whose other side is a person and
for a movement, and with `unknown_line` for a name the current month's budget lacks, including when the
budget in force for the transaction's own month has that name (two budget versions in the fixture); it
accepts `Tarifas e juros` when the current month's budget has at least one line and refuses it with
`unknown_line` when that budget has none.
- [ ] A default line whose line the current month's budget no longer has is answered as
`counterparty.defaultLine: null` while its row keeps the line id.
- [ ] `addFixedTag` twice with the same tag stores it once, and the tag then shows in `tags` of every
listed transaction of the key and in `counterparty.fixedTags`; `removeFixedTag` takes it off all of
them.
- [ ] Each of the seven methods that take one transaction id answers 409 `refused` / `not_found` for an
unknown id, for a tax row folded into its purchase (`tx-foreign-tax` in the full invented ledger) and
for a pot movement (`tx-pot-transfer`), with no table changed.
- [ ] A write that changes nothing (a tag already there, the same note, the same nickname, a tag that
normalises to nothing, an empty list of ids) answers a change id, adds no row to `change_effects`, and
its `changes.undo` succeeds and changes nothing.
- [ ] With the snapshot file missing, a write answers 503 `ledger_unavailable` and no table changes.
- [ ] The behaviour chosen for `setNickname`, `addFixedTag` and `removeFixedTag` on a movement is pinned
by one test and named in the pull request body.
- [ ] `authoredReadCases` has calls over an invented authored state that holds a nickname, an own tag, a
fixed tag, a note and a default line, and their golden files in `testdata/golden/full-authored/` show
each of the five.
- [ ] The commits of this slice change no file under `internal/api/testdata/golden/full/` or
`internal/api/testdata/golden/empty/`, and no file under `web/`.
- [ ] The no-leak test runs the new write cases and fails when a handler of this slice is made to log
one of its arguments.
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, each against its own deliberate break, named in the final
report: the second trim removed from the normalisation; `addFixedTag` storing its argument raw; fixed
tags listed before own ones; the bulk write validating inside its loop; `purchaseWireOf` reading the
ledger's name directly; `setDefaultLine` resolving the name in the transaction's month; the person and
movement check of `setDefaultLine` removed; the unknown-target refusal turned into an empty change; a
position renumbered on removal.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, the eight methods are out of `writesWithoutHandler`, and
for each of the five fields a golden effects file, a read that shows the value and an undo that restores
the dump are in the suite.

## Tests
- Table (Go, the normalisation function): the rows of the criterion above, through each of the three
  methods that add a tag.
- Conformance, recorded-change mode, over the full invented ledger of `internal/api/fixtures_test.go`
  and an authored state built by `authoredtest`: at least one case per method, with effects golden files
  under `testdata/golden/writes/` and the undo check of the harness.
- Conformance, refusal cases: `not_found` (unknown id, folded tax row, pot movement, a person and a
  movement for `setDefaultLine`, one unknown id in `addTagToMany`) and `unknown_line`
  (`setDefaultLine`); if either reason is still in the list of reasons with no producer, remove it there.
- Unit (Go, handlers over the full invented ledger): empty changes; tag order and positions across a
  removal and its undo; own tags before fixed ones; the known and suggested tags; the nickname on every
  transaction of a key and its clearing; the default line resolved in the current month against a
  fixture with two budget versions; the bulk undo that removes only what it added.
- Unit (Go, `internal/api/card_test.go`, over a ledger built for the test with `addCardPurchase`): the
  nickname in the card's three lists and in the closing view's card bill.
- Golden: the authored read cases in `testdata/golden/full-authored/`; `full/` and `empty/` unchanged.
- Unit: the no-leak test over the new write cases, with a handler that logs.
- Unit (`internal/authored`): every new statement is registered and prepares against the migrated
  schema; the store functions take an establishment key.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/api/transaction_tag_writes.go`, `internal/api/establishment_writes.go`,
`internal/api/card.go`, `internal/api/transactions_wire.go`, `internal/api/transaction_detail.go`,
`internal/api/transactions.go`, `internal/authored/`, `internal/authored/authoredtest/`,
`internal/api/transaction_tag_writes_test.go`, `internal/api/establishment_writes_test.go`,
`internal/api/card_test.go`, `internal/api/testdata/golden/writes/`,
`internal/api/testdata/golden/full-authored/`
**Reads only:** `web/src/api/fake/transaction-edits.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/transaction-writes.ts`,
`web/src/api/fake/transaction-detail.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/rules.ts`,
`web/src/api/fake/panel-writes.test.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/writes.test.ts`,
`web/src/components/transaction-panel/`, `web/src/components/transactions/useTransactionActions.ts`,
`web/src/api/contract/transaction-detail.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/transactions.ts`,
`internal/txrules/`, `internal/api/review_closing.go`, `internal/api/testdata/golden/full/`,
`internal/api/testdata/golden/empty/`, `internal/contract/contract.json`, `bin/ci`

Two new handler files in `internal/api` (the names are a proposal), the store functions for tags, the
note and the establishment's row in `internal/authored`, the builders `authoredtest` needs for them, and
one read that changes for certain: `card.go`, where two functions stop reading the ledger's name
directly. `transactions_wire.go`, `transaction_detail.go` and `transactions.go` are edited only where a
