- [ ] The user has unlocked the app at the desktop against a copy of the real ledger.
- [ ] The user has opened every screen in the list above.
- [ ] Each thing found wrong is a bead of its own, described without any real value.
- [ ] Done when: the user says the read-only app is good enough to plan the write side on.

## Tests
- Manual: the walk through the screens above, by the user.

## Blast radius
No file is edited. The check only reads: the built binary, a copy of the snapshot, and the interface in a browser.
close_reason: Done by the agent in a browser, at the user's request, instead of by the user. Chromium drove the production build of the interface against the built backend over a copy of the real ledger, printing counts, booleans, routes and status codes only. 64 screens on two viewports: no failed read, no broken text, no empty screen, no horizontal overflow. For each of the 15 months the sum of what the API lists equals an independent sum taken from the ledger with its own reading of sign and of what leaves the list. The parts of the net worth sum to its total. The PIN, the session cookie, a reload, a transaction's panel, a pot opened from the list and the lock all behave. Found and fixed through beads: the three reads that show a yield took about fifteen seconds; editing the budget looped on its refused evaluation; the scenarios screen toasted on open and then lost the toast; a pot's page could not be opened from the list. Not done, and not something a script can do: comparing a figure on screen with what the bank shows. The rules written where the sources were silent, listed in this bead's body, are still unconfirmed by the person whose money it is.

title: Create and migrate the app's own database behind `serve --db`, refusing any file that is not its own
description:
## What changes for the user
Today the app shows a person their money and can keep nothing they say about it: a budget line, the
category of a purchase, a tag or a note is answered with "Somente leitura por enquanto. Nada foi
alterado.", because the program has no place of its own to keep it. This work gives it that place: a
file that belongs to the app, created the first time the program is started with it, that survives a
restart and is never the file the bank records arrive in. Nothing on screen changes yet, and every
button still answers the same sentence. What the person would notice if this were wrong is the worst
kind of failure: the program started over the wrong file and damaged it, an update that quietly
scrambled what they had typed, or the app one day asking them about years of old purchases because it
forgot the month in which they began using it.

## Outcome
A new package, `internal/authored`, owns the app's database, `finwise.db`. It recognises a file by
its first hundred bytes before writing a byte to it, opens it with fixed connection settings, applies
embedded migrations recorded by name and checksum, creates the journal tables and `meta` (migration
`0001_journal`), records once the month in which the database was created, and keeps every SQL
statement as a registered constant under test. `finwise serve` gains `--db` / `FINWISE_DB`: absent,
the server is exactly today's read-only server; present, the database is created if missing or empty,
migrated and kept open for the life of the process, and a file that is not finwise's, or a migration
history the binary cannot vouch for, stops the start with the file untouched. No route answers
differently than before.

## Context
finwise is a personal finance app for one person. It has two stores. The **ledger** is a SQLite file,
`pluggy-snapshot.db`, that a separate program, the **collector** (pluggy-sync), fills from the banks
every night and replaces by an atomic rename; each such file is a **snapshot**, and finwise only ever
reads it, through `internal/ledger`. The second store does not exist yet: the **app's own database**,
`finwise.db`, where everything the person authors will live (the budget, the category of each
transaction, tags, notes, settings). Today the Go backend (`cmd/finwise`, `internal/api`) performs no
write to any SQLite file, and every method of the API that changes something answers `read_only`.
This bead creates the database and the discipline around it. Nothing reads or writes authored data
yet; that is later work, and all of it stands on what is built here.

The failure that matters in this app is a wrong total or a silently dropped transaction; the write
side adds a second one: a change the person made that is lost, or applied to the wrong thing. Here
that means three things: never write to a file that is not ours, never run a schema change that cannot
be traced or taken back, and never lose the month the person started.

**Decisions already taken, with what lost.**

| decision | why | what lost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The server runs read-only when no `--db` is given, and a write method without a handler keeps answering `read_only` | the write side lands one domain at a time and the app is never half-broken; the interface already handles `read_only` | a switch that turns every write on at once |
| Migrations are recorded by name in a table and every missing one is applied; the names are assigned in advance, one owner each | work lands in parallel, so a lower number can arrive after a higher one | `PRAGMA user_version` as "the number applied" |
| The two stores are never joined in SQL: rows are joined in Go | the ledger reader hands out rows, never a connection, and the snapshot is swapped under it | `ATTACH`; copying the ledger into `finwise.db` |

One more was decided by the person who uses the app, on 2026-11-21: the app asks about uncategorised
transactions from the month in which `finwise.db` is first created. Earlier transactions are never
put in the review queue (the list of transactions the app asks the person to categorise); they can
still be categorised by hand, or reached by the action that applies a category to every purchase of
one establishment. The month is one value in the database. What lost: all history in the queue on day
one, and a month chosen by hand.

**The package.** `internal/authored` owns `finwise.db`: opening, migrations and, in later work, the
recorder, the journal and undo, with one file per group of tables. It is the only package that
executes SQL against `finwise.db`. It depends on `internal/money` (amounts as integer cents) and
`internal/brday` (a day and a month in Brazil time) and on nothing else of this repository: not on
`internal/ledger`, not on `internal/api`. It never attaches or opens the snapshot. It logs nothing and
prints nothing; it returns errors and `cmd/finwise` reports them. A sibling package
`internal/authored/authoredtest`, which will build invented authored states for other packages'
tests, is later work and is not created here; this bead's tests keep their helpers in their own test
files.

**The setting.** `--db` / `FINWISE_DB` is a file path; the flag wins over the variable, as
`firstNonEmpty` already does for `--listen` and `--ledger` in `readServeSettings`
(`cmd/finwise/serve.go`). Absent: the server is today's, unchanged, and no file is created. Present:
the file is created if missing (its directory must exist and is never created), migrated, and kept
open for the life of the process, then closed on shutdown. It is not reopened per call the way the
ledger reader reopens the snapshot (`Reader.read` in `internal/ledger/open.go`): unlike the snapshot,
nobody swaps this file. `FINWISE_PIN_HASH` stays required at start either way
(`completeServeSettings`); later work lets a changed PIN be stored in the database, and until then
the variable is the only source. The database is opened before the server accepts a connection, so a
refused database never leaves a server answering. With `--db` given, every write still answers
`read_only` after this bead: `internal/api` is not touched, and its test that all write and evaluate
methods are refused (`TestEveryWriteAndEvaluationIsRefusedWithASession` in `router_test.go`) keeps
passing as it is.

**Recognition comes before anything is written, and does not open the file as a database at all:** it
reads the file's first hundred bytes. A file that does not exist or is empty is a new database.
Anything else must be an SQLite file whose header carries the application id finwise stamps,
`0x46494E57` (decimal 1179209303, the bytes `FINW`); any other file, the collector's snapshot
included, is refused. Only then is the file opened for writing. In SQLite's file format the header is
those first hundred bytes: bytes 0 to 15 hold the text `SQLite format 3` and a zero byte, and bytes 68
to 71 hold the application id as a big-endian integer. A file shorter than that and not empty is not
an SQLite file and is refused like any other. Reading bytes is what keeps a refused file untouched: by
SQLite's documentation, even a read-only open of a database in write-ahead mode can leave a `-shm` and
a `-wal` file beside it in a writable directory, and opening for writing with `journal_mode(WAL)`
rewrites the header.

A new database gets its application id written and flushed to the main file before it is put in
write-ahead mode, so a crash right after creation cannot leave a file finwise would refuse. The reason
is the same reading of bytes: in write-ahead mode a committed change stays in the `-wal` file until a
checkpoint copies it into the main file, so an id stamped after the switch may not be in the header
when the process dies, and recognition, which looks only at the main file, would then refuse the
app's own database. A file that stopped right after the stamp (the header with the id and no table) is
ours, and the next start finishes creating it.

The proof uses a foreign database in write-ahead mode, compares its bytes before and after and
requires that no file appeared beside it; an invented collector snapshot is refused the same way,
byte for byte. `TestQueriesLeaveTheSnapshotByteForByteUntouched` (`internal/ledger/safety_test.go`,
with `fileHash` in `support_test.go` and `listDirectory`) is the model for that comparison.

**Connection settings travel in the DSN**, so every connection of the pool has them, as the ledger
reader does with `_pragma`: `foreign_keys(1)`, `busy_timeout(5000)`, `synchronous(FULL)`,
`journal_mode(WAL)`, and immediate write transactions (`_txlock=immediate`). Reads use read-only
transactions, which the driver begins without taking the write lock. That last sentence was checked
against the driver in `go.mod` (`modernc.org/sqlite` v1.62.0): `newTx` in its `tx.go` issues a plain
`begin` when the transaction options say read-only and `begin immediate` otherwise, and `_txlock`
accepts `deferred`, `immediate` and `exclusive`. Unlike the ledger reader, which holds one connection
(`SetMaxOpenConns(1)`), this handle is a pool: a reader must not wait for a writer. What the handle
offers to later work is exactly two kinds of transaction, a read-only one and an immediate write one;
the recorder, the layer through which every change to the app's database will be written and
journaled ({{F2}}), builds on the write kind, and the per-request views of both stores that handlers
will receive ({{F3b}}) build on the read kind. The pool's DSN asks for write-ahead mode on every
connection, so for a new file the stamp of the paragraph above has to happen before the first
connection of that pool is made. A write that fails at run time, including when the
five-second wait for the lock runs out, rolls back and returns an error with nothing kept; the API
will answer it as `internal`.

**Migrations.** SQL files embedded from `internal/authored/migrations/`. A table
`schema_migrations(name, sha256)` records each one applied; it is the runner's own table, not part of
any migration file. A migration's name is its file name without the extension. At start every file
not recorded is applied in name order, each in one transaction together with its own
`schema_migrations` row. A recorded name whose checksum differs from the embedded file, or a recorded
name the binary does not have, is refused: the start fails and nothing is applied. Because every
*missing* one is applied, a database that records `0001` and `0003` and meets a binary that also has
`0002` gets `0002`; there is no "highest number applied". Before migrating a database that already
holds data, the file is copied with `VACUUM INTO` to `<name>.before-<UTC timestamp>` beside it, where
`<name>` is the database's file name; an existing copy is never overwritten, and a migration never
runs when the copy could not be written. If a migration fails, its transaction rolls back, the copy
taken before it stays beside the file, earlier migrations of the same start stay applied, and the
start fails. The runner takes its set of files as a value (the embedded one in production) so a test
can hand it a changed, an unknown, a failing or an out-of-order set.

The names are fixed in advance and this bead creates only the first: `0001_journal` (here), then
`0002_budget`, `0003_transactions`, `0004_settings`, `0005_pots`, `0006_subscriptions`, `0007_review`,
`0008_session`, each created by the later work that owns its tables. Rules every migration file
follows, this one included: every table declares its primary key, `NOT NULL` where a value is
required, foreign keys to `lines`, `tx_index`, `budget_versions` and `changes` (of which only
`changes` exists here), and `CHECK`s for every closed set of values and for amounts that cannot be
negative; each owner proves with a test that a duplicate, an invalid value and a negative amount are
refused by the database itself. The column lists are the starting point; an owner may add a column it
proves it needs, in its own file. A file, once applied anywhere, is frozen by its checksum.

**`0001_journal`.** The **journal** is the record of every change made to authored data: each write
is one change with an author, and can be undone. This migration creates its tables and `meta`; nothing
writes them yet.

- `changes(id, at, day, author, method, extended, undone_at)`. `id` is
  `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT`, as every id this database mints, so an id is never reused and a
  stale handle can never point at a newer object; on the wire it is the handle of a change, written
  as a decimal string. `at` is the instant the change was made and `day` its Brazil day
  (`YYYY-MM-DD`). `author` is one of `person` (an HTTP session), `rule` (the step that brings the
  database up to date with a new snapshot and classifies new transactions by rule) and `model`
  (reserved for a later nightly model call). `method` is the API method that made the change.
  `extended` says whether a later write appended its effects to this change. `undone_at` is null
  until the change is undone.
- `change_effects(change_id, seq, tbl, key, col, before, after)`. One row per recorded effect, in the
  order `seq` within its change, with a foreign key to `changes`. `tbl` is the table written, `key`
  the row's key as canonical JSON (an array in column order), `col` the column for a table of
  independent facts per key and null for a table whose rows are facts by existing, `before` and
  `after` the content on each side, null when there was none.
- `meta(key, value)`: the tracking start month, and later the last collector run the app has taken in
  and the instant of the last backup.

The recorder is written later against exactly these columns, and by then this file is frozen by its
checksum in every database that has started with it, so what it will record must fit `change_effects`
as it is created here: one column of one key changing; one row appearing or disappearing; and, for a
table of things that are created whole (a subscription), the creation of a row, which the recorder
treats as a unit of its own.

Not every table of this database is journaled. The ones deliberately left out are named: `changes`
and `change_effects` (the journal itself), `schema_migrations`, `meta`, `tx_index` and `tx_ids` (what
the database remembers about the transactions it has seen: observations, not decisions), `lines` (a
budget line's id, once minted, exists for good) and `pin`. Every table created here is on that list,
so its rows are written by plain registered statements of this package. The guard that fails when a
table is in neither list arrives with the recorder ({{F2}}) and carries the whole list from the
start, including the names whose tables arrive later (`tx_index`, `tx_ids`, `lines`, `pin`).

No column here is an amount, so "a negative amount is refused" has nothing to bite on in this file;
its proof is a duplicate, an invalid value and a dangling foreign key. How an instant is written in
`at` and `undone_at`, the key names inside `meta`, and the column types are the implementer's, bound
by the rules above. Later work reads `meta` through functions of this package, never by key.

**The tracking start month, and the clock.** Creation sets, in the same transaction as the first
migration and from the injected clock, the month in which the database was created: `YYYY-MM` in
Brazil time (`brday.MonthOf`). Nothing later sets it again: not a migration, not the first time the
database is brought up to date with a snapshot, not a restore from a copy. The package offers it as a
read. The clock is a required part of the configuration: opening the database without one fails at
once, nothing in `internal/authored` falls back to the host's clock, and only `cmd/finwise` supplies
the host's. Today `cmd/finwise` has none to give: `environment` in `cmd/finwise/main.go` carries the
streams, `getenv` and `listening`, and `serve` leaves `api.Config.Now` unset so `withDefaults` in
`internal/api/router.go` falls back to `time.Now`. `environment` gains a clock, which `main` fills
with the host's and a test with a fixed one; the copy's timestamp comes from the same clock. Making
the clock required in the API's own configuration as well, and removing that fallback, belongs to the
work that hands each handler a view of each store per request ({{F3b}}); `api.Config` is not changed
here.

**Statement discipline, mirroring the ledger's.** Every statement is a registered constant, a test
prepares each against the migrated schema, and a test fails on a statement that is not registered.
The ledger's version is `internal/ledger/queries.go` (constants named `query…` and the map
`allQueries`), `export_test.go` (`AllQueries`), and three tests in `schema_test.go`:
`TestEveryQueryPreparesAgainstTheCollectorsSchema`, `TestEveryQueryConstantIsRegistered` and
`TestNoStatementEscapesTheRegistry`. Mirror the intent, not the blind spots. The ledger's
registration test parses only `queries.go`, because the ledger keeps every statement there; this
package keeps one file per group of tables, so its test looks at every non-test file, including files
later work adds. The ledger's escape test inspects only calls to `QueryContext`, `QueryRowContext`,
`ExecContext` and `PrepareContext`, so a call to `Exec`, `Query`, `QueryRow` or `Prepare` would pass
unseen; here both families are covered. It allows one literal, `PRAGMA user_version`; here the
exceptions are named one by one (the execution of an embedded migration file, which is checked by
checksum instead, and whatever pragma cannot be a prepared constant), and it keeps the ledger's floor
that fails when the scan has stopped seeing calls. No SQL text is assembled at run time.

**Failure, and what a message may say.** If the database cannot be opened, recognised or migrated at
start, `serve` exits non-zero with a message naming the path and the reason, never the content
(`runServe` already prints `finwise: <error>` and returns `exitFailure`). Use errors with fixed
sentences, as `UnreadableSnapshotError` in `internal/ledger/open.go` does: a raw SQLite error can
quote a value. Failure paths this bead owns:

| what goes wrong | what happens |
| --- | --- |
| `--db` points at a file that is not ours | refused at start, file untouched, no side file created |
| the database holds a migration the binary does not know, or a changed one | refused at start |
| a migration fails | its transaction rolls back; the copy taken before it is beside the file; `serve` exits |
| a write fails halfway, or waits out the lock | one transaction: nothing of it is kept; `internal` |

**Left to the implementer, and what binds each** (these are what make this bead `spec:open`).

- The layout of the UTC timestamp in the copy's name: UTC, from the injected clock.
- What "already holds data" means for taking the copy: at least any database in which a migration is
  already recorded; a file this start created, or found missing or empty, needs none.
- What happens when the copy's name is taken: refuse the start or use another unused name, never
  overwrite.
- How the application id of a new file is written and flushed before the switch to write-ahead mode,
  as long as the main file's own bytes 68 to 71 hold it while the database is still open and before
  any checkpoint.

Each choice is stated in a comment where it is made.

**Privacy.** No test here touches a real ledger: the "collector's snapshot" of the refusal proof is an
invented one built by `ledgertest.New` (`internal/ledger/ledgertest`), which loads the collector's
schema and stamps no application id, and the foreign database in write-ahead mode is one the test
creates. Fixtures are invented. The pre-migration copy is a whole copy of
what the person authored, and `.gitignore` today ignores `*.db` and `*.db-*`, neither of which matches
`finwise.db.before-…`; it gains a pattern so a copy made inside the tree cannot be committed.

**Conventions.** Work happens in the worktree it was given and ends at local commits: atomic,
Conventional Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a work item or a plan in a
commit message. Money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path; this package gets
the same source guard `internal/api` has (`TestNoSourceFileOfTheHTTPLayerTouchesAFloat` in
`internal/api/reais_test.go`). Every SQL statement over the app's database is a registered constant.
Interface text is Brazilian Portuguese and everything else is English; a design value in a component
comes from a token (neither arises here). The standard library and the driver already in `go.mod` are
enough.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Started with neither `--db` nor `FINWISE_DB`, `finwise serve` behaves as before: the existing
tests of `cmd/finwise` and `internal/api` pass unchanged and no database file is created.
- [ ] `serve --db <dir>/finwise.db`, file missing and `<dir>` existing: the server starts; the file's
`PRAGMA application_id` is 1179209303; it holds the tables `schema_migrations`, `changes`,
`change_effects` and `meta` and no other besides SQLite's own `sqlite_sequence`; `schema_migrations`
has exactly one row, named `0001_journal`, whose `sha256` is the SHA-256 of the embedded file;
`PRAGMA journal_mode` answers `wal`. A graceful stop exits 0.
- [ ] `FINWISE_DB` supplies the path when the flag is absent, and the flag wins when both are given.
- [ ] `--db` in a directory that does not exist exits non-zero, names the path on standard error and
creates no directory. `--db` without `FINWISE_PIN_HASH` exits non-zero as today.
- [ ] Given as `--db`, each of these is refused with a non-zero exit, its SHA-256 equal before and
after, and its directory listing equal before and after (no `-wal`, `-shm`, `-journal`, no copy): a
foreign database in write-ahead mode with one table; an invented collector snapshot built by
`ledgertest`; a database with one table and application id 1; an SQLite database with no table and no
application id; a text file of more than a hundred bytes that is not a database; a file of ten bytes.
The message names the path and contains no sentinel string the test stored inside the file.
- [ ] A file of zero bytes given as `--db` is accepted and becomes a database as in the second
criterion, exactly as a missing one does.
- [ ] While a newly created database is still open, and before any checkpoint, bytes 68 to 71 of the
main file, read directly from disk, are `46 49 4E 57`.
- [ ] A file that holds only an SQLite header with application id 1179209303 and no table (a creation
that stopped right after the stamp) is accepted, becomes a database as in the second criterion, and
takes its tracking start month from the clock of the start that finishes it.
- [ ] Opening the database without a clock returns an error. `time.Now` is named in no non-test file
of `internal/authored`, and in `cmd/finwise` only where `main` builds `environment`.
- [ ] Created with the clock at 2026-12-01T01:30:00Z, the tracking start month reads `2026-11`.
Reopened with the clock at 2027-02-10T12:00:00Z it still reads `2026-11`, and it still does after a
start that applies a further, test-supplied migration.
- [ ] A second start with nothing pending applies nothing, leaves `schema_migrations` as it was and
creates no `.before-` file.
- [ ] A database recording `0001_journal` and a test migration `0003_x`, started with a set that also
has `0002_x`, ends with three recorded rows and `0002_x` applied.
- [ ] A set in which one byte of an applied file differs is refused; so is a database recording a
name the set lacks. In both, nothing is applied, `schema_migrations` is unchanged and no copy is made.
- [ ] A pending migration over a database that already records one: before it runs, a file named
`<database file name>.before-<UTC timestamp>` appears beside the database, carries application id
1179209303, answers `ok` to `PRAGMA integrity_check`, and does not record the pending name. A file
already at that name is byte-identical afterwards.
- [ ] A migration that fails (test-supplied) leaves its tables absent and its name unrecorded, leaves
earlier migrations of the same start applied, leaves the copy beside the file and makes the open fail;
through `serve` the exit is non-zero and names the path. When the first migration of a new file is the
one that fails, the next start with a correct set succeeds on that same file.
- [ ] On three connections held at once from each of two handles on one file, `PRAGMA foreign_keys`
answers 1, `busy_timeout` 5000, `synchronous` 2 and `journal_mode` `wal`.
- [ ] With two handles on one file: a `change_effects` row for a change that does not exist is refused
through each; a second write transaction begun while the first is open returns only after the first
commits; a read-only transaction begun on the other handle while a write transaction is open returns
at once and reads the state from before that write.
- [ ] The database itself refuses: a second `change_effects` row with the same `change_id` and `seq`;
a second `meta` row with the same key; a `changes` row whose `author` is not `person`, `rule` or
`model`; a `changes` row with `at`, `day`, `author` or `method` missing; an `extended` outside its two
values.
- [ ] After the highest row of `changes` is deleted, the next row gets a higher id, never the deleted
one.
- [ ] Every statement constant of `internal/authored` is registered and prepares against the migrated
schema. A constant left out of the registry fails a test; a statement executed from a non-test file
that is not a registered constant or a named exception fails a test, through the `…Context` methods
and through `Exec`, `Query`, `QueryRow` and `Prepare` alike; the scan fails when it inspects no call.
- [ ] A source test fails on `float64`, `float32`, `ParseFloat`, `FromFloat` or a float literal in a
non-test file of `internal/authored`.
- [ ] `git check-ignore` matches `finwise.db.before-x`.
- [ ] No file under `internal/api`, `internal/ledger` or `web/` is changed.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, and the report names the break used for each: recognition
done by opening the file as a database, or moved after the write-open (the byte and side-file
comparison fails on the foreign database in write-ahead mode); the application id stamped after the
switch to write-ahead mode (the main file's header lacks it while the database is open); the clock
defaulted to the host's when none is given; the checksum comparison removed;
the unknown-name check removed; the copy skipped; `foreign_keys` dropped from the DSN;
`_txlock=immediate` dropped (the second writer no longer waits at its begin); the tracking start month
written on every open; a statement constant left unregistered; a `float64` added.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, a foreign database in write-ahead mode and an invented
collector snapshot given as `--db` are each refused byte for byte with nothing appearing beside them,
and a changed or unknown migration stops the start.

## Tests
- Integration, `cmd/finwise` (the existing `runCommand`, `refusalVars`, `cancelledContext` and
`startServer` of `finwise_test.go`), over temporary directories: start with and without `--db`, the
environment variable, the missing directory, the refused files with hashes and directory listings,
the zero-byte file, a failing migration's exit.
- Unit, `internal/authored`, over temporary files: recognition case by case from the first hundred
bytes (missing, empty, ours, ours with no table yet, foreign in write-ahead mode, foreign with another
id, no id, not SQLite, too short); the header bytes of a new database read from disk while it is
open; the tracking start month with a fixed clock on both sides of midnight in Brazil; opening without
a clock.
- Table, `internal/authored`, over test-supplied migration sets: nothing pending, out of order, changed
checksum, unknown recorded name, failing migration, first migration failing, the copy and its checks,
a name already taken.
- Unit, two handles on one temporary file: the four pragmas on several pooled connections, the foreign
key on both, the waiting writer, the reader that does not wait.
- Unit, the migrated schema: each constraint of `0001_journal` refused by the database; ids not
reused.
- Unit, source scans: every statement registered and prepared; no statement outside the registry; no
float.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/authored/`, `cmd/finwise/serve.go`, `cmd/finwise/main.go`,
`cmd/finwise/finwise_test.go`, `.gitignore`
**Reads only:** `internal/ledger/open.go`, `internal/ledger/queries.go`, `internal/ledger/schema_test.go`,
`internal/ledger/safety_test.go`, `internal/ledger/ledgertest/`, `internal/brday/`, `internal/money/`,
`internal/api/`, `bin/ci`

One new package (opening and recognition, the migration runner, the one migration file, the statement
registry, the read of the tracking start month, and their tests) and the wiring of one flag in
`cmd/finwise`, which also gains a clock in `environment`. About eight code files in two packages, and
the first schema of a new database, hence `size:L`. `internal/api` is read to see what must not
change and is not edited: handlers do not receive the database in this bead.

## Recovery path
The database is new, so there is nothing to convert and nothing this bead can lose but the file it
creates. To stop using it, start the server without `--db`: it is today's read-only server and the
file is left alone. To restore a database from a copy (the one a migration takes before it runs, or
any consistent copy): stop the server; check the copy (`PRAGMA integrity_check` answers `ok`, the
application id is 1179209303); put it in place of the database with no `-wal` or `-shm` file beside
it; start the server. A binary older than the database refuses it at start (it records a migration
that binary does not know) instead of guessing, so going back to an older binary means going back to
the copy taken before the migration. Deleting a database also deletes the month it was created in;
the next creation records a new one.

title: Returning from the scenarios to the budget loses the read-only message
description:
## What changes for the user
Against the real backend, which only reads for now, pressing "Cenários" on the budget sends the person straight back to the budget with nothing on screen to say why. After this lands the read-only message is there when they arrive.

## Outcome
When the scenarios screen returns to the budget because its evaluation was refused, the read-only toast is visible on the budget.

## Context
finwise's interface runs against a backend that is read-only for now: every evaluation of the contract answers a `read_only` error, and one function (`web/src/api/failures.ts`) turns that into a toast, "Somente leitura por enquanto. Nada foi alterado.".

`web/src/screens/budget/ScenariosScreen.vue` evaluates a scenario as soon as it opens. When that is refused it now returns to the budget and rethrows, so the central function shows the toast. But the frame around every screen closes everything floating when a screen is left, the toast included, and the return to the budget is such a leave: the screen starts the navigation, the toast is shown at once, and the navigation then completes and clears it. Seen in Chromium against the built backend over a real ledger: one refused call, the route ends at the budget, and no toast is on screen.

The component test of the scenarios screen passes because it mounts the screen without the frame, so nothing clears the toast there. The fix is the order: the return to the budget completes before the error goes on to the central function. The regression test has to include the frame's clearing, or it cannot fail.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Mount the app's frame with its router over the stand-in wrapped by the read-only helper (`web/src/test/readOnly.ts`), on the budget.
2. Go to the scenarios route.
3. Observed: the route ends at the budget and no toast is shown.
4. Expected: the route ends at the budget and the read-only toast is shown.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Through the mounted frame over the read-only stand-in, going to the scenarios route ends at the budget with the read-only toast visible, and `budget.evaluateScenario` was called exactly once.
- [ ] The same test fails when the screen rethrows before its navigation has completed.
- [ ] Over the plain stand-in the scenarios screen opens and stays, as before, and `npm --prefix web run parity` still reports every state at or under 0.05%.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and the regression test fails with the fix removed.

## Tests
- Component, regression: the frame, the router and the scenarios route over the read-only stand-in.
- Parity: the full run, unchanged.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `web/src/screens/budget/ScenariosScreen.vue`, `web/src/api/refused-writes.test.ts`
**Reads only:** `web/src/components/shell/AppShell.vue`, `web/src/stores/overlay.ts`, `web/src/api/failures.ts`, `web/src/test/readOnly.ts`, `bin/ci`

One reordering in one screen and one regression test that mounts the frame.
close_reason: ScenariosScreen.vue completes its return to the budget before the refused evaluation's error goes on to the central function, so the frame's clearing of everything floating no longer takes the toast with it. The regression test mounts the frame with its router over the read-only stand-in; it failed on the toast alone before the fix and again with the old order put back. bin/ci: CI green on the tree merged with main, 941 tests. Parity: 174 checked, 0 over 0.05%. Confirmed in Chromium against the built backend over a real ledger: one refused call, the route ends at the budget, the toast is on screen.

title: Say why a write was refused, what became of a save that failed or never answered, and how long a locked PIN screen must wait
description:
## What changes for the user
Today every button that changes something answers "Somente leitura por enquanto. Nada foi alterado.",
because the app only reads. Once it starts accepting changes, some will still be declined for a reason
the person can act on: closing a month that still has purchases waiting for review, undoing something
that was changed again afterwards, saving a budget with two lines of the same name. Without this work
each of those would read "Não foi possível carregar os dados." with a "Tentar de novo" button, which is
what a page that failed to load says, and tells the person nothing about why. After this lands each
refusal says why in one sentence and the screen goes back to what is really stored. A save the app
could not complete says it was not saved. When the connection drops in the middle of a save, the app
says it could not confirm whether it was saved and refreshes the screen, instead of claiming the change
was lost. A budget being edited survives a save that failed, so what the message names can be fixed,
unless the month was closed meanwhile. And when the app locks itself after too many wrong PINs, the PIN
screen that comes back says how long to wait, where today it shows an ordinary keypad and only says so
after six digits are typed.

## Outcome
A failed call carries, besides its kind, the class of the method that failed and, for a refusal, its
reason. The one function every failure of the interface ends in shows a fixed sentence for each of the
nine reasons a write can be refused for, a sentence for a reason it does not know, the wording of a
failed save for a write the server could not complete, and the wording of an unconfirmed save for a
write whose answer never arrived; none of these carries an action, and each refetches at once. "Tentar
de novo" stays on failed reads. A PIN screen brought back by a `locked` answer loads the session status
and shows the hold. A budget save that fails keeps the draft and the edit, except that a month found
closed ends the edit and a lost session goes to the PIN screen; a scenario applied to a month found
closed leaves the scenarios screen with its sentence still showing. A test helper refuses one chosen
method with a chosen kind and reason, so a screen test can produce any of this without a server.

## Context
**What finwise is, and the words used below.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The
ledger* is a SQLite snapshot that a separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app only
reads it. The app is gaining a *write side*: its own database, `finwise.db`, where everything the
person authors (budget, categories, tags, notes) will live. *The contract* is the TypeScript interface
`FinwiseApi` (`web/src/api/types.ts` and `web/src/api/contract/`), 82 methods; *the manifest* is
`internal/contract/contract.json`, generated from it by `npm --prefix web run contract`, which states
for every method its route, its arguments, its result and its *class*: `session`, `read`, `evaluate`
(takes a draft, computes, stores nothing) or `write` (`web/src/api/contract/classification.ts`; today 3,
23, 1 and 55 methods). *The stand-in* is the in-memory fake backend under `web/src/api/fake/` that the
design prototype runs on (`createFakeApi`); it is the only existing statement of how writes behave, and
this work does not change it. *The revision* is a counter (`web/src/stores/revision.ts`) that every
screen watches: bumping it makes every screen fetch again. *The frame* is the shell around every
screen (`web/src/components/shell/AppShell.vue`); it also draws the toast. *The gate* is `bin/ci`, the
exact checks CI runs. *The parity check* is `npm --prefix web run parity`: it builds the app on the
stand-in and measures every screen against the design's reference screenshots in a real browser; it is
not part of the gate.

**The failure path as it is today** (each point read in the file named):

- Call sites do not catch. Every rejection of the API reaches `createFailureHandler` in
  `web/src/api/failures.ts`, through Vue's error handler or through the window's `unhandledrejection`
  (`failureListeners`, `installFailureHandling`). About sixty call sites funnel there. Two screens catch
  only to end themselves before rethrowing: `web/src/screens/budget/BudgetScreen.vue` discards its draft
  when the evaluation of a draft is refused with `read_only`, and
  `web/src/screens/budget/ScenariosScreen.vue` returns to the budget on the same refusal, awaiting that
  navigation before it rethrows. The reason for the order is in the frame: `AppShell.vue` closes
  everything that floats, the toast included, when the screen is left, so a toast shown before the
  navigation completed would be cleared by it.
- The handler switches on the kind alone. `read_only`: toast `READ_ONLY_MESSAGE` ("Somente leitura por
  enquanto. Nada foi alterado.") with no action, and a revision bump. `locked`:
  `useSessionStore().markLocked()`, no toast. `ledger_unavailable`: "Dados do banco indisponíveis no
  momento." with the action "Tentar de novo". Anything else (`bad_request`, `unknown_method`,
  `internal`, `network`): "Não foi possível carregar os dados." with "Tentar de novo". That action
  (`tryAgain`) dismisses the toast, resumes the first reads of the app if they never arrived
  (`resumeStartup`) and bumps the revision. It only refetches.
- `ApiFailure` (`web/src/api/http/failure.ts`) carries a kind and nothing else. Its constructor takes
  the kind alone, and about twenty call sites in tests and in `web/src/test/replay.ts` build one that
  way.
- The HTTP client (`web/src/api/http/client.ts`) is built from the manifest. Its `ManifestMethod`
  interface reads `domain`, `name`, `route` and `result`, not `class`, although every entry of the
  manifest has one. `failureKind` reads `error.kind` from the answer and turns any kind it does not know,
  and any answer it cannot read, into `internal`. A `fetch` that throws becomes `network`, the one kind
  that never travels on the wire.
- No write is optimistic: a screen changes only after the server answered and the revision was bumped.
  The handle that undoes a change lives in a toast for eight seconds (`TOAST_LIFETIME_MS` in
  `web/src/stores/overlay.ts`), and the overlay holds one toast at a time: a new one replaces the old.
- `markLocked()` in `web/src/stores/session.ts` sets `locked`, clears the typed digits and the message,
  and makes no call ("no call has to be made to put the PIN screen back"). `load()`, run once at start,
  is the only place that reads `session.status()` and calls `holdKeypad(retryAfterSeconds)`, which
  disables the keypad, shows "Muitas tentativas. Tente de novo em 1 minuto." or "... em N minutos."
  (N is the seconds divided by sixty, rounded up, at least 1) and releases both when the wait ends. So a
  PIN screen brought back by a `locked` answer shows no wait even while the server is holding.
- `save()` in `BudgetScreen.vue` awaits `api.budget.save` and only then discards the draft, so a save
  that fails for any reason leaves the draft where it was. `apply()` in `ScenariosScreen.vue` awaits
  `api.budget.applyScenario`, bumps the revision and leaves; a failure stops it before either. That
  screen also leaves by itself when its month becomes closed (a watch on `month.isClosed`).
- `web/src/test/readOnly.ts` has `readOnlyApi(api)`, which wraps a `FinwiseApi` so that every `write`
  and `evaluate` method rejects with `read_only`, and `mountWithFailures`, which mounts a screen with
  the failure handling installed as the app installs it and records every toast, every unclaimed
  rejection and the revision. `web/src/api/refused-writes.test.ts` sends one refused write through each
  of the seven ways the interface makes one (the transaction panel, the list's change of line, the
  selection, the settings writes, the "announce" helpers of the subscriptions and of the review, the
  closing's writes with the budget's save, the PIN form) and requires the same single toast each time.

**What this work finds already in place.** It depends on the work that adds a seventh wire kind,
`refused`, with its closed list of reasons, to the contract's error types
(`web/src/api/contract/errors.ts`) and to the manifest ({{F4a}}). Before that work, `errors.ts` lists
six wire kinds and `network`, and the envelope is `{"error":{"kind":"..."}}` with no other field.
After it, the envelope is a closed union: every kind but `refused` has no other field, and `refused`
always carries one reason. The server will answer it with HTTP 409:

```
{"error": {"kind": "refused", "reason": "<one of the nine below>"}}
```

The server starts answering refusals in later work; nothing here waits for it, because the helper
below produces them in tests. Read `errors.ts` as you find it and take the kind and the list of reasons
from there; do not redeclare them. If the reasons are there only as a type, export them as a value
beside `API_ERROR_KINDS`: that changes no schema, so the manifest must come out byte for byte the same.

**Decisions already taken, with what lost.**

- One new kind, `refused`, with a reason from a closed list; the texts stay in the interface. A closed
  month or a stale undo must be readable by the person, and `bad_request` keeps meaning a bug in a
  client. Rejected: one kind per refusal; free text sent by the server.
- No shared write wrapper in the interface. The central failure function learns `refused` and the
  wording of a failed write, because the call sites already funnel there and nothing is optimistic.
  Rejected: wrapping every call site.
- The stand-in keeps throwing plain errors where the server will refuse (its `assertOpen` throws an
  `Error` for a closed month). It is not taught the typed refusals; that is why the test helper below
  exists.

**The reasons, when the server answers each, and the sentence the person reads.** The sentences are
exact; they are interface text and stay in Brazilian Portuguese.

| reason | when | what the person reads |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `month_closed` | saving or applying a budget for a closed month; closing a month already closed | "Esse mês já está fechado." |
| `future_month` | closing a month after the current one | "Esse mês ainda não chegou." |
| `pending_reviews` | closing a month while a transaction of that month or an earlier one waits for review | "Resolva as pendências do mês antes de fechar." |
| `stale_change` | undoing or extending a change that is unknown, already undone, already extended, or overwritten since | "Isso já foi alterado depois e não pode mais ser desfeito." |
| `not_found` | a write whose result cannot be null names a transaction, pot, subscription or establishment that the ledger does not list or `finwise.db` does not have | "Esse item não existe mais." |
| `unknown_line` | a write names a budget line that the budget of the month it is resolved in does not have | "Essa linha não existe no budget desse mês." |
| `invalid_budget` | saving a budget with a duplicate or empty line name, an unknown or repeated line id, an unknown group | "O budget tem linha sem nome ou repetida." |
| `unstable_pot` | a write to a pot whose identity the bank does not keep stable | "O banco não identifica esse cofrinho de forma estável." |
| `split_with_reimbursement` | splitting a purchase that has a linked reimbursement, or linking one to a split purchase | "Uma compra dividida não pode ter reembolso ligado." |

Three more sentences: for a `refused` whose reason the interface does not know (a newer server, or a
reason that is missing or not a string), "Não foi possível concluir."; for a write the server answered
and did not carry out, "Não foi possível salvar."; for a write whose answer never arrived, "Não deu
para confirmar se foi salvo. Atualizando a tela."

What the other kinds mean does not change. `bad_request`: the arguments do not match the method's
schema or cannot be parsed, a bug in a client. `read_only`: a server started without its database, or a
write that has no handler yet; it keeps its sentence and its tests. `ledger_unavailable`: answered by a
write exactly as by a read when the snapshot it needs is missing. Where a method's result type allows
null, "nothing to do" and "no such target" both answer null, which the screens already treat as
"nothing happened"; `not_found` is only for results that cannot be null.

**What the failure carries.** `ApiFailure` gains the class of the method that failed and, for
`refused`, the reason. The HTTP client takes the class from the manifest entry it is calling (so every
failure it raises has one: an error envelope, an answer it cannot read, a `fetch` that throws) and the
reason from the envelope. A `refused` with a reason outside the list stays `refused`; it must not be
turned into `internal`, because the server did say that nothing was changed. How an unknown reason is
held on the object is yours to choose. Constructing a failure from a kind alone must keep working, so
that `web/src/test/replay.ts`, `web/src/test/sweep.ts` and the existing tests need no edit; a failure
that names no class is shown as a failed read, which is what those tests expect.

**What the handler shows.** After this work:

| kind | class of the method | toast | action | revision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `refused`, a known reason | any | the reason's sentence | none | bumped once, at once |
| `refused`, an unknown reason | any | "Não foi possível concluir." | none | bumped once, at once |
| `internal`, `bad_request`, `unknown_method` | `write` | "Não foi possível salvar." | none | bumped once, at once |
| `network` | `write` | "Não deu para confirmar se foi salvo. Atualizando a tela." | none | bumped once, at once |
| `internal`, `network`, `bad_request`, `unknown_method` | `read`, `session`, `evaluate`, or none | "Não foi possível carregar os dados." | "Tentar de novo" | as today: when the action runs |
| `ledger_unavailable` | any | "Dados do banco indisponíveis no momento." | "Tentar de novo" | as today |
| `read_only` | any | "Somente leitura por enquanto. Nada foi alterado." | none | as today: bumped at once |
| `locked` | any | none; the PIN screen comes back | | not bumped |

The reasoning behind the rows that are new. A refusal is the server saying that it changed nothing and
why, so the screen returns to what the server holds and there is nothing to retry. A write answered
`internal` was rolled back whole on the server (one transaction: nothing of it is kept, including when
the wait for the database's lock runs out), and one answered `bad_request` or `unknown_method` never
ran, so "it was not saved" is true of all three. A write whose answer never arrived may have been
stored: the process can stop between the commit and the answer. The interface therefore never says
that change was lost; it says it could not confirm. Neither toast offers an action: a write is never
sent again by the interface, and there is nothing to refetch by hand because the revision is bumped at
once, so that the screen shows what the server holds. "Tentar de novo" stays where it is today, on
failed reads; it refetches and never replays a write. A failed evaluation is shown as a failed read,
since nothing was being saved: `budget.evaluateScenario` is of class `evaluate`, and `budget.view` with
a draft is of class `read`. `session.changePin` and `changes.undo` are of class `write` and follow the
write rows. The `ledger_unavailable` branch is not touched: a write that meets a missing snapshot
shows what a read shows, and its action refetches only. Nothing here changes how a failed read is
shown, so when the server is really unreachable the refetch fails too and its own toast replaces the
one about the write; a test for the unconfirmed write therefore fails only the write.

**What the bump puts back, and what it does not.** The point of bumping at once is that a field the
person typed into goes back to what the server holds. A field redrawn from the refetched answer does:
in the transaction panel the note, the reasons and the amounts (each section is given the new detail)
and in the subscription editor the note and the review date. Three places hold what was typed where a
refetch does not reach it, and keep it after a failed or refused write as they already do after
`read_only`: the nickname and card-label fields of the settings screen
(`web/src/screens/config/NicknameInput.vue` is given only the stored text, which did not change, so it
is not redrawn), the threshold slider there (a local value in `CategorizationSection.vue`, set again
only when the stored one changes), and the panel's nickname editor of an establishment
(`EstablishmentSection.vue` stays open with its draft). This work does not change those three and its
criteria do not claim them. Forms that keep what was typed on purpose, the budget draft first among
them, are not fields in this sense.

**The hold after `locked`.** Three wrong PINs make the server hold every attempt for 300 seconds,
globally. A `locked` answer can arrive while that hold is running: the session expired during it, or,
once the PIN can be changed on the server ({{P1}}, the work that stores a new PIN and counts a wrong
current PIN in the same lockout), the third wrong current PIN, and any attempt while the hold is
already running, removes the session and answers `locked`. The person must land on a PIN screen that
shows the wait. So `markLocked()` locks at once, and then loads the session status for the hold alone:
the PIN screen is back without waiting for that answer; when the answer reports `retryAfterSeconds`
above zero the keypad is held with the same message and the same release as at start (`holdKeypad`);
what was typed is forgotten, as today. A `locked` answer means the session is gone, so a status that
says `locked: false` must not take the PIN screen away (the existing screen test in
`web/src/api/failures-on-screen.test.ts` rejects one read with `locked` over a stand-in whose session
is still open, and must keep passing). A failure of that status call shows nothing: no toast on the
PIN screen, no message, the keypad free. That is the one rejection this work catches without
rethrowing, and it is caught in the store. Whether `lock()`, the person locking by hand, also loads the
status is yours to choose.

**The budget's edit and a failed save.** A save that fails keeps the draft and the edit, so the person
can fix what the toast names. Two exceptions. `month_closed` ends the edit and shows the closed month:
the month was closed elsewhere after the edit began, and no correction of the draft can make it
saveable. `locked` goes to the PIN screen, as it does from anywhere. Four outcomes, each with a test:

| the save is answered | the draft and the edit | what the person sees |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a validation refusal, `invalid_budget` | kept | "O budget tem linha sem nome ou repetida."; the figures of the same draft again |
| `month_closed` | ended | "Esse mês já está fechado."; the month drawn as closed: its notice "Budget de <mês> · fechado", no "Editar budget", no "Salvar" |
| `locked` | gone with the screen | the PIN screen; no toast |
| `internal` | kept | "Não foi possível salvar."; the figures of the same draft again |

The first and the last already hold by the shape of `save()`: the bump that follows only makes the
screen ask again for the figures of the draft it still has. For `month_closed` follow the pattern the
file has for a refused evaluation: catch only to discard the draft, then rethrow so the central handler
shows the sentence. The month is drawn as closed because the bump makes the shell fetch its overview
again and the month store learns the closed month from it; a test over the stand-in closes the month
in the stand-in's state before the refused save, so that refetch finds it closed. What `read_only`
does today is not to change: a `read_only` save keeps the edit, and a `read_only` evaluation of a
draft ends it.

**A scenario applied to a month found closed.** `applyScenario` refused with `month_closed` leaves
the scenarios screen, back to the budget, with the sentence still showing, as a refused evaluation
does there today. The navigation must complete before the failure is rethrown, or the frame clears the
toast as it leaves the screen.

**The test helper.** Beside `readOnlyApi` in `web/src/test/readOnly.ts`: a function that wraps a
`FinwiseApi` (in practice `createFakeApi(...)`) and makes exactly one named method, such as
`budget.save`, reject with an `ApiFailure` of the kind given, the reason given when the kind is
`refused`, and the class that method has in `METHOD_CLASSES`. Every other method stays the wrapped
API's own. Its name and signature are yours; it must be usable as the `api` option of
`mountWithFailures`, and naming a method the contract does not have must fail loudly instead of
refusing nothing.

**Out of scope.** The stand-in; the contract's types and the manifest (unless the list of reasons has
to be exported as a value, as said above); any Go file; the wording or behaviour of `read_only`,
`ledger_unavailable` and of a failed read; the three places named above that keep what was typed; a
debounce or a retry of writes.

**Conventions.** Work in your own git worktree on a branch of your own and stop at local commits:
atomic, Conventional Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a plan in a
commit message. Interface text is Brazilian Portuguese; everything else in the repository is English.
A design value in a component comes from a token (`design/tokens/finwise.tokens.json`); this work
needs none. Money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path, and every SQL statement
over the app's database is a registered constant; this work touches neither. Fixtures are invented:
nothing derived from a real account is committed. The backend is faked at the API boundary with
`createFakeApi`; only the HTTP client's own tests stub `fetch`.

`month_closed` and `invalid_budget` through the budget's save; `future_month` and `pending_reviews`
through closing the month in the closing tab; `stale_change` through "Desfazer" on the toast of a line
change in the transaction list (`changes.undo`); `unknown_line` through the list's change of line;
`not_found` through a write of the transaction panel; `unstable_pot` through the bucket menu of the
settings screen; `split_with_reimbursement` through the panel's split. Another write is fine where the
table's "when" covers it.
- Screen tests of a failed budget save, one per outcome, four in all (new file
`web/src/screens/budget/failed-save.test.ts`): `invalid_budget`, `internal` and `month_closed` over the
budget screen with `mountWithFailures`, the third with the month closed in the stand-in's state before
the save; `locked` over the whole app, mounted as `web/src/api/failures-on-screen.test.ts` mounts it.
In the same file, the scenario applied to a closed month, with the frame around the scenarios screen
as the existing read-only case in `refused-writes.test.ts` mounts it.
- Screen tests in `web/src/api/refusal-reasons.test.ts`: a write that fails with `network` (the
sentence, no action, the immediate bump); the panel's note going back after `internal`; a write
answered `ledger_unavailable` followed by "Tentar de novo" (the write is not replayed).
- Screen test (`web/src/api/failures-on-screen.test.ts`): the PIN screen with the wait after a `locked`
answer, and with nothing shown when the status call fails.
- The gate and the parity check, run once at the end. The review breaks each new guard once more
before the work is accepted.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `web/src/api/http/failure.ts`, `web/src/api/http/client.ts`, `web/src/api/http/client.test.ts`,
`web/src/api/failures.ts`, `web/src/api/failures.test.ts`, `web/src/api/failures-on-screen.test.ts`,
`web/src/api/refused-writes.test.ts`, `web/src/api/refusal-reasons.test.ts`, `web/src/stores/session.ts`,
`web/src/stores/session.test.ts`, `web/src/test/readOnly.ts`, `web/src/test/readOnly.test.ts`,
`web/src/screens/budget/BudgetScreen.vue`, `web/src/screens/budget/ScenariosScreen.vue`,
`web/src/screens/budget/failed-save.test.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/errors.ts`, `AGENTS.md`
**Reads only:** `web/src/api/contract/classification.ts`, `internal/contract/contract.json`,
`web/src/stores/overlay.ts`, `web/src/stores/revision.ts`, `web/src/stores/shell.ts`,
`web/src/stores/month.ts`, `web/src/components/shell/AppShell.vue`, `web/src/App.vue`,
`web/src/test/replay.ts`, `web/src/test/sweep.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/`,
`web/src/screens/config/NicknameInput.vue`, `web/src/screens/config/CategorizationSection.vue`,
`web/src/components/transaction-panel/EstablishmentSection.vue`, `bin/ci`

Seven source files in one module, the interface: the failure object, the HTTP client, the failure
handler, the session store, the test support file and the save of two budget screens. That is over the
count of a medium bead, hence `size:L`; each change is small and they share one thread, what a failure
carries and what is done with it. The rest are their tests, three of them new, and two sentences of
`AGENTS.md`. `web/src/api/contract/errors.ts` is edited only if the list of reasons has to be exported
as a value, and then the generated manifest must not change. The stand-in, the settings screen, the
transaction panel, the contract's method types and every Go file are not touched.

title: Answer the monthly closing and the settings as a fresh install
description:
## What changes for the user
The monthly closing and the settings are the last two screens still answered by nothing. After this lands they open against the real backend the way they would on the day the app is first installed: a closing with every step still to do and nothing to review, and settings at their defaults, with what the bank's records do support (the card's bill and closing day, the last synchronisation, the connections, the pots) shown for real. With them every screen of the app has a real answer behind it.

## Outcome
The backend answers the last two read methods of the interface's contract, `review.closing` and `settings.overview`. With them every read of the contract has a handler, and the list of reads still waiting for one is gone.

## Context
finwise's read-only backend already answers every other read: the frame, the accounts, the transactions, the card, the pots, net worth, the home summary, the budget, the subscriptions, the weekly review and payday. Its HTTP package (`internal/api`) has handlers registered per contract method, a money type that encodes integer cents as an exact decimal, a conformance test that validates every answer against the method's schema in `internal/contract/contract.json` over two fixture ledgers, golden files, the choice of the card in use, each pot with the bucket its bank declares, and a test-side list of reads still without a handler. The backend has no database of its own: the part of the app that stores what the person authors has no reviewed plan yet, so what only that part will know comes back as on a fresh install. The contract is already nullable where a fresh install has no honest value, and the stand-in's fresh-install state in `web/src/api/fake/first-run-data.ts` shows what these two methods answer on a first day.

| method | answer |
| --- | --- |
| `review.closing` | the month, not closed, pending count 0, the card's real bill or `null`, the closing steps all not done, every list empty |
| `settings.overview` | the card's title, the default label, the default categorisation thresholds, the bank's closing day, the last synchronisation, no backup, the real connections, the real pots each in the bucket the pots answer already gives it and with no linked line, no establishments, no people |

**The closing steps.** `review.closing` lists the steps of closing a month. On a fresh install each exists and none is done: the list is the full set of `ClosingStepId` values in `web/src/api/contract/review-closing.ts`, in the order the stand-in gives them, not an empty array.

**The card and the pots are already chosen.** Which card account is "the card", its bill and its closing day, and each pot with its bucket, are worked out by the handlers of the card and the pots. Call what they use; do not choose a card or a bucket a second time.

**Defaults.** The categorisation threshold, the minimum of examples and the manual closing day have no decided default. Take the values the stand-in starts with in `web/src/api/fake/`, keep them in one place in Go, and list them in the report so the user can change them. The suggested threshold has no data behind it on a fresh install and is the contract's empty value.

**Money, messages, privacy.** As everywhere in this package: cents in, an exact decimal out; any string the person reads is Brazilian Portuguese and lives in the one messages file; no value from a real ledger is printed, logged or committed.

**What the first reads left in place.** `internal/api/bank.go` has `bankLabels(accounts)`, the one place that says which bank an account belongs to. `nowOf(ctx)` gives the injected clock in Brazil time. The conformance test validates the answer of every registered read handler over both fixture ledgers, and the golden test records them, once it knows the argument sets of a new method. `fixtures_test.go` builds the two fixture ledgers: extend them instead of building a third. Golden files are named as the README in `internal/api/testdata/golden/` says. `shell.overview` already reports the sync state. The opt-in test over a real ledger walks every registered handler and logs counts only.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Both methods answer 200 with a valid session and their answers validate against their result schemas over both fixture ledgers.
- [ ] `review.closing` lists every `ClosingStepId` exactly once, none done; a test fails when the contract gains a step the handler does not list.
- [ ] `review.closing` reports the same bill for the card as `card.overview` does over the fixture, and `null` over a ledger with no card.
- [ ] `settings.overview` reports the fixture's last complete run as the last synchronisation, one connection per fixture item, each fixture pot with the same bucket `savingsPots.list` gives it, and no backup.
- [ ] The defaults are defined once and a test reads them from that place.
- [ ] The list of reads without a handler is empty and removed, and the test that every `read` in the manifest has a handler stays.
- [ ] The opt-in test over a real snapshot validates every answer and logs counts only.
- [ ] `go.mod` gains no direct dependency.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and a POST to every `read` route of the manifest answers 200 or a contract-valid `null` over both fixture ledgers.

## Tests
- Conformance: every answer against the manifest's schema, over both fixture ledgers.
- Golden: every answer against its file.
- Unit: the closing steps against the contract's list; the defaults.
- Integration with `httptest`: every `read` route of the manifest through the router with a session.
- Integration, opt-in: a real snapshot, counts only.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/api/`
**Reads only:** `internal/contract/contract.json`, `internal/ledger/`, `web/src/api/contract/`, `web/src/api/fake/`, `bin/ci`

New handler and test files in the HTTP package with their golden files, and the removal of the pending list. Existing handlers are called, not changed.
close_reason: The backend answers review.closing and settings.overview, and with them every read of the contract has a handler; the list of reads waiting for one is removed and a test still requires every read of the manifest to have a handler. The closing lists every step of the contract once, shows the card's real next-bill amount or null, and the budget's groups at zero; the settings show the card in use, the bank's closing day, the last complete synchronisation, the connections, each open pot with the bucket the pots list gives it, and the stand-in's defaults, defined once. Both probe the ledger first. bin/ci: CI green. Over a real snapshot every answer validated. Departures from the bead's table, following the stand-in: the pending step is done when nothing waits, and the planned-against-actual list shows the budget's groups; the closing's report is empty, where the stand-in's fresh install still carries prototype sentences.

title: Store the budget by month in the app's database, with stable line ids, saved scenarios and the line menu of each month
description:
## What changes for the user
Today the app keeps no budget: the budget screen opens on five empty groups, the list of scenarios is
always empty, "Salvar" answers that the app is read-only, and no menu anywhere offers a line to put a
transaction on. This work is the server keeping a budget: one that holds from the month it was saved
for, while a closed month keeps the budget it had; scenarios kept under a name; and every menu of lines
offering the lines of the budget of the month it is asked about, with "Tarifas e juros" among them once
that budget has any line. On its own it is not yet something the person can do from the budget screen,
because the screen still cannot work out its figures for a budget that is being edited and ends the edit;
that arrives with the budget's arithmetic. What the person would notice if this were wrong, later and not
at the moment it went wrong: a line they renamed losing everything that was spent on it, a month they
closed showing a budget they wrote afterwards, a budget that is gone after a restart, or a menu offering
a line the transaction's month never had.

## Outcome
Migration `0002_budget` adds the budget's tables to the app's database: line ids with the built-in fees
line seeded, budget versions and their lines, saved scenarios, and closed months. `budget.save`,
`budget.applyScenario` and `budget.saveScenario` have handlers: each validates its document, refuses a
closed month where it has a month, mints an id for every new line when a budget is saved or applied,
writes the versions the month rule asks for, and is one recorded change that `changes.undo` takes back.
`budget.document`, `budget.scenarios` and the line menu of `transactions.filterOptions(month)` answer from
that database, with names owned by each budget version; on a server without the database they answer
exactly what they answer today. `budget.view`, `budget.establishments` and `budget.evaluateScenario` are
not touched.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is a SQLite snapshot that a
separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app only reads it. *The app's database* is
`finwise.db`, owned by the Go package `internal/authored`, where everything the person authors is kept;
the server has one only when started with `--db`. *The stand-in* is the in-memory fake backend under
`web/src/api/fake/` that the design prototype runs on; it is the only existing statement of how writes
behave, so where this text says "as the stand-in does" the file named is the reference. *The contract*
is the TypeScript interface `FinwiseApi` (`web/src/api/contract/`); *the manifest* is
`internal/contract/contract.json`, generated from it, with a schema for every method's arguments and
result. *A budget document* (`BudgetDoc`) is a list of groups, each with a key, a name and its lines; a
line has a name, an amount and an optional `flag` (a marker such as "Não garantida"). The five editable
groups are `rec` (income), `fix`, `var`, `prov` (provisions) and `res` (reserves). *A version* is a
budget document valid from a month on. *A closed month* is one the person closed in the monthly review;
its budget no longer changes. *The line menu* is the list `lines` of `transactions.filterOptions`, each
entry a name and its group's name, from which every menu that puts something on a line is drawn. *The
fees line* is the built-in line "Tarifas e juros": it belongs to no group and no document. *The current
month* is the Brazil month of the instant in the request's context (`brday.MonthOf(nowOf(ctx))`), never
the host's clock. *The recorder* is the layer of `internal/authored` through which every change to the
app's database is written; *the journal* is what it writes (one row per change, one per effect); *undo*
is the inverse of a change's recorded effects. *A golden file* is the committed, exact answer of one call
over an invented fixture. *The gate* is `bin/ci`, the exact checks CI runs.

**What the code is today** (each point read in the file named).

- `internal/api/budget.go`: `registerBudget` registers four reads. `readBudgetDocument` parses its month
  with `onlyMonthArgument` (`fresh_install.go`), calls `requireReadableLedger` and answers
  `emptyBudgetDocument()`: the five groups with no lines. `readBudgetScenarios` answers `[]` after the same
  ledger check. `readBudgetView` answers a fresh install's figures and refuses any draft with `read_only`;
  `readBudgetEstablishments` answers `[]`. This work replaces the first two and leaves the last two
  exactly as they are.
- `internal/api/budget_view.go`: `editableGroupNames` is the fixed order and the names of the five
  groups: `rec` "Receita", `fix` "Fixos e essenciais", `var` "Variáveis", `prov` "Provisões", `res`
  "Reservas de desejo". The names are constants of `internal/api/messages.go`, the one file that holds
  what the server writes for a person to read; `budgetGroupFees` there is "Tarifas e juros".
- `internal/api/transactions.go`: `readTransactionFilterOptions` answers every account, `tags: []` and
  `lines: []`; `budgetLineOption` (`name`, `group`) already exists.
- Tests that pin today's answers and must keep passing unchanged on a server without the app's database:
  `TestTheBudgetAnswersAsAFreshInstallOverBothLedgers` and `TestTheBudgetViewRefusesAnyDraftAsAWriteIsRefused`
  (`internal/api/budget_test.go`, the second also expects `budget.save` to answer `read_only`), the golden
  files under `internal/api/testdata/golden/full/` and `empty/`, and
  `TestEveryReadAnswersLedgerUnavailableForAFileThatIsNotADatabase` (`unreadable_snapshot_test.go`), which
  requires every read case, the budget's included, to answer `ledger_unavailable` over a snapshot that
  cannot be read. `web/src/test/empty-ledger.test.ts` compares the files of `empty/` with the stand-in
  over an empty ledger and finds its calls by scanning the Go test sources for the written shape
  ``readCase{"domain.method", `[...]`}``.
- The stand-in: `web/src/api/fake/budget.ts` (the methods; `UNNAMED_SCENARIO` is "Cenário sem nome"),
  `budget-versions.ts` (`budgetFor`, `saveFrom`, `assertOpen`, `cleanDraft`), `transactions.ts`
  (`lineOptions`, `LINE_MENU_ORDER`, `FEES_LINE`), `first-run-data.ts` (`EMPTY_BUDGET`, the five empty
  groups a fresh install has), and the tests `budget.test.ts` (the groups "versioning by month" and
  "scenarios"), `transactions.test.ts` and `first-run-line-menu.test.ts`. It validates nothing: `cleanDraft`
  only turns an amount that is not a finite number into zero and drops an empty flag. It joins everything
  by a line's name.
- The interface: in edit mode `web/src/screens/budget/BudgetScreen.vue` asks `budget.view(month, draft)`
  after every change of the draft and discards the edit when that answers `read_only`; the scenarios
  screen leaves when `budget.evaluateScenario` does. Both still answer `read_only` after this work, so
  the save cannot yet be reached from the browser; it is reached over HTTP and by the tests.
- `internal/brday` has `Month`, `ParseMonth`, `MonthOf` and `MonthPeriod`, and no "month after";
  `internal/api/net_worth_chart.go` has a private `nextMonth`.

**What earlier work provides.** None of the following is in the repository when this text is written;
each is delivered before this bead starts, and its interfaces are to be read in the code as that work
left them.

- The app's database ({{F1}}): `internal/authored` recognises, opens and migrates `finwise.db`. A
  migration is an SQL file embedded from `internal/authored/migrations/`, recorded by name and checksum in
  `schema_migrations` once applied; at start every file not recorded is applied in name order, each in one
  transaction, after a copy of a database that already holds data is taken beside it. A recorded name
  whose checksum differs from the embedded file is refused at start. Every SQL statement over the
  database is a registered constant: one test prepares each against the migrated schema and another fails
  on a statement that is not registered.
- The recorder ({{F2}}): it works from a closed, hand-written registry of the journaled tables. Each
  entry says which of two shapes the table has. An *attribute table* holds one row of independent facts
  per key, and an effect is one column changing. A *set table* holds rows that are facts by existing, and
  an effect is one row appearing or disappearing. A table that is in neither the registry nor the named
  list of tables deliberately not journaled fails a test, and so does a statement that inserts, updates or
  deletes in an authored table outside the recorder. `lines` is on that named list already: an id, once
  minted, exists for good.
- The views ({{F3b}}): a handler's third parameter is one value carrying a view of each store, opened
  for the request. The authored view is one read-only transaction, so an answer is wholly before or wholly
  after a concurrent write; on a server without `--db` it is an empty view that answers "nothing
  authored", so read code has one path. Each slice adds to that view the reads of the tables it owns.
- The `refused` kind ({{F4a}}): an error envelope `{"error":{"kind":"refused","reason":"<reason>"}}`,
  HTTP 409, with a reason from a closed list; the sentences a person reads stay in the interface.
- Money in ({{F4b}}): `ParseReais` turns a JSON number into integer cents from its decimal text, with no
  float, rounding half away from zero beyond two places and refusing anything that is not a finite number
  within one billion reais; `Reais` decodes through it.
- Write dispatch ({{F4c}}): a write that has a registered handler, on a server with the app's database,
  has its arguments validated against the method's schema in the manifest, then runs inside one immediate
  transaction with a recorder that holds one open change (author `person`, the method's qualified name,
  the instant and the Brazil day); the dispatcher commits, and any failure rolls everything back. Without
  the database, or without a handler, the method answers `read_only` before its body is read. A test walks
  the manifest: every write has a handler or is named in an explicit list, `writesWithoutHandler`.
  `changes.undo` is the first handler.
- The write conformance harness ({{F5}}): every write has a case in its mode. For a recorded change: the
  answer validates against the manifest, its effects match a golden file under
  `internal/api/testdata/golden/writes/`, and undoing it returns a canonical dump of every journaled table
  to the dump taken before. One refusal case is owed per reason, and the reasons that have no producer yet
  are named in a list in a test file. `internal/authored/authoredtest` builds invented states of the app's
  database, one builder per group of tables, added by the slice that owns the tables. Read conformance has
  a third state, the full invented ledger with an invented authored state, in
  `internal/api/testdata/golden/full-authored/`, whose cases are a list of their own (`authoredReadCases`)
  with a type and constructor of their own, precisely so that the interface's equality test does not find
  them. The test that proves no handler logs what it reads runs every write case.
- The contract change ({{B1}}): `BudgetLineDoc` carries an optional `id`, and
  `transactions.filterOptions` takes the month it is asked for; the Go handler already reads that month
