wrapper that opens a view for that one call, so no file outside `internal/ledger` changes and every
existing test passes untouched.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is a SQLite file,
`pluggy-snapshot.db`, that a separate collector (pluggy-sync) fills from the banks every night and
replaces by an atomic rename; the app only reads it, and "the snapshot" below is that file. *The
reader* is `ledger.Reader`, the type through which the HTTP backend (`internal/api`) and the tests of
the rule packages ask the snapshot for accounts, transactions, bills, pots and so on. A *read handler*
is the function of `internal/api` that answers one method of the API.

**What the code is today (each point checked in the file named).**

- `internal/ledger/open.go`: a `Reader` holds only a path and `New` does not touch the file. Every
  public query goes through `read`, which opens a fresh handle with `openReadOnly` (it stats the file,
  opens it with `mode=ro`, `query_only(1)` and `busy_timeout(5000)` in the DSN, one connection), begins
  one read-only transaction, checks `PRAGMA user_version` with `requireSupportedVersion`, runs one
  function, passes its error through `asUnreadable` and closes. The package comment says why: the
  snapshot is replaced by an atomic rename and nothing promises what an open handle sees across the
  swap, so every call opens the file, runs and closes.
- There are 13 public query methods on `*Reader`, in 11 files: `Accounts` (`accounts.go`), `Bills`
  (`bills.go`), `BalanceHistory` and `ReserveHistory` (`history.go`), `Identities` (`identities.go`),
  `InvestmentPrincipals` (`investment_principal.go`), `Investments` and `InvestmentHistory`
  (`investments.go`), `Pots` (`pots.go`), `PotYields` (`pot_yield.go`), `SyncState` (`sync.go`),
  `CleanTransactions` (`transactions.go`), `YieldHistory` (`yield_history.go`). Each runs its
  statements inside the function it hands to `read`, which receives the `*sql.Tx` (`Accounts`, for
  example, calls `queryAccountRows(ctx, tx)` there).
- A read handler makes several of those calls, so it opens the snapshot several times and can see two
  snapshots across the swap: `readShellOverview` (`internal/api/shell.go`) calls `Accounts`,
  `SyncState` and `CleanTransactions`.
- The typed errors: a missing file is `fs.ErrNotExist` wrapped by `openReadOnly`; another schema
  version is `UnsupportedVersionError`; a file SQLite cannot read as a database, or a damaged one, is
  `UnreadableSnapshotError`. `internal/api/errors.go` answers all three as `ledger_unavailable`.
- Every SQL statement over the snapshot is a registered constant of `queries.go`, and
  `TestEveryQueryPreparesAgainstTheCollectorsSchema` (`schema_test.go`) prepares each against the
  collector's schema.
- `internal/ledger/safety_test.go` pins the package's promises: every query refuses an unsupported
  version; the open path refuses writes; `TestQueriesLeaveTheSnapshotByteForByteUntouched` (the file's
  hash and its directory's listing are the same after every query);
  `TestEachCallSeesTheFileThatIsThereNow` (a call after a rename sees the new file); a missing file is
  an error; a file that is not a database, or a damaged one, is unreadable. `everyQuery` in
  `support_test.go` walks 12 of the 13 queries; `PotYields` has its own tests in `pot_yield_test.go`.
- Who holds the reader: 21 source files of `internal/api` that call its methods or pass it on,
  `cmd/finwise/serve.go` (which only builds it), and test files of `internal/ledger`, `internal/api`,
  `internal/cardrules`, `internal/potrules` and `internal/txrules`.
- `internal/api/pots_yield_guard_test.go` scans every non-test file under `internal/` and `cmd/` for
  the identifier `PotYields` (the collector's slow reference statement, which no request may reach)
  and exempts only `internal/ledger/pot_yield.go` and `queries.go`, by path.

**What changes.**

1. *The view.* The package gains a view of the snapshot: one handle and one read-only transaction, the
   version checked once, kept for as long as the view is open and released when it is closed. Every
   one of the 13 queries can run on it. Every query made through one view sees the same snapshot even
   when the collector renames a new file over the path meanwhile; a view opened after the rename sees
   the new file. The open path stays read-only twice over (`mode=ro` and `query_only`), the statements
   stay the registered constants of `queries.go`, and each query's error still passes through
   `asUnreadable`.
2. *The reader's methods stay, as wrappers.* Each of the reader's 13 methods becomes a wrapper that
   opens a view, runs that one query on it and closes it: exactly what a call does today. Twelve of
   them are gathered in one new file, so that the slice that removes them later deletes one file. The
   thirteenth, the reader's `PotYields`, stays in `pot_yield.go` beside the view's own, because the
   guard described above fails on that name in any other file. For the same reason nothing outside
   `pot_yield.go` may name `PotYields`, an interface that lists the view's methods included.
3. *Nothing outside the package changes.* No file of `internal/api`, of the rule packages or of
   `cmd/finwise` is edited, and no existing test file of `internal/ledger` is edited: they all keep
   calling the reader and keep passing, `TestEachCallSeesTheFileThatIsThereNow` among them, because a
   wrapper still opens the file that is there now. The view's own promises are proved in a new test
   file.

**Who uses the view next, so the design can be checked against real use.** The slice after this one
({{F3b}}: every read handler receives a view of each store, opened for its request, and the reader's
wrappers are removed) hands one ledger view to each request and closes it when the request ends,
whether it answered, failed or panicked. Two things it needs constrain this slice. A request that never
asks the ledger anything must not fail because the snapshot is missing, so it must be possible to hold
a view that has not touched the file yet, or to open one only when first needed; whether that lives in
the view (opened at its first query) or in its caller is the implementer's, as long as all the queries
of one view see one snapshot. And the errors of a view are the same typed errors as today, returned by
whichever call first touches the file, so the API's answers do not change. Later the job that brings a
new snapshot into the app's own database reads the run that produced the rows and the rows themselves
through one view, for the same reason.

**Left to the implementer.** The names of the view type, of what opens it and of the wrapper file.

**Why it is done this way, and what lost.** Ledger rows are handed out as rows, never as a connection,
and the snapshot is swapped under the reader; what a request needs is one snapshot for all its queries.
A fresh handle per query, which is what the code does today, lost: it is exactly what lets one answer
mix two snapshots. Changing the reader and every caller in one step also lost, to this slice and the
next: the callers are some sixty files in five packages, and a view that lands first, with the old
methods still answering, can be proved on its own with no caller touched.

**The failure path this slice prepares.** The snapshot is swapped during a request: the request
finishes on the snapshot it opened, and the next one sees the new one. Here it is proved for a view;
the next slice makes it true for a request.

**Privacy.** The repository is public and a real ledger is a person's whole financial history. Nothing
in this slice needs a real ledger and the opt-in test that reads one
(`internal/ledger/realsnapshot_test.go`) is not edited. The rule stands all the same: a real snapshot
may be opened read-only; no value from it (amount, description, name, document, id) is ever printed,
logged, copied into a file, a commit, a bead or a pull request; a count may be shown to the person
running the test and goes into no file; such a test runs only when `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` names a
file. Fixtures are invented (`internal/ledger/ledgertest`), and no `.db` file is opened by hand.

**Conventions.** Work happens in a git worktree of its own and ends at local commits: atomic,
Conventional Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a plan in a commit
message. Money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path; this slice changes how rows
are fetched, not how an amount is decoded. Every SQL statement over the snapshot stays a registered
constant, as every statement over the app's own database must be. Interface text is Brazilian
Portuguese and everything else is English; a design value in a component comes from a token (this slice
touches no component).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] On one view over the `populated` fixture, each of the 13 queries returns what the reader's method
of the same name returns.
- [ ] A view answers `Accounts`; a second invented snapshot holding a different account is renamed over
the path; the same view then answers `Accounts` and `CleanTransactions` from the first snapshot; a view
opened after the rename answers from the second.
- [ ] A view kept open across all 13 queries leaves the file's hash and its directory's listing as they
were: no `-journal`, `-wal` or `-shm` file appears.
- [ ] Through a view, a snapshot with `user_version` 2 is `UnsupportedVersionError`, a file that is not
a database and a damaged database are `UnreadableSnapshotError`, and a missing file satisfies
`errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist)`; none of them yields a row.
- [ ] A query on a closed view is an error, not a fresh open of the file.
- [ ] `git diff --stat main -- . ':(exclude)internal/ledger'` is empty, and among the test files of
`internal/ledger` the diff against `main` shows only added files.
- [ ] `git diff main -- internal/ledger/queries.go` is empty and
`TestEveryQueryPreparesAgainstTheCollectorsSchema` passes.
- [ ] Both `PotYields` methods are in `internal/ledger/pot_yield.go`, and
`go test ./internal/api -run TestNoReadHandlerReachesTheCollectorsYieldStatement` passes.
- [ ] `go test ./...` passes with no test edited, the golden comparison of `internal/api`
(`TestEveryAnswerMatchesItsGoldenFile`) included, without `-update`.
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, each against its own deliberate break, named in the final
report: the swap test against a view that reopens the file for each query; the closed-view test against
a view that reopens after it was closed; the untouched-file test against a handle opened without
`mode=ro`; the parity test against one query left running on a handle of its own.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, a snapshot swap between two queries on one view is not
seen in a test that was seen failing, and no file outside `internal/ledger` differs from `main`.

## Tests
- Unit, over two invented snapshots built with `ledgertest` (`ledgertest.NewAt` at a second path and
  `os.Rename`, as `TestEachCallSeesTheFileThatIsThereNow` builds them): a view keeps its snapshot
  across the swap for every later query; a new view sees the new file.
- Unit, over the `populated` fixture of `support_test.go`: the 13 queries on one view against the
  reader's 13 methods; the file and its directory untouched after a long-lived view.
- Unit, over the same fixture with its version changed (`SetUserVersion`), over a text file and over a
  database with its pages overwritten (as `TestADamagedDatabaseIsUnreadableToo` builds one), and over a
  missing path: the view's typed errors.
- Unit: a query on a closed view.
- The existing tests of `internal/ledger`, `internal/api` and the rule packages, unedited, as the proof
  that the wrappers answer as the methods did; golden, the 59 files of each of
  `internal/api/testdata/golden/full/` and `empty/`, unchanged.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/ledger/open.go`, `internal/ledger/accounts.go`, `internal/ledger/bills.go`,
`internal/ledger/history.go`, `internal/ledger/identities.go`, `internal/ledger/investment_principal.go`,
`internal/ledger/investments.go`, `internal/ledger/pots.go`, `internal/ledger/pot_yield.go`,
`internal/ledger/sync.go`, `internal/ledger/transactions.go`, `internal/ledger/yield_history.go`
**Reads only:** `internal/ledger/queries.go`, `internal/ledger/schema_test.go`,
`internal/ledger/safety_test.go`, `internal/ledger/support_test.go`, `internal/ledger/ledgertest/`,
`internal/api/`, `internal/cardrules/`, `internal/potrules/`, `internal/txrules/`,
`cmd/finwise/serve.go`, `bin/ci`

One package: `open.go` and the 11 files that hold the 13 queries change, and three files are new (the
view, the reader's twelve wrappers, the view's tests). It is labelled large for the count of files, not
for the reach: nothing outside `internal/ledger` is edited, no existing test is edited, and the
statements of `queries.go` are not touched. The callers in `internal/api`, the rule packages and
`cmd/finwise` are read only to confirm they still compile and pass.

title: Show a pot's day with an unknown yield as unknown
description:
## What changes for the user
A savings pot's month opens into the days behind its yield. When the bank's records cannot support one of those days, the month's total rightly reads as unknown, but the day itself is simply missing from the list, so nothing on screen says which day broke the month. After this lands that day is listed with a dash.

## Outcome
A pot's daily yield row can carry an unknown amount in the contract, the backend answers such a day instead of leaving it out, and the pot's page shows a dash for it.

## Context
finwise's interface reaches its backend through a TypeScript contract (`web/src/api/contract/`), described for Go by a generated manifest the gate keeps current (`npm --prefix web run contract`). The convention in `AGENTS.md`: a field the ledger cannot always answer is nullable in the contract and a screen shows its absence as a dash; a zero is for a figure that is truly zero.

The backend computes a pot's yield per pair of nightly sightings (`internal/potrules`), and a pair it cannot support gets a row whose yield is unknown, with a reason. `savingsPots.detail` puts the known rows in `yield.days`. The contract's `PotYieldDay.amount` is a required number, so the handler in `internal/api/pots_detail.go` leaves an unknown row out, and the month's total is `null`.

No pair on the real ledger examined so far was unknown, so the case is not on screen today.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] In the contract, `PotYieldDay.amount` is nullable and the manifest is regenerated.
- [ ] Over a fixture pot whose month has a day the rules cannot support, `savingsPots.detail` lists that day with a `null` amount, in order among the others, and the month's total is `null`.
- [ ] The pot's page shows a dash for that day and no "R$ 0,00"; a test mounts it over the stand-in with such a day.
- [ ] Over the prototype dataset nothing changes: `npm --prefix web run parity` still reports every state at or under 0.05%.
- [ ] The backend's golden files for the pot detail are re-recorded from the fixture ledgers and its answers still validate against the schema.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, parity is unchanged, and an unknown day shows a dash.

## Tests
- Unit: the handler over a month with an unknown day.
- Component: the pot's page over the stand-in with an unknown day.
- Conformance: the stand-in's and the backend's pot answers against the regenerated schema.
- Golden: the pot detail's answers.
- Parity: the full run, unchanged.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `web/src/api/contract/savings-pots.ts`, `web/src/screens/cofrinhos/`, `web/src/api/fake/savings-rules.ts`, `web/src/test/`, `internal/contract/contract.json`, `internal/api/pots_detail.go`, `internal/api/pots_test.go`, `internal/api/testdata/golden/`
**Reads only:** `internal/potrules/`, `web/src/lib/format.ts`, `AGENTS.md`, `bin/ci`

One field of one contract type becomes nullable, one screen and one handler follow, and the generated manifest and the pot detail's golden files are refreshed.
close_reason: PotYieldDay.amount is nullable in the contract and the manifest is regenerated. The pot detail handler lists a day whose yield is unknown, in order, with a null amount, and the month's total is null; a day with a deposit and no yield stays a known zero. The pot's page shows a dash for such a day and for the total; the stand-in can carry an unknown day and its answers validate against the schema as a new state. bin/ci: CI green on the tree merged with main, 940 tests. Parity: 174 checked, 0 over 0.05%. No golden file changed: neither recorded ledger holds an unknown day, so the case is covered by the handler's test.

title: Answer each request from one snapshot of the ledger and one of the app's database, and require the clock
description:
## What changes for the user
The app builds a screen by asking the bank's records several questions, one after another, and a separate
collector replaces those records every night. A screen opened at the moment of the replacement can be put
together half from yesterday's records and half from today's: a total that does not match the rows under
it, with nothing on screen saying so. After this lands a screen is always built from one state of the
records, the one that was there when it was asked for, and the next screen sees the new one. Nothing else
changes: every figure and every sentence the app shows today stays the same. It is also the ground the
rest of the work on saving stands on, because once the app keeps what the person types (a budget, a
category, a note) each screen has to show the bank's records and the person's own entries as they were at
one same moment. If this were wrong the person would see, for one refresh around the nightly update or
while another tab is saving, a figure that disagrees with its own breakdown, or a screen that fails to
open.

## Outcome
Every read handler of the HTTP backend receives, as its third parameter, one value that carries a view of
each store, opened for that request: the ledger's view (one handle and one read-only transaction on the
snapshot) and a view of the app's own database that is one read-only transaction, or an empty view that
answers nothing when the server runs without that database. No file of `internal/api` or of `cmd/finwise`
calls a query method of the reader any more, tests included: the queries are reached through the view. The
reader's own wrappers stay in place after this slice; removing them, and moving the tests of
`internal/ledger`, `internal/cardrules`, `internal/potrules` and `internal/txrules` onto the view, is the next
piece of work (finwise-qet: it deletes the reader's thirteen query methods, which only tests still call, and
makes those four packages' tests open a view instead). The clock is a required part of the API's configuration, supplied by
`cmd/finwise` alone; asking for "now" without one panics, and a source test keeps `time.Now` out of the
HTTP layer and of the packages that hold rules. No answer changes: every golden file is byte for byte
what it was.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is a SQLite file,
`pluggy-snapshot.db`, that a separate collector (pluggy-sync) fills from the banks every night and
replaces by an atomic rename; the app only reads it, and "the snapshot" below is that file. *The ledger's
view* is delivered by finwise-gn5: a type of `internal/ledger` that is one handle and one read-only
transaction on the snapshot, on which each of the 13 query methods can run, so that all the queries made
through one view see one snapshot; that slice kept the reader's own 13 methods as wrappers that open a
view per call, twelve of them in one file of their own and `PotYields` in `pot_yield.go`. *The app's
database* is `finwise.db`, a second SQLite file that will hold what the person authors; unlike the
snapshot nobody swaps it, so it is opened once and kept open for the life of the process. It is owned by
the package `internal/authored`, delivered by finwise-9h2 (recognising the file, opening it with its
connection settings, the migrations table and runner, the first migration with the tables of the journal
that will record every change, the tracking start month, which is the month the database was first
created in and is kept as one value of the table `meta`, the registry of SQL statements, and the `--db`
/ `FINWISE_DB` setting of `finwise serve`). Without `--db` the server is today's read-only server. *The
manifest* is `internal/contract/contract.json`, the generated description of the 82 methods of the API,
of which 23 are of class `read`. A *read handler* is the Go function that answers one read method. The
*golden files* under `internal/api/testdata/golden/full/` and `empty/` (59 files each) are the exact
answers of every read over two invented ledgers, compared byte for byte by
`TestEveryAnswerMatchesItsGoldenFile`.

**What the code is today (each point checked in the file named; the ledger's view is the one thing
described from the slice that delivers it).**

- `internal/api/reads.go`: `ReadHandler` is `func(ctx context.Context, args []json.RawMessage, reader
  *ledger.Reader) (any, error)`. `Registry.Register` panics on a duplicate. `domainRegistrations` lists
  twelve `register<Domain>` functions that together make 23 registrations (22 functions:
  `subscriptions.candidates` and `subscriptions.recurring` share `readNothingListed`).
- `internal/api/router.go`: `serveRead` calls `handler(withNow(r.Context(), found.now), arguments,
  found.reader)`. `Config.Ledger` is a `*ledger.Reader`; `Config` has no field for the app's database.
  `withDefaults` sets `config.Now = time.Now` when the `Config` has none.
- A handler makes several calls to the reader, each of which opens the snapshot anew, so it can see two
  snapshots across the swap. `readShellOverview` (`shell.go`) calls `Accounts`, `SyncState` and
  `CleanTransactions`; `readSettingsOverview` (`settings.go`) calls `loadCard`, `loadPots` and
  `SyncState`. A handler that answers a fixed value still asks the ledger one question first,
  `requireReadableLedger` in `fresh_install.go`, so that it never answers over a snapshot that is gone.
  A handler that takes arguments checks them before its first ledger call.
- `internal/api/now.go`: `withNow` puts the clock function in the context and `nowOf` calls it; when the
  context has none, `nowOf` returns `time.Now()`. `nowOf` is called in `accounts.go`, `shell.go`,
  `card.go`, `pots_model.go` and `settings.go`. `cmd/finwise/serve.go` builds its `api.Config` without a
  clock, so the server's clock today is the default in `withDefaults`.
- `internal/api/errors.go`: `kindOfReadError` answers `ledger_unavailable` for a missing file
  (`fs.ErrNotExist`), an unreadable one (`fs.ErrPermission`, `ledger.IsUnreadableSnapshot`) and an
  unsupported version; anything else is `internal`. `internal/api/logging.go` recovers a handler's panic
  and answers `internal`.
- The reader's methods are called, outside `internal/api`, only by tests: 8 test files of
  `internal/ledger`, and `internal/cardrules/forecast_test.go`, `internal/cardrules/realsnapshot_test.go`,
  `internal/potrules/realsnapshot_test.go` and `internal/txrules/realsnapshot_test.go`.

**What changes.**

1. *One value per request.* The third parameter of a handler becomes one value carrying a view of each
   store, opened for the request. The router builds it for each read and closes it when the handler has
   returned, on every path: an answer, an error, a panic. Every ledger query of the request runs on the
   request's one ledger view, so it sees the same snapshot even when the collector swaps the file
   meanwhile.
2. *The authored view.* For the app's database a handler never holds the connection pool. The router
   opens one read-only transaction per read (and, once evaluations are dispatched, per evaluation) and
   hands the handler a view of it, so an answer is wholly before or wholly after a concurrent write. A
   write handler will instead receive the recorder, the layer through which every change to the app's
   database is written and journaled (finwise-wi4); wiring that in is the write dispatch (finwise-2s5: the router
   running a handler for a write inside one transaction and one recorded change), not this slice.
   Without `--db` the authored view is an empty one that answers nothing, so read code has one path: no
   handler ever asks whether a database is configured. This is the standing rule for every read method a
   later slice adds to the view: on the empty view it answers "nothing authored", the contract's empty
   value. `Config` gains the app's database and `cmd/finwise/serve.go` passes the one it opened.
3. *The signature change.* All 23 registrations change signature in one commit that lands alone.
4. *The reader's wrappers stay.* With no handler left on the reader, its 13 wrappers have no caller in
   `internal/api` or `cmd/finwise`; the tests of `internal/api` that called them (the opt-in real-ledger
   tests, `pots_yield_reference_test.go`, `review_payday_test.go` and the test helpers) open a view instead.
   The wrappers themselves are not touched here: the wrapper file, the reader's `PotYields` in
   `pot_yield.go` and the tests of the four packages outside `internal/api` that still call them are the
   next piece of work (finwise-qet), so no file of `internal/ledger`, `internal/cardrules`, `internal/potrules`
   or `internal/txrules` is edited by this slice.
5. *The clock.* "Today" and "the current month" are the Brazil day and month of the instant in the
   request's context. The clock is a required part of the API's configuration: building the handler
   without one fails at once, and only `cmd/finwise` supplies the host's clock. The router always
   installs it; `nowOf` without one panics instead of reading the host's clock; and a source test forbids
   `time.Now` in the non-test files of `internal/api`, `internal/ingest` and the rule packages
   `internal/budgetrules`, `internal/classrules` and `internal/subrules`.

**What is left to the implementer, and what constrains each choice.**

- *Names.* The per-request value and the authored view are named by the implementer. `Registry.Register`
  and `domainRegistrations` keep their names: the repository's `AGENTS.md` documents them.
- *When the snapshot is opened.* Whether the request's ledger view touches the file when the request
  starts or at the handler's first query is the implementer's. Three things constrain it. A request must
  see one snapshot for all its queries. A handler that asks the ledger nothing must not fail because the
  snapshot is missing: the write side needs this (undoing a change touches no snapshot, and a write
  answers `ledger_unavailable` only when the snapshot it needs is missing), and the router's own tests
  already run handlers on a `Config` with no ledger at all (`newTestEnv` in `helpers_test.go`,
  `withRead`, `returnsNothing`). And no existing answer may change: a missing or unreadable snapshot is
  still `ledger_unavailable` through `kindOfReadError`, and malformed arguments are still `bad_request`.
- *What the authored view can read.* The read methods of the authored view are added by the slices that
  own each group of tables. When this lands the only table with content is `meta`, so the view needs
  just enough to make its own proof observable: one read of a value another connection can change. The
  tracking start month is the natural one; which value it is stays the implementer's.
- *One instant or one clock per request.* Today the context carries the clock function and `nowOf` calls
  it on every use. Reading the clock once per request, so a request cannot see two days around midnight,
  is consistent with the rule in point 5 and is the implementer's to adopt. What is required is the
  failure at construction, the panic and the source test.
- *The packages that do not exist yet.* `internal/ingest` and the three rule packages are created by
  later slices. The source test must already name them, so each is covered from its first file without
  anyone editing the test. How a directory that is not there yet is treated is the implementer's, but a
  missing directory must not fail the gate and a present one must not be skipped. The three rule packages
  that exist (`internal/txrules`, `internal/cardrules`, `internal/potrules`) name no `time.Now` today and
  may be added to the list at no cost; that is allowed, not required.

**What follows from the code and is not optional.**

- The `time.Now` default in `withDefaults` (`router.go`) goes: the source test has no exemption inside
  `internal/api`. `NewHandler` returns an error for a `Config` with no clock, as it already does for one
  with no PIN verifier, and `cmd/finwise/serve.go` hands in the host's clock; if `cmd/finwise` already
  carries a clock of its own for creating the app's database, it is that same one.
  `TestAHandlerCannotBeRegisteredForAWrite` and `TestNewHandlerNeedsAPINVerifier` (`router_test.go`)
  build a `Config` without `Now`: give them a clock, or they will keep passing for the wrong reason.
- `PotYields`, the collector's slow reference statement, stays in `internal/ledger/pot_yield.go`, the
  reader's wrapper beside the view's method: `internal/api/pots_yield_guard_test.go` scans every package for
  that name and exempts that file and `queries.go` by path. This slice adds no other mention of it in a
  non-test file, and the tests of `internal/api` that read yields (`pots_yield_reference_test.go`, the
  opt-in `pots_yield_realsnapshot_test.go` and `pots_yield_months_realsnapshot_test.go`) are test files,
  which that scan does not read.
- The tests of `internal/ledger` (among them `TestEachCallSeesTheFileThatIsThereNow`, which is true only
  while the wrappers open the file on every call), of `internal/cardrules`, `internal/potrules` and
  `internal/txrules` are not edited here and keep passing, because the wrappers still answer as before.
- `TestAReadHandlerGetsTheContextTheArgumentsAndTheReader` (`router_test.go`) asserts the old third
  parameter and is rewritten to assert the new one. Every hand-written handler in `router_test.go`,
  `logging_test.go` and `helpers_test.go` changes signature with the rest.
- Test code that calls a helper directly (`loadPots`, `loadCard`, `loadContext`) must pass a context with
  a clock, as `card_test.go` and `net_worth_test.go` already do with `withNow`. The opt-in tests that
  read a real ledger are skipped in the gate, so a bare context there would panic only when someone runs
  them: check those by reading.
- `internal/api/handler_silence_test.go` allows only `logging.go` and `router.go` to name a logging
  package. Any new file of `internal/api` logs nothing.
- The per-request value and the handler signature carry no `net/http` type: a later command-line client
  is expected to call the handlers as plain functions, outside HTTP.
- The recorder (finwise-wi4) is being built in `internal/authored` at the same time as this slice. Keep this
  slice's additions to that package in a file of their own, so the two do not edit the same lines.

**Why it is done this way, and what lost.** Ledger rows and authored rows are joined in Go, by key,
inside one request that sees one snapshot of each store, because the reader hands out rows, never a
connection, and the snapshot is swapped under it. Three alternatives lost: attaching the snapshot to the
app's database connection with `ATTACH`; copying the ledger into `finwise.db`; and a fresh ledger handle
per query, which is what the handlers do today and is exactly what lets one answer mix two snapshots. The
app's database is not reopened per call because, unlike the snapshot, nobody swaps it.

**The failure path this slice owns.** The snapshot is swapped during a request: the request finishes on
the snapshot it opened, and the next one sees the new one. Its named proof: a request that pauses
between two ledger queries while the snapshot is swapped answers wholly from the first snapshot.

**Why the signature change is one commit.** The package compiles only when the handler type, the
registry, the router's call and every handler agree, and the proof of this slice is that no golden file
changes. A commit that holds only the mechanical change can be reviewed by that one property.

**Privacy.** The repository is public and a real ledger is a person's whole financial history. This slice
edits the plumbing of the opt-in tests of `internal/api` that read a real ledger (`realsnapshot_test.go`,
`realsnapshot_money_test.go`, `fresh_install_realsnapshot_test.go`, `pots_yield_realsnapshot_test.go` and
`pots_yield_months_realsnapshot_test.go`), so the rule applies in full: a real snapshot may be opened read-only; no value from it (amount, description, name, document,
id) is ever printed, logged, copied into a file, a commit, a bead or a pull request; a count may be shown
to the person running the test and goes into no file; those tests run only when
`FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` names a file. Fixtures are invented, and no `.db` file is opened by hand.

**Conventions.** Work happens in a git worktree of its own and ends at local commits: atomic,
Conventional Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a plan in a commit
message. Money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path. Every SQL statement over the
app's database is a registered constant, as every statement over the ledger already is. Interface text is
Brazilian Portuguese and everything else is English; a design value in a component comes from a token
(this slice touches no component).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The third parameter of every registered handler is the per-request value;
`command grep -l "ledger\.Reader" internal/api/*.go` lists, among non-test files, at most `router.go`
and the file that opens the views.
- [ ] Nothing in `internal/api` or `cmd/finwise`, test files included, calls a query method of the
reader: with the reader's wrappers temporarily removed in a scratch copy (the wrapper file moved aside and
the reader's `PotYields` deleted from `pot_yield.go`), `go vet ./internal/api/... ./cmd/...` still
compiles; the repository's own tree keeps the wrappers.
- [ ] HTTP level: a test handler that makes two ledger queries with a second invented snapshot renamed
over the path between them answers wholly from the first snapshot, and the next request answers from the
second.
- [ ] Authored level: a test handler that reads the app's database twice, with another connection
committing a change to what it reads between the two, gets the same value both times; the next request
gets the new value.
- [ ] With no app database configured the handler receives the empty authored view and every existing
test passes; no handler branches on whether a database is configured.
- [ ] `git diff --stat main -- internal/api/testdata` is empty, and `TestEveryAnswerMatchesItsGoldenFile`
passes without `-update`.
- [ ] A handler that asks the ledger nothing is answered normally when the snapshot file is missing; a
handler that asks it something is answered 503 `ledger_unavailable`, and
`TestEveryReadAnswersLedgerUnavailableForAFileThatIsNotADatabase` passes unchanged.
- [ ] After a request ends (answered, failed or panicked) the ledger handle it opened is closed and the
app database's connection is back in its pool: a test shows it for the three endings.
- [ ] The commit that changes the handler signature holds all 23 registrations, the handler type, the
router's call and the hand-written test handlers, and nothing that the package does not need to compile
and pass at that commit; `go build ./... && go test ./...` is green at that commit.
- [ ] `NewHandler` returns an error for a `Config` with no clock; `cmd/finwise/serve.go` passes the
host's clock and the app's database; `nowOf` on a context with no clock panics, and a test recovers the
panic.
- [ ] A source test fails for a `time.Now` in any non-test file of `internal/api`, `internal/ingest`,
`internal/budgetrules`, `internal/classrules` or `internal/subrules`, passes while four of those five
directories do not exist, and `command grep -rn "time\.Now" internal/api --include='*.go'` shows matches
only in `_test.go` files.
- [ ] `git diff --stat main -- internal/ledger internal/cardrules internal/potrules internal/txrules` is
empty, and `go test ./internal/ledger ./internal/cardrules ./internal/potrules ./internal/txrules` passes.
- [ ] `TestOnlyTheRequestLogWritesAnything`, `TestNoHandlerLogsWhatItReads` and
`TestNoReadHandlerReachesTheCollectorsYieldStatement` pass unchanged.
- [ ] The five opt-in real-ledger tests of `internal/api` compile, and are run once **by the review**, not
by the implementer, with `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` set, printing counts only.
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, each against its own deliberate break, named in the final
report: the HTTP swap test against a request value that opens a new ledger view for each query; the
authored test against a view that reads outside its transaction; the release test against a view that is
never closed; the construction test against the old default clock; the panic test against the old
fallback in `nowOf`; the source test against a `time.Now` planted in a scratch file of a covered
directory.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, no golden file differs from `main`, and the two proofs (a
snapshot swap inside one request, a commit to the app's database inside one request) each pass and were
each seen failing.

## Tests
- Integration with `httptest`, over two invented snapshots built with `ledgertest` (`ledgertest.NewAt`
  at a second path and `os.Rename`): a test handler registered through `withRead` has the snapshot
  swapped between its two queries; the next request sees the new file.
- Integration with `httptest`, over a scratch `finwise.db` in the test's temporary directory: a commit by
  another connection between two reads of one request is not seen.
- Integration: the three endings of a request (answer, error, panic) release both views.
- Integration: a handler that asks the ledger nothing, with the snapshot file missing.
- Golden: the existing 59 files of each of `full/` and `empty/`, unchanged.
- Unit: `NewHandler` refuses a `Config` without a clock; `nowOf` panics without one.
- Source test (Go AST or text, as `handler_silence_test.go` and `reais_test.go` already do): no
  `time.Now` in the non-test files of the five named directories, with a test of the test over a scratch
  directory.
- Existing tests of `internal/api` that called the reader's methods, moved to a view with no change of
  expectation; the tests of the other four packages are unedited and pass as the proof that the wrappers
  still answer.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/api/` (its source and test files that name the reader), one new file of
`internal/authored` (the read view and the empty view), `cmd/finwise/serve.go`
**Reads only:** `internal/ledger/` (`open.go`, `queries.go`, the wrapper file, `pot_yield.go`, its tests and
`ledgertest/`), `internal/cardrules/`, `internal/potrules/`, `internal/txrules/`,
`internal/api/testdata/golden/`, `internal/contract/contract.json`, `AGENTS.md`, `bin/ci`

In `internal/api`, 23 source files name `*ledger.Reader` today and all of them change: the 21 files that
hold the handlers and their helpers (`accounts.go`, `budget.go`, `budget_view.go`, `card.go`,
`fresh_install.go`, `home.go`, `net_worth.go`, `pots.go`, `pots_detail.go`, `pots_investments.go`,
`pots_model.go`, `pots_yield.go`, `review.go`, `review_closing.go`, `review_payday.go`, `settings.go`,
`shell.go`, `subscriptions.go`, `transaction_detail.go`, `transactions.go`, `transactions_period.go`),
plus `reads.go` and `router.go`; `now.go` changes for the clock. Fifteen test files of that package build
a reader or a handler by hand and change with them, and two or three new test files carry the proofs. In
`internal/authored` the read view and the empty view are new files, kept apart from the recorder's; no file
that package already has is edited. `internal/ledger` and the three rule packages are read and not edited:
the wrappers stay, and their removal is finwise-qet. That is about 45 files in three packages (`internal/api`,
`internal/authored`, `cmd/finwise`), almost all of them in `internal/api`; it is labelled large for that
count, and it cannot be divided further because the package does not compile half-changed and the handler
type, the clock and the router all edit `router.go`.

The change of the handler signature must land alone, in one commit and with no other slice in flight in
`internal/api`, for three reasons. The package does not compile unless the handler type, the registry,
the router's call and every one of the 23 registrations agree, so it cannot be spread over commits that
each build. Every later slice of the write side adds or edits handlers in these same 21 files, so any of
them open at the same time would conflict in every file it touches and would have to be redone against
the new signature. And the proof is that no golden file changes, which is only readable when the diff
holds nothing but the mechanical change.

The golden files, the manifest, the statements of `queries.go`, the reader's wrappers and the fixture
builders of `ledgertest` are read and not edited. `AGENTS.md` is not edited here.

title: Answer the budget, the subscriptions, the weekly review and payday as a fresh install
description:
## What changes for the user
Budget, subscriptions and the reviews are things the person builds inside the app, and the app cannot store anything yet. After this lands the Budget and Assinaturas screens, the weekly review and the payday review open against the real backend the way they would on the day the app is first installed: an empty budget, no subscriptions, nothing waiting for review, and the one figure the bank's records do support, the balance of the account the salary lands on, shown for real. Trying to edit a budget answers that the app is read-only for now.

## Outcome
The backend answers ten more read methods of the interface's contract: the four of `budget`, the four of `subscriptions`, `review.weekly` and `review.payday`.

## Context
finwise's read-only backend already answers the frame, the accounts and the transactions from the ledger. Its HTTP package (`internal/api`) has handlers registered per contract method, a money type that encodes integer cents as an exact decimal, a conformance test that validates every answer against the method's schema in `internal/contract/contract.json` over two fixture ledgers, golden files, and a test-side list of reads still without a handler. The backend has no database of its own: the part of the app that stores what the person authors has no reviewed plan yet, so what only that part will know comes back as on a fresh install. The contract is already nullable where a fresh install has no honest value, and the stand-in's fresh-install state in `web/src/api/fake/first-run-data.ts` shows what each of these methods answers on a first day.

| method | answer |
| --- | --- |
| `budget.document` | the budget's authored groups, each with no line, exactly as the stand-in's fresh-install state gives them |
| `budget.view` | the month, not closed, income 0, allocated 0, an unknown investment rate, and the same groups plus the derived ones, zero wherever the figure comes from the budget; the fees subtotal is the month's real fees |
| `budget.establishments`, `budget.scenarios` | `[]` |
| `subscriptions.list` | totals 0, no groups, no suggestion |
| `subscriptions.detail` | `null` |
| `subscriptions.candidates`, `subscriptions.recurring` | `[]` |
| `review.weekly` | the limit with cap 0 and spent 0 (the contract's "spent" is what was spent on the budget's variable lines, and there are none); no week, an empty queue, no approvals, no warnings |
| `review.payday` | the real balance of the account the salary lands on and its label, a cushion of 0, no transfers; the comparison with the cushion as the contract's fresh-install value |

**A budget draft is refused.** `budget.view` takes an optional draft and then evaluates it; that is the budget's arithmetic, which belongs to the part of the app not built yet. With a draft that is not `null` the method answers the `read_only` error, the same one every write answers. Without a draft it answers the table's row.

**Recurring purchases and subscription candidates** could in principle be detected from the ledger. Detecting them is not decided and belongs with the write side; they are empty here on purpose.

**An empty budget still has its groups.** The Budget screen draws its first-day state from the groups the API returns, so an answer with no groups would leave a blank area. The stand-in's fresh-install state is the reference for both budget reads, field by field. The one derived figure the bank's records support is the fees subtotal, taken from the month's listed transactions that the transaction rules flag as a fee, read through the same widened period the transaction list uses.

**The account the salary lands on.** The contract's payday figures use one account and the ledger has several. It is the bank account with the latest settled credit whose `operationType` is `FOLHA_PAGAMENTO`: a salary can move to another account, and the latest one is where it lands now. A real ledger was found to hold two accounts with such credits, an older one with many and a newer one with few, which is what a change of account looks like. The check over a real ledger asserts that the latest credit does not tie between two accounts and reports, as a count, how many accounts ever received one. With none, the balance and its label are the contract's empty value, and so is the comparison with the cushion: with no cushion set there is nothing to be above or below.

**Work in parallel.** Another change is adding the card, the pots, net worth and the home summary to the same package at the same time. Keep to files of your own, add one line per domain to the registration list, extend the shared fixture ledgers only by adding to them, and take from the pending list exactly the ten names of this bead.

**Money, messages, privacy.** As everywhere in this package: cents in, an exact decimal out; any string the person reads is Brazilian Portuguese and lives in the one messages file; no value from a real ledger is printed, logged or committed.

**What the first reads left in place.** `internal/api/bank.go` has `bankLabels(accounts)`, the one place that says which bank an account belongs to: use it wherever the bank matters and write no second one. `nowOf(ctx)` gives the injected clock in Brazil time. The conformance test validates the answer of every registered read handler over both fixture ledgers, and the golden test records them, once it knows the argument sets of a new method. `fixtures_test.go` builds the two fixture ledgers. Golden files are named as the README in `internal/api/testdata/golden/` says. The opt-in test over a real ledger walks every registered handler and logs counts only.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Each of the ten methods answers 200 with a valid session and its answer validates against its result schema over both fixture ledgers.
- [ ] `budget.view` with a draft of `[]` answers 403 `read_only`; with no draft and with `null` it answers the empty view.
- [ ] `review.weekly` reports a limit of cap 0 and spent 0 over a fixture month that has purchases.
- [ ] `review.payday` reports the balance of the fixture account that received the latest `FOLHA_PAGAMENTO` credit, and the contract's empty value over a ledger with no such credit.
- [ ] `subscriptions.detail` answers `null` for any id.
- [ ] The pending list of reads without a handler no longer names these ten methods.
- [ ] `budget.document` and `budget.view` answer the same groups, in the same order, as the stand-in's fresh-install state, and over a fixture month with a fee the fees subtotal is that fee.
- [ ] The opt-in test over a real snapshot validates every answer, asserts that the latest payroll credit is not tied between two accounts, and logs counts only.
- [ ] `go.mod` gains no direct dependency.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and each of the ten routes answers 200 or a contract-valid `null` over both fixture ledgers.

## Tests
- Conformance: every answer against the manifest's schema, over both fixture ledgers.
- Golden: every answer against its file.
- Unit: the draft refusal; the choice of the salary account.
- Integration with `httptest`: each of the ten routes through the router with a session.
- Integration, opt-in: a real snapshot, counts only.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/api/`
**Reads only:** `internal/contract/contract.json`, `internal/ledger/`, `internal/txrules/`, `web/src/api/contract/`, `web/src/api/fake/`, `bin/ci`

New handler and test files in the HTTP package with their golden files, one line per domain in the registration list, and ten names fewer in the pending list. Existing handlers are called, not changed.
close_reason: The backend answers the four budget reads, the four subscription reads, review.weekly and review.payday. An empty budget answers the stand-in's groups, with the fees subtotal taken from the month's real fees through the same widened read the transaction list uses; a budget draft answers read_only through the path a refused write uses. The payday shows the balance of the bank account with the latest settled payroll credit, and no comparison with a cushion that is not set. Every answer validates against its schema over both fixture ledgers and is recorded as a golden file. bin/ci: CI green. Over a real snapshot every answer validated and the latest payroll credit is not tied between accounts; two accounts were found to have received payroll, which is why the check no longer demands one.

title: Answer the card, the pots, net worth and the home summary from the ledger
description:
## What changes for the user
After the accounts and the transactions, the rest of what the bank's records can answer becomes real: the card page with its open bill, its closing and due dates and how much of this month's spending falls on the next bill; the savings pots with what each holds and what it yielded; net worth and its history; and the summary at the top of the home screen. Where the records cannot support a figure the screen says it is not known, and nothing that needs a budget pretends to have one.

## Outcome
The backend answers five more methods of the interface's contract from the ledger: `card.overview`, `savingsPots.list`, `savingsPots.detail`, `netWorth.overview` and `home.summary`, each checked against the contract's schema and recorded as golden files from invented data.

## Context
finwise's read-only backend already answers the frame, the accounts and the transactions. Its HTTP package (`internal/api`) has the machinery this bead reuses: handlers registered per contract method, a money type that encodes integer cents as an exact decimal, a conformance test that validates every answer against the method's schema in `internal/contract/contract.json` over two fixture ledgers (one with every shape, one empty), golden files, and an opt-in test over a real ledger that logs counts only. `internal/cardrules` predicts the card's closing date, places a purchase on its bill and computes the amount that falls on the next bill; `internal/potrules` gives each pot's identity, latest balance and monthly yield, and attributes movements to pots.

**Same rule as before.** A figure the ledger supports is real; anything only the person can author is the contract's empty value; nothing is invented. The contract is already nullable where a fresh install has no honest value.

**Which card.** The contract models one card; the ledger may hold several card accounts, and the interview with the user says one card is in use. A bank keeps issuing bills for a card nobody uses, so a recent bill does not tell which card is in use. "The card" is the card account with the most recent purchase; ties go to the later bill by due date, then to the account id; when no card account has a purchase it is the one with the latest bill. A real ledger was found with several card accounts that still receive bills and only one with purchases. An opt-in check over a real ledger asserts that exactly one card account has a purchase in the last 60 days; when it finds another number the work stops and the count is reported. With no card account at all, `card.overview` answers the contract empty value. The other card accounts are reachable as accounts.

| method | from the ledger | empty for now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `card.overview` | the open bill, when it closes and falls due, the best day to buy, the limit and what is left of it, the amount that falls on the next bill with its purchases, past bills | the card's label is the default; the closing mode is the bank's |
| `savingsPots.list`, `savingsPots.detail` | each pot's name as the bank gives it, balance, movements, the month's yield with its daily rows and its base (net or gross); closed pots when asked | target, planned contribution, linked budget lines; the bucket is the default below |
| `netWorth.overview` | the total, what is available, reserved and invested, the chart from the first month the ledger has a reading for, the pots' yields | planned contribution and planned investment rate 0 |
| `home.summary` | net worth's three parts, the amount that falls on the next bill | the limit is cap 0 and spent 0 (the contract's "spent" is what was spent on the budget's variable lines, and there are none), weeks `[]`, pending count 0 |

**Net worth.** Available is the balance of the bank accounts; reserved is the pots; invested is the investments at their net amount (`amount_net` of the latest day; `amountOriginal` is never summed). The stand-in's rules in `web/src/api/fake/` state how the three parts and the total relate; follow them. The balance history has one reading per night and starts recently, so the chart starts at the first month with a reading: a month before it is absent, never zero.

**A pot's bucket, decided with the user.** The person assigns each pot to a bucket (`Disponível`, `Reservado`, `Investido`), and nothing can be assigned yet. A pot counted in no bucket would be missing from the net worth, so until the person says otherwise the bucket is what the bank says the pot is: a reserve entry (a "caixinha") is `Reservado` and an investment is `Investido`. Bank accounts are available. The stand-in's fresh-install state follows the same rule. Rejected: counting an unassigned pot nowhere, which understates the total for as long as nothing can be assigned; and a fourth "no bucket" group, which adds interface outside the design for a state that ends when assignment exists.

**The same money must not be counted twice.** Some banks back a pot with investments, so one sum can appear both as a reserve entry and among the investments. The sources do not say how those investments divide between the pots. Count the reserve entries; leave out an investment only when the ledger itself shows it backs a reserve; otherwise keep both and report, as a count, how many investments sit on an account that also has reserve entries, so the case is seen and decided rather than guessed.

**Yield.** A month whose yield cannot be computed is unknown, not zero. Two bases are never added into one figure.

**What the card and pot rules expect of their caller.**
- `cardrules.Card` is built by the caller from the card account's bills, the closing table and an optional manual closing day. The rules do not know which bank a card belongs to: the caller picks `cardrules.C6ClosingTable()` for a C6 card and no table for any other, using the bank identification that `internal/txrules` already has. A card with no table has an unknown closing date and an unknown next-bill amount, and both reach the screen as unknown.
- `Card.AmountOnNextBill` sums the purchases it is handed with the sign they carry. Hand it the listed card purchases of `internal/txrules` (negative for money out) and present the figure as the contract expects.
- A pot's yield comes from `ledger.PotYields` between two days and `potrules.YieldOfMonth`, which needs the pot's base: net for Nubank, gross for Mercado Pago, by the account's bank. `MonthYield.Since` precedes the month when the account was not sighted on the days before; the total then holds yield earned before the month began, and the pot's page says since when.
- The yield statement of the collector's README does not prepare as one statement in this module's SQLite and runs as three statements over the same CTEs. Asking it once per pair of consecutive sightings took about 70 seconds over a real ledger. A request must not do that: ask for the range the screen needs in as few calls as the query allows, and measure.
- `potrules` attributes a deposit or a withdrawal to a pot only when a sighting within three days after it shows exactly one pot whose balance moved by that amount. The balance history is one reading per night and starts recently, so most past movements stay unattributed on their account. They are shown on the account's side of the pots screen as the contract allows, never dropped and never guessed onto a pot.
- `ledger.Pots` returns no row for a sighting in which the account holds no pot, so an account that emptied every pot does not make them read as closed. If the pots screen needs that case, the reader gains it here, with a test.

**Money, messages, privacy.** As everywhere in this package: cents in, an exact decimal out; any string the person reads is Brazilian Portuguese and lives in the one messages file; no value from a real ledger is printed, logged or committed, and golden files come only from the fixture builder.

**What the first reads left in place.** `internal/api/bank.go` has `bankLabels(accounts)`, the one place that says which bank an account belongs to: use it wherever the bank matters and write no second one. `nowOf(ctx)` gives the injected clock in Brazil time. The conformance test validates the answer of every registered read handler over both fixture ledgers, and the golden test records them, once it knows the argument sets of a new method. `fixtures_test.go` builds the two fixture ledgers: extend them with what this bead needs instead of building a third. Golden files are named as the README in `internal/api/testdata/golden/` says. Strings a person reads live in the one messages file. `accounts.detail` already answers a bank account with the bucket `Disponível`, and `shell.overview` already reports the sync state. The opt-in test over a real ledger walks every registered handler and logs counts only.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Each of the five methods answers 200 with a valid session, and its answer validates against its result schema over both fixture ledgers.
- [ ] Over a fixture with two card accounts, `card.overview` describes the one with the more recent purchase, even when the other has the later bill; with no purchase on either it describes the one with the later bill.
- [ ] Over the empty ledger `card.overview` answers the contract's empty value, the pot list is `[]`, and net worth is zero with an empty chart.
- [ ] A fixture purchase dated on the predicted closing date is among the purchases that fall on the next bill; one dated the day before with the closed bill's id is not.
- [ ] A fixture pot whose month has a day the yield query cannot compute reports an unknown yield for that month.
- [ ] A fixture with one net pot and one gross pot never yields a single summed figure.
- [ ] Net worth's total equals available plus reserved plus invested for the fixture, to the cent; a fixture reserve entry is counted in reserved and a fixture investment in invested, and each pot's answer names that bucket.
- [ ] The chart has no month before the fixture's first balance reading.
- [ ] `home.summary` reports a limit of cap 0 and spent 0 over a fixture month that has purchases, and its net worth equals what `netWorth.overview` reports for the same ledger.
- [ ] `savingsPots.list` omits a closed pot by default and includes it when asked.
- [ ] A fixture card of a bank with no closing table answers `card.overview` with an unknown closing date and an unknown next-bill amount, neither shown as zero.
- [ ] A fixture movement no pot can claim is present in the pots answer as unattributed on its account.
- [ ] `savingsPots.list` and `savingsPots.detail` each run the yield query a number of times that does not grow with the number of sightings in the range; a test counts the calls.
- [ ] The time `savingsPots.list` takes over a real ledger is measured **by the review**, not by the lane, three runs on a quiet machine, and recorded on the pull request.
- [ ] The pending list of reads without a handler no longer names these five methods.
- [ ] The opt-in test over a real snapshot validates every answer, asserts exactly one card account with a purchase in the last 60 days, and logs counts only.
- [ ] `go.mod` gains no direct dependency.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and the opt-in run reports every answer valid and one card in use.

## Tests
- Conformance: every answer against the manifest's schema, over both fixture ledgers.
- Golden: every answer against its file.
- Unit: the choice of the card; net worth's parts and total; the chart's first month; unknown yield.
- Integration with `httptest`: each method through the router with a session.
- Integration, opt-in: a real snapshot, counts only.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/api/`, `internal/ledger/`
**Reads only:** `internal/contract/contract.json`, `internal/cardrules/`, `internal/potrules/`, `internal/txrules/`, `web/src/api/contract/`, `web/src/api/fake/`, `bin/ci`

New handler and test files in the HTTP package with their golden files, and new history queries in the reader (balances, reserves and investments per day), each as a new file with its test. Existing handlers are not changed.
close_reason: The backend answers card.overview, savingsPots.list, savingsPots.detail, netWorth.overview and home.summary from the ledger. The card in use is the card account with the most recent purchase. A reserve entry counts as reserved and an investment as invested; an investment is left out only when the ledger shows it backs the reserves. Yield is unknown rather than zero when it cannot be computed, and two bases are never summed. Every answer validates against its schema over both fixture ledgers and is recorded as a golden file. bin/ci: CI green on the tree merged with main. Over a real snapshot every answer validated and exactly one card account has a purchase in the last 60 days. Measured by the review on the built server over a real ledger, three runs each: savingsPots.list, savingsPots.detail and netWorth.overview take 12 to 15 seconds because of the collector's yield statement; every other read is under 0.4 s. That, and the daily yield rows that are always empty, are carried by a follow-up bead; a card with no closing rule answering blanks and a zero is carried by another.

title: Serve the contract over HTTP behind the PIN and refuse every write
description:
## What changes for the user
Today the PIN screen guards nothing: the lock lives in the browser's memory and the data is an invented dataset bundled with the page. After this lands there is a real program to start, `finwise serve`, that keeps the person's data behind the six-digit PIN on the server side, locks for five minutes after three wrong attempts, and answers every attempt to change something with one clear refusal, because this first backend only reads.

## Outcome
A `finwise` binary with `serve` and `hash-pin`. Its HTTP server exposes one route per method of the interface's API contract, built from the contract's manifest: session methods work, every write and every evaluation is refused, reads are dispatched to handlers registered by later work, and nothing but the session's own two routes answers without a valid session.

## Context
finwise is a personal finance app. Its interface (`web/`) talks to a backend through a TypeScript contract of 82 methods. A generated file, `internal/contract/contract.json`, describes that contract for Go: for every method its route (`/api/<domain>/<method>`), its class (`session`, `read`, `evaluate` or `write`), a schema for its arguments and one for its result, and the schema of the error envelope. The Go module and a read-only ledger reader (`internal/ledger`) already exist. This bead is the HTTP layer between them; the read handlers themselves come later.

**The wire.** Every method is `POST /api/<domain>/<method>`. The body is the JSON array of the method's arguments in declaration order; the answer is the method's result as JSON, `null` for a method that returns nothing. An error is `{"error":{"kind":"<kind>"}}`:

| kind | status | when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `locked` | 401 | no valid session |
| `read_only` | 403 | the method's class is `write` or `evaluate` |
| `ledger_unavailable` | 503 | the reader reports a missing or unreadable snapshot, or an unsupported version |
| `bad_request` | 400 | the body is not a JSON array the method accepts, the content type is not JSON, the body is over 1 MiB, or the verb is not POST |
| `unknown_method` | 404 | no such route under `/api/` |
| `internal` | 500 | anything else |

**Refusing writes without a handler per write.** The router is built from the manifest. A `write` or `evaluate` method is refused before its body is read, and no handler exists for it. The session check comes first: without a session a write answers `locked`, not `read_only`. `session.changePin` is a write and is refused without comparing any PIN. This backend is read-only on purpose: the part of the app that changes data has no reviewed plan yet.

**Reads.** A `read` method is served by a handler registered for it, receiving the request context, the raw arguments and a way to open the ledger. This bead registers none. A test holds the list of `read` methods still without a handler and fails when the manifest's reads differ from registered plus listed; later work empties that list. A `read` with no handler answers `internal`.

**The PIN.** One six-digit PIN, no user name. The server never stores it: it reads `FINWISE_PIN_HASH`, a string of the form `pbkdf2-sha256$<iterations>$<salt>$<key>` (base64 fields, at least 600000 iterations), derives the key from the attempt with the standard library's `crypto/pbkdf2` and compares in constant time. `finwise hash-pin` reads a PIN from standard input, refuses anything but six digits, and prints that string. `finwise serve` refuses to start when the variable is missing or malformed, and its message never contains the value. A six-digit PIN cannot be protected against someone who holds the hash; the hash keeps the PIN out of configuration in the clear, and the lockout protects against guessing over the network.

**Lockout.** Three wrong attempts lock every attempt out for 300 seconds, the right PIN included; a correct attempt resets the count. The lock is global, not per client: there is one user. `session.status` answers `{locked, retryAfterSeconds}` and `session.unlock` answers the contract's `UnlockResult` (see `web/src/api/contract/session.ts`). The in-memory stand-in in `web/src/api/fake/index.ts` is the statement of the same behaviour. The clock is injected so tests do not wait.

**Sessions.** A successful unlock creates a random 256-bit token kept in memory and sets a cookie named `__Host-finwise-session` with `Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict` and no `Domain`. A session expires after 12 hours without a request (`FINWISE_SESSION_TTL` overrides it); the server decides expiry and the cookie lives at least as long. `session.lock` removes the session and clears the cookie. Sessions are lost when the process restarts, which only means typing the PIN again. A flag `--dev-insecure-cookie`, off by default, drops `Secure` and the `__Host-` prefix for a plain-HTTP development setup.

**Cross-origin.** Wrap the mux in the standard library's `http.CrossOriginProtection`, and require `Content-Type: application/json` on every `/api/` request.

**Logs.** `log/slog` to standard output: method, route, status, duration. Never a body, an argument, a cookie, the PIN, the hash, or a value from the ledger. The person's whole financial history passes through this process. An error returned by the ledger reader may carry a row id in its text: log the error's kind, never its message.

**Serving.** `finwise serve --listen <addr> --ledger <path>` (`FINWISE_LISTEN`, `FINWISE_LEDGER`; the default address is `127.0.0.1:8080`). It starts even when the snapshot file does not exist: the PIN works and reads answer `ledger_unavailable`. `GET /healthz` answers 200 without a session and says nothing about the ledger. Read and write timeouts are set, and `SIGTERM` shuts down gracefully. Serving the built interface from the binary is later work.

No dependency is added: everything here is in the standard library.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] For every `write` and `evaluate` method in the manifest, a POST with a valid session answers 403 with `{"error":{"kind":"read_only"}}`, including when the body is not valid JSON.
- [ ] For every route in the manifest except `session.status` and `session.unlock`, a POST without a session answers 401 `locked`.
- [ ] `POST /api/nope/nothing` answers 404 `unknown_method` as JSON; a GET on a method route answers `bad_request`.
- [ ] A correct unlock sets a cookie named `__Host-finwise-session` whose attributes are exactly `Path=/`, `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict` plus an expiry, with no `Domain`; with `--dev-insecure-cookie` the name has no prefix and `Secure` is absent.
- [ ] After three wrong PINs a fourth attempt with the right PIN is refused and `retryAfterSeconds` is between 1 and 300; after the clock advances 300 seconds the right PIN unlocks; a correct unlock after two wrong attempts resets the count.
- [ ] `session.status` reports `locked: true` without a cookie and `locked: false` with one.
- [ ] After `session.lock` the same cookie answers 401.
- [ ] A session unused for 12 hours answers 401; a request at 11 hours keeps it valid at 20 hours.
- [ ] `session.changePin` answers `read_only` and the PIN comparison function is not called.
- [ ] `finwise hash-pin` rejects `12345` and `abcdef`, and the string it prints for `123456` unlocks a server started with it; a server started with no hash, or with `not-a-hash`, exits non-zero.
- [ ] A POST with `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` answers 403; a POST with `Content-Type: text/plain` answers `bad_request`; a body over 1 MiB answers `bad_request`.
- [ ] A request carrying a sentinel string in its body, another as its PIN and a valid cookie produces log output containing none of the three.
- [ ] A test handler returning the reader's unsupported-version error answers 503 `ledger_unavailable`; one returning any other error answers 500 `internal`.
- [ ] The set of `read` methods in the manifest equals the registered handlers plus the pending list, and removing one name from the pending list makes that test fail.
- [ ] `finwise serve --listen 127.0.0.1:0 --ledger /nonexistent` starts, and `GET /healthz` answers 200.
- [ ] `go.mod` gains no direct dependency.
- [ ] `AGENTS.md` says how to run the backend.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and every row of the error table above has a test that produces it.

## Tests
- Unit: the hash format and its round trip; the lockout and the session expiry with an injected clock.
- Integration with `httptest`: the manifest-driven refusal of every write and evaluation; the session requirement on every route; the cookie's attributes; cross-origin, content type and size limits; the error mapping.
- Unit: the log line for a request with sentinels.
- Integration: the `serve` command started on a free port without a snapshot.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `cmd/finwise/`, `internal/api/`, `internal/contract/contract.go`, `internal/contract/contract_test.go`, `AGENTS.md`, `.gitignore`
**Reads only:** `internal/contract/contract.json`, `internal/ledger/`, `web/src/api/contract/session.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/index.ts`, `bin/ci`

A new command and a new package for the HTTP layer and the session, plus the Go side of the manifest. The generated manifest and the reader are read, not changed.
close_reason: The finwise command serves one route per contract method, built from the manifest: session methods work, every write and evaluation answers read_only before its body is read, reads dispatch to handlers registered per domain, and only session.status and session.unlock answer without a session. The PIN is checked against a PBKDF2 hash in constant time, three wrong attempts hold the keypad for 300 seconds globally, sessions are 256-bit tokens kept in memory behind a __Host- cookie and expire after 12 idle hours. Every row of the error table has a test. bin/ci: CI green. Review added tests for two gaps: a forged cookie beside a live session, and the wrong-attempt count after a hold ends. Left for the first reads: a snapshot file that is not a database answers internal instead of ledger_unavailable.

title: Give every budget line an id in the contract and make every line menu ask for the month it is for
description:
## What changes for the user
Almost nothing the person can see. Today the app knows a budget line only by its name, and every menu
that offers lines offers one and the same list whichever month the transaction is from; nothing gets in
the way yet, because the app does not store a budget. This work is what lets the app, once it does,
rename or reorder a line without losing the history of what was spent on it, and offer for each
transaction the lines of the budget of that transaction's own month, so that a purchase of last March
is put on a line last March really had. Two small things do show: the menus of lines and tags in a
transaction's panel and on a subscription's page keep up with a change just made, where today they
show what they loaded when the page opened, and the filter by line above the transaction list offers
every line the listed transactions are on, also one a later budget renamed or dropped. If the rest
were wrong the person would notice later, and not at the moment it went wrong: a renamed line whose
past spending vanished from every total, the history of a removed line turning up on another one, or a
menu offering a line the transaction's month does not have, so that picking it is refused.

## Outcome
The contract's budget line carries an optional `id`, a decimal string, and the line menu
`transactions.filterOptions` takes the month it is asked for. The generated manifest says both. Every
place of the interface that shows a menu of lines sends the month that menu is for: the transaction's
own month where the line belongs to a transaction, the current month where it belongs to something
that has no month; and every one of them asks again when the revision is bumped. The list's filter by
line also offers every line name its rows carry. The budget draft carries each line's id through
copying, renaming, moving and editing; a new line has none, and removing a line never hands its id to
another. The stand-in keeps an id it is given instead of dropping it and accepts the month, and
behaves otherwise as before. The Go read handler of the menu takes the month, and its recorded cases
and golden files follow, so the gate stays green.

## Context
**What finwise is, and the words used below.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The
ledger* is a SQLite snapshot that a separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app only
reads it, through `finwise serve`, a read-only Go server. The app is gaining a *write side*: its own
database, `finwise.db`, where everything the person authors will live. None of that database exists in
this work; this is the contract change the budget's storage is built on. *The contract* is the
TypeScript interface `FinwiseApi` (`web/src/api/types.ts` and `web/src/api/contract/`). *The manifest*
is `internal/contract/contract.json`, generated from the contract by `npm --prefix web run contract`
(`web/scripts/contract-manifest.mjs`), versioned and never edited by hand; the Go server builds its
routes from it and `bin/ci` fails when it is stale. *The stand-in* is the in-memory fake backend under
`web/src/api/fake/` (`createFakeApi`) that the design prototype runs on; it is the only existing
statement of how writes behave. *A budget document* (`BudgetDoc`) is five editable groups (`rec`
income, `fix`, `var`, `prov` provisions, `res` reserves), each a list of lines. A budget is kept as
*versions*, each valid from a month on; a month uses the latest version at or before it. *The line
menu* is the list `lines` of `TransactionFilterOptions`, each entry a `BudgetLineOption` of a name and
its group's name, which every menu that puts something on a line is drawn from. *The draft* is the
budget document while it is being edited on the budget screen or the scenarios screen. *The current
month* is the month of today as the server tells it. *A closed month* is one the person closed in the
monthly review; its budget no longer changes. *The revision* is a counter
(`web/src/stores/revision.ts`) bumped after every write and undo; what shows data a write can change
watches it and fetches again. *The gate* is `bin/ci`, the exact checks CI runs: among them the
manifest being current, the type check, the interface's tests, and Go's `gofmt`, `vet` and tests. *A
golden file* is the recorded, exact answer of one read method over one of two invented ledgers
(`internal/api/testdata/golden/full/` and `empty/`), which a Go test compares every answer with.

**The contract and its callers as they are today** (each point read in the file named):

- `BudgetLineDoc` in `web/src/api/contract/budget.ts` has `name`, `amount` and an optional `flag`. A
  line has no identity but its name, and the stand-in joins everything by name.
- `TransactionsApi.filterOptions()` in `web/src/api/contract/transactions.ts` takes no argument. It
  answers the accounts and tags to filter by and the line menu.
