the reasons cannot be found, is refused at start instead of being half-honoured. How the reasons are
located in the manifest (the definition the generator emits for the list, or a field the generator is
taught to write) is the implementer's; the shape of what Go receives, beyond the two things named, is
too. The existing `Method` fields and `Load` keep working for the router as it is: no file of
`internal/api` changes in this slice.

**Another slice regenerates the same manifest.** The budget line's id and the month of the line menu are
added to the contract at the same time ({{B1}}), and that work regenerates
`internal/contract/contract.json` and may edit `manifest.test.ts` too. A conflict in the generated file
is resolved by regenerating it from the merged TypeScript (`npm --prefix web run contract`), never by
merging the JSON by hand.

**Decision, with what lost.** One new error kind, `refused`, with a `reason` from a closed list, and the
texts in the interface: a closed month or a stale undo must be readable by the person, and `bad_request`
means a client bug. Lost: one kind per refusal; free text from the server.

**Where the server departs from the stand-in on purpose.** Typed refusals instead of thrown errors; the
envelope carries a reason. The stand-in throws a plain `Error`; nothing in it changes here. The test
that pins this slice's part is the envelope test of `manifest.test.ts`.

**Privacy.** The repository is public and a real ledger is a person's whole financial history. Nothing
in this slice touches a ledger, real or invented; no value from a real snapshot (amount, description,
name, document, id) is ever printed, logged, copied into a file, a commit, a bead or a pull request.

**Conventions.** Work happens in a git worktree of its own and ends at local commits: atomic,
Conventional Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a plan in a commit
message. Money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path. Every SQL statement over the
app's database is a registered constant (this slice runs none). Interface text is Brazilian Portuguese
and everything else is English; a design value in a component comes from a token (this slice touches no
component). The manifest is generated, never edited by hand.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `API_ERROR_KINDS` holds the six older wire kinds, `refused` and `network`; the list of reasons
holds exactly the nine of the table, in that order; `npm --prefix web run typecheck` passes.
- [ ] `npm --prefix web run contract:check` passes, and the diff of `internal/contract/contract.json`
against the commit this work started from shows only the error envelope and the definitions it needs.
- [ ] In `manifest.test.ts`, the manifest's `error` schema accepts `{error:{kind}}` for each of the six
older wire kinds and `{error:{kind:"refused",reason}}` for each of the nine reasons, and rejects
`{error:{kind:"refused"}}`, `{error:{kind:"refused",reason:"nope"}}`,
`{error:{kind:"refused",reason:"stale_change",detail:"x"}}`,
`{error:{kind:"read_only",reason:"month_closed"}}`, `{error:{kind:"network"}}` and `{kind:"read_only"}`.
- [ ] `internal/contract` hands out an argument schema for each of the 82 methods; a test compiles all
82 with the schema library the conformance tests already use, and for `budget.save` accepts
`["2026-03",[{"key":"rec","name":"Receita","lines":[{"name":"Salário","amount":8000}]}]]` and rejects
the same array with `amount` as a string, with an extra field on the line, and with a third element.
- [ ] `internal/contract` hands out the nine reasons in the order of the table, read from the manifest
and not written a second time in Go; a test compares them with the table above.
- [ ] `parse` refuses a manifest whose method has no argument schema and one in which the reasons cannot
be found, in the style of `TestParseRefusesWhatItDoesNotUnderstand`.
- [ ] No file under `internal/api`, `web/src/api/http/`, `web/src/api/fake/` or `web/src/api/failures.ts`
is changed, and `go test ./...` and `npm --prefix web test` pass.
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, each against its own deliberate break, named in the final
report: the envelope test against a `reason` allowed on every kind and against `refused` with an
optional reason; the reasons test against a reason removed from the TypeScript list without
regenerating; the schema test against definitions left out of what Go hands out.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` with the manifest current, and an envelope with a reason on
another kind, or `refused` without one, does not validate against the manifest.

## Tests
- Unit (vitest, `web/src/api/contract/manifest.test.ts`), over the generated manifest: the envelopes the
  error schema accepts and rejects.
- Unit (`internal/contract/contract_test.go`), over the embedded manifest: an argument schema for every
  method; all 82 compile; the `budget.save` vectors; the nine reasons in order.
- Table (`internal/contract/contract_test.go`), over hand-written manifests: what `parse` refuses.
- The gate's own checks: the manifest is current; the types check.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `web/src/api/contract/errors.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/manifest.test.ts`,
`web/scripts/contract-manifest.mjs`, `internal/contract/contract.json`, `internal/contract/contract.go`,
`internal/contract/contract_test.go`
**Reads only:** `web/src/api/http/client.ts`, `web/src/api/http/failure.ts`, `web/src/api/failures.ts`,
`web/src/api/fake/changes.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/classification.ts`,
`internal/api/conformance_test.go`, `internal/api/errors.go`, `internal/api/router.go`, `go.mod`,
`bin/ci`

Two small modules: the contract's error type with its test and generated manifest, and the Go package
that reads the manifest. Three code files at most (`errors.ts`, `contract.go`, and the generator only if
it cannot express the union), two test files and one generated file. The HTTP client, the failure
handler, the stand-in and every file of `internal/api` are read and left as they are: what the interface
does with a refusal and how the server answers one are other slices'. `go.mod` gains no requirement: the
schema library is already there, and here only a test uses it. Only `bin/ci` proves the whole, because
the change spans the TypeScript types, the generated manifest and Go.

title: Read money and whole numbers from JSON into integers with no float
description:
## What changes for the user
Nothing the person sees changes with this piece. Today the app only shows amounts; it never receives
one, because every button that changes something is refused. Once the person can type a budget line, a
part of a split purchase or the amount they expect back, the server has to read that number, and this
piece is how: to the cent, exactly as typed, with a fixed rule for a third decimal place and a refusal
for anything that is not an amount. If it were wrong the person would find a line saved one cent off
what they typed, an empty field saved as zero, or a setting rounded the wrong way, and no screen would
say so.

## Outcome
`internal/api` has `ParseReais`, which turns a JSON number into integer cents from its decimal text, and
`ParseWholeNumber`, which turns one into a whole number; the money type `Reais` decodes itself through
the first. Neither touches a float, and the test that forbids floats in the HTTP layer covers the
packages the write side adds. No handler uses them yet.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. Its Go backend answers the API the
interface calls; today it is read-only, and it is about to gain handlers that save what the person
types. Money is held as integer cents (`money.Cents`, an `int64`, in `internal/money`). On the wire an
amount is a JSON number in reais with two decimals (`19.99`, `-65.10`). *The stand-in* is the in-memory
fake backend under `web/src/api/fake/` that the design prototype runs on, and the only existing
statement of how writes behave.

**What the code is today (each point checked in the file named).**

- `internal/api/reais.go`: `Reais` is `money.Cents` with a `MarshalJSON` that writes the decimal from
  the integer itself (`decimalOf` works on the magnitude as unsigned so the most negative integer does
  not overflow). There is no way to read an amount: `Reais` has no `UnmarshalJSON`.
- `internal/api/reais_test.go`: `TestMoneyIsWrittenAsADecimalWithTwoPlaces` (a table up to the limits of
  `int64`); `TestAnAbsentFigureIsNullAndNotZero` (a `*Reais` that is nil is written `null`); and
  `TestNoSourceFileOfTheHTTPLayerTouchesAFloat`, which parses every non-test file of `internal/api` and
  fails on the identifiers `float64` and `float32`, on a call named `ParseFloat` or `FromFloat`, and on
  a float literal.
- `internal/money/money.go`: `FromFloat` converts what the ledger hands over (floats read out of JSON),
  rounding half away from zero on the shortest decimal the float prints as, and refuses a magnitude of
  `1e12` or more. That is the boundary with the bank's records and is not used for what a person types.
- `internal/api/arguments.go`: `decodeArgument` decodes one argument strictly (`DisallowUnknownFields`,
  nothing after the value) and answers `badArgumentsError`, which the router turns into `bad_request`.
- `internal/api/percent.go`: `Percent` is a rate the bank states, kept as text with two decimals.
- The stand-in rounds and clamps three settings with `clamp` in `web/src/api/fake/settings-rules.ts`:
  `Math.round`, then the range's minimum and maximum, a non-finite value becoming the minimum.
  `web/src/api/contract/settings.ts` types those three as `number`: `setThreshold(percent)`,
  `setMinExamples(count)` and the manual day of `setClosing(mode, manualDay)`.

**`ParseReais(raw) (money.Cents, error)`.** It turns a JSON number into integer cents from its decimal
text, exponent form included, with no float. It rounds half away from zero beyond two places. It refuses
anything that is not a finite number within one billion reais: the bound is inclusive and is on the
result, 100,000,000,000 cents in magnitude, so exactly one billion reais is accepted, positive or
negative, and one cent more is not. What is not a JSON number is refused: `null`, a string, a boolean,
an array, an object, an empty input, and the spellings JSON does not have (`1.`, `.5`, `+1`, `01`,
`NaN`, `Infinity`). It must not do work proportional to the size of an exponent: `1e999999999` is
refused at once, without building the number, and `0e999999999` is zero.

**`Reais.UnmarshalJSON`.** `Reais` gains `UnmarshalJSON` on top of `ParseReais`, so a budget line's
amount and a split part's amount decode directly inside the struct a handler decodes. It refuses `null`
like everything else that is not a number, so an absent amount can never read as zero; a field that may
be absent is a `*Reais`, which Go leaves nil for `null` without calling the method.

**A negative amount.** An amount that cannot be negative (a budget line, a split part, an expected
reimbursement) is `bad_request` when it is. `ParseReais` itself accepts a negative, because other
amounts can be one; the handler that takes such an amount applies the rule. Those handlers belong to
later slices.

**`ParseWholeNumber(raw) (int, error)`.** It reads the three settings the contract types as `number`. It
rounds to the nearest whole number, a half upward (72.5 becomes 73, -72.5 becomes -72), which is what
the stand-in's `Math.round` gives. It answers an error, which its caller turns into `bad_request`, for a
number beyond one billion in magnitude or not finite, and for anything that is not a JSON number; the
bound is on the result, as it is for money, so one billion itself is accepted. The handler then clamps
to the contract's range, as the stand-in does (for the threshold's 50 to 99, 72.6 becomes 73 and 10
becomes 50); the clamping and the ranges belong to the settings' own slice ({{S1}}: the confidence
threshold, the minimum of examples, the card's label and the closing day), not here. No float, and the
same rule about exponents.

**The rule both parsers serve, binding on every later handler.** All arithmetic is integer cents. Where
the stand-in rounds a float, the port states its rounding in cents, and a table test pins each case
including a negative half. A percentage the server computes (a progress, a fill, a bar, a confidence) is
a whole number rounded half up, as the existing reads already answer them; the stand-in's fractions are
not copied. A rate the bank states, such as a pot's share of the CDI, keeps the two decimals it has
today (`Percent`).

**The float guard widens.** The test that forbids floats covers the new packages too:
`internal/authored` (the package that owns the app's own database, `finwise.db`), `internal/ingest` (the
job that brings a new snapshot of the bank's records into that database) and the three rule packages
`internal/budgetrules`, `internal/classrules` and `internal/subrules`. None of the five may exist when
this lands. The test must already name them, so each is covered from its first file without anyone
editing the test; a directory that is not there yet must not fail the gate, and a present one must not
be skipped. If `internal/authored` arrives with a guard of its own, the overlap is harmless.
`big.Float` is a float too, although the guard's patterns do not see it.

**Why here, and what lost.** A JSON decoder that reads a number into a `float64` and multiplies by a
hundred is right on round figures and wrong on `1.005`, silently; so the amount is read from its text.
`money.FromFloat` is not reused: it starts from a float. The two bounds differ on purpose: what the
ledger hands over is trusted up to `1e12`, what a person types up to one billion.

**Privacy.** The repository is public and a real ledger is a person's whole financial history. Nothing
in this slice touches a ledger; every amount in its tests is invented, and no value from a real snapshot
(amount, description, name, document, id) is ever printed, logged, copied into a file, a commit, a bead
or a pull request.

**Conventions.** Work happens in a git worktree of its own and ends at local commits: atomic,
Conventional Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a plan in a commit
message. Money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path, which is this slice's whole
subject. Every SQL statement over the app's database is a registered constant (this slice runs none).
Interface text is Brazilian Portuguese and everything else is English; a design value in a component
comes from a token (this slice touches no component).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `ParseReais` returns, in cents: `0` and `-0` 0; `19.99` 1999; `-65.10` -6510; `8000` 800000;
`0.005` 1; `-0.005` -1; `1.005` 101; `-1.005` -101; `1.0049` 100; `2.675` 268; `0.994999` 99; `1e2`
10000; `1.5e-1` 15; `12E-1` 120; `1e-400` 0; `0e999999999` 0.
- [ ] At the bound, `ParseReais` returns 99999999999 for `999999999.99`, 100000000000 for `1000000000`,
`1000000000.00`, `1e9` and `1000000000.004`, and -100000000000 for `-1000000000`; it refuses
`1000000000.005`, `1000000000.01`, `-1000000000.01`, `1e10`, `1e400` and `1e999999999`.
- [ ] `ParseReais` refuses `"19.99"`, `null`, `true`, `[1]`, `{}`, the empty input, `1.`, `.5`, `+1`,
`01`, `NaN`, `Infinity` and `1 2`.
- [ ] For every amount in a generated range of cents that includes negatives and both bounds,
`ParseReais` of what `Reais` writes is the same amount.
- [ ] A struct field of type `Reais` decodes `19.99` to 1999 and makes the decode fail for `null` and
for `"19.99"`; a field of type `*Reais` is nil for `null`.
- [ ] `ParseWholeNumber` returns 73 for `73`, `72.6`, `72.5` and `7.3e1`; 72 for `72.4`; -72 for
`-72.5`; -73 for `-72.6`; 1 for `0.5`; 0 for `-0.5`, `0.4` and `-0`; 1000000000 for `1000000000` and
`1000000000.4`; -1000000000 for `-1000000000.5`.
- [ ] `ParseWholeNumber` refuses `1000000000.5`, `1000000001`, `-1000000001`, `1e400`, `1e999999999`,
`"73"`, `null`, `true` and the empty input.
- [ ] Neither parser builds the number for an enormous exponent: a test shows that each allocates no
more bytes for `1e999999999` than for `1e400`.
- [ ] The float test fails for a float planted in a non-test file of `internal/api` and of a scratch
directory standing for each of the five packages named above, and passes while those five do not exist.
- [ ] `git diff --stat` against the commit this work started from lists only `internal/api/reais.go`,
`internal/api/reais_test.go` and the new files of `ParseWholeNumber`; no handler is changed.
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, each against its own deliberate break, named in the final
report: the rounding rows against truncation and against rounding half to even; the bound rows against
an exclusive bound; the `null` row against an `UnmarshalJSON` that returns without error; the whole
number's negative half against rounding half away from zero; one row of each table against
`strconv.ParseFloat`, which the float test must catch too.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, every vector above (decimal, exponent, huge, negative half,
out of bound) is a row of a table test, and no non-test file of `internal/api` names a float.

## Tests
- Table (`internal/api`), over the vectors of the criteria: `ParseReais`, accepted and refused, with the
  rows at the bound.
- Property: `ParseReais` over what `Reais.MarshalJSON` writes, for generated cents between the two
  bounds, negatives included.
- Unit: `Reais` and `*Reais` as struct fields decoded with `decodeArgument`.
- Table: `ParseWholeNumber`, accepted and refused, with the halves of both signs and the rows at the
  bound.
- Unit: the bytes each parser allocates on `1e999999999` against `1e400`.
- Source test: the float guard over `internal/api` and the five packages to come, with a test of the
  test over scratch directories.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/api/reais.go`, `internal/api/reais_test.go`
**Reads only:** `internal/api/arguments.go`, `internal/api/percent.go`, `internal/money/money.go`,
`web/src/api/fake/settings-rules.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/settings.ts`, `bin/ci`

One package and two existing files, plus one new file for `ParseWholeNumber` and its test file. No
handler, no router code and no contract type changes, and nothing calls the parsers yet: their first
callers are the handlers of later slices. It is labelled critical although it is small: a parser that
rounds wrongly passes every test on round figures and is wrong about someone's money in silence.
close_reason: ParseReais reads a JSON number into integer cents from its decimal text (exponent form included, half away from zero beyond two places, refused beyond one billion reais inclusive) and Reais decodes through it, refusing null; ParseWholeNumber rounds a half upward and refuses beyond one billion. Neither builds the number for a huge exponent. The float guard now covers the write side's packages and is itself tested with a planted float in each. bin/ci: CI green on the branch. Review: four independent mutations (half not rounding up, leading zeros accepted, negative exponent read as positive, whole-number half rounding down) each failed a test; the implementer's eighteen breaks each failed one too. Nothing calls the parsers yet.

title: Remove the ledger reader's wrapper methods and move the tests that still call them onto the view
description:
## What changes for the user
Nothing the person sees changes with this piece, and no answer of the app changes. Every screen is by
now built from one state of the bank's records, the one that was there when the screen was asked for.
But the older way of asking those records a question, which goes back to them for each question and so
can see yesterday's records for one answer and today's for the next, is still in the code beside the new
one, kept alive only by the app's own tests. This piece removes it. What it prevents is two ways of
reading the bank's records living side by side, one of which can put a single screen together from two
states of them: anything written later could pick the old one up by mistake, and nothing would say so.
If this piece were wrong the person would notice nothing; a test would stop building.

## Outcome
`ledger.Reader` has no query method left: the file that holds its twelve wrappers is deleted and its
thirteenth, `PotYields`, is removed from `internal/ledger/pot_yield.go`. The queries live on the
ledger's view only. The twelve test files that still called the reader's methods, in `internal/ledger`,
`internal/cardrules`, `internal/potrules` and `internal/txrules`, open a view instead, with no change
to what they expect.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is a SQLite file,
`pluggy-snapshot.db`, that a separate collector fills from the banks every night and replaces by an
atomic rename; the app only reads it, and "the snapshot" is that file. *The reader* is `ledger.Reader`
in `internal/ledger`, built with `ledger.New(path)`; it holds only the path. *The ledger's view* is a
type of the same package that is one handle and one read-only transaction on the snapshot, on which
each of the 13 queries runs, so that all the queries made through one view see one snapshot even when
the collector swaps the file meanwhile.

**How the code got here.** The view was added first, with the reader's own 13 methods kept as wrappers,
each opening a view for one call, so that no caller had to change: twelve of them gathered in one file
of their own, and `PotYields` left in `pot_yield.go` beside the view's method of the same name. Then
the HTTP backend was moved onto views: every read handler of `internal/api` receives a view of each
store, opened for its request ({{F3b}}), and no file of `internal/api`, tests included, calls a query
method of the reader any more. What is left on the wrappers is tests outside that package, and this
slice is the last step.

**The 13 queries** (checked in `internal/ledger` as it is before the view exists; the view's methods
carry the same names): `Accounts`, `Bills`, `BalanceHistory`, `ReserveHistory`, `Identities`,
`InvestmentPrincipals`, `Investments`, `InvestmentHistory`, `Pots`, `PotYields`, `SyncState`,
`CleanTransactions`, `YieldHistory`.

**The tests that still call the reader** (each checked in the file named, before the earlier steps):

- `internal/ledger`: `records_test.go`, `transactions_test.go`, `pot_yield_test.go`, `history_test.go`,
  `yield_history_test.go`, `safety_test.go`, `support_test.go` (whose `everyQuery` walks 12 of the 13
  queries on a reader and whose `populated` fixture most of them use) and `realsnapshot_test.go`.
- `internal/cardrules`: `forecast_test.go` (it reads `Bills` and `CleanTransactions` of an invented
  snapshot) and `realsnapshot_test.go`.
- `internal/potrules`: `realsnapshot_test.go`, which passes the reader to helpers typed
  `*ledger.Reader`, calls `Accounts`, `Pots` and `PotYields`, and hands `reader.CleanTransactions` on as
  a method value.
- `internal/txrules`: `realsnapshot_test.go` (`Accounts`, `Identities`, `CleanTransactions`).

Five of those twelve are opt-in tests that read a real ledger and are skipped unless
`FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set: the four files named `realsnapshot_test.go`, and nothing else in this
list. Because they are skipped in the gate, they are checked by compiling and by reading.

**What changes.**

1. The wrapper file is deleted, and the reader's `PotYields` is removed from `pot_yield.go`. After
   this, `*ledger.Reader` keeps `New` and what opens a view, and has no query method.
2. Each of the twelve test files opens a view where it called the reader, and closes it. No
   expectation changes: the same rows, the same typed errors. Where a test expects an error of the
   snapshot itself (a missing file, another schema version, a file that is not a database, a damaged
   one), the error is the one returned by whichever call first touches the file, opening the view or
   its first query; the test keeps asserting the same kind of error for the same file.
3. One test states the old rule and cannot simply be moved: `TestEachCallSeesTheFileThatIsThereNow` in
   `safety_test.go` says that a call made after the snapshot is renamed sees the new file, which was
   true of a reader that opened the file on every call. It is replaced by the rule of the view: a view
   opened after the rename answers from the new file. That a view opened before the rename keeps
   answering from the old one is already proved by the view's own tests, and is not repeated.
4. The other promises of `safety_test.go` are kept over a view, unchanged in what they assert: every
   query refuses an unsupported version; the open path refuses writes
   (`TestSnapshotOpenPathRefusesWrites`, which goes through `ledger.OpenReadOnly` in `export_test.go`
   and does not use the reader); `TestQueriesLeaveTheSnapshotByteForByteUntouched`; a missing snapshot
   is an error and not an empty ledger; a file that is not a database, and a damaged one, are
   unreadable.

**The guard that must stay true.** `internal/api/pots_yield_guard_test.go` scans every non-test file
under `internal/` and `cmd/` for the identifier `PotYields`, the collector's slow reference statement
that no request may reach, and exempts only `internal/ledger/pot_yield.go` and `queries.go`, by path.
The view's `PotYields` therefore stays in `pot_yield.go`, and no other non-test file may come to name
it. The tests that call it (`internal/ledger/pot_yield_test.go`, `internal/potrules/realsnapshot_test.go`)
are test files, which the scan does not read. Remove the reader's `PotYields` only once nothing calls
it: after the tests are moved, `go vet ./...` says so.

**Why it is done, and what lost.** A fresh handle per query is exactly what lets one answer mix two
snapshots; that is the fault the view exists to remove, and a wrapper is that fault kept available.
Leaving the wrappers for the convenience of tests lost: later work that reads the ledger outside a
request (the job that brings a new snapshot into the app's own database must read the run that produced
the rows and the rows themselves from one snapshot) would find two ways to ask and no warning on the
wrong one.

**Why it is one step.** The deletion and the tests that call the deleted methods have to land
together: with a wrapper gone, a test file that still calls it does not compile, and `go vet ./...`
fails for the whole module. The tests may be moved in commits before the one that deletes, package by
package, each of which builds.

**Privacy.** The repository is public and a real ledger is a person's whole financial history. This
slice edits four opt-in tests that read a real ledger, so the rule applies in full: a real snapshot may
be opened read-only; no value from it (amount, description, name, document, id) is ever printed,
logged, copied into a file, a commit, a bead or a pull request; a count may be shown to the person
running the test and goes into no file; those tests run only when `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` names a
file. The edits here change how a query is reached and nothing about what those tests log. Fixtures are
invented (`internal/ledger/ledgertest`), and no `.db` file is opened by hand.

**Conventions.** Work happens in a git worktree of its own and ends at local commits: atomic,
Conventional Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a plan in a commit
message. Money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path (this slice touches no
amount). Every SQL statement over the snapshot stays a registered constant of `queries.go`, as every
statement over the app's own database must be; this slice adds none. Interface text is Brazilian
Portuguese and everything else is English; a design value in a component comes from a token (this slice
touches no component).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `command grep -n "^func (reader \*Reader) [A-Z]" internal/ledger/*.go` lists no query method: the
wrapper file is gone and `pot_yield.go` holds only the view's `PotYields`.
- [ ] `go build ./... && go vet ./...` pass, which includes the four opt-in test files compiling.
- [ ] `go test ./internal/ledger ./internal/cardrules ./internal/potrules ./internal/txrules` passes,
and in the twelve test files the only changes are how a query is reached: no expected value, no
fixture and no assertion is changed, except the replacement of
`TestEachCallSeesTheFileThatIsThereNow`.
- [ ] In `internal/ledger`, a view opened after a second invented snapshot is renamed over the path
answers from the second snapshot.
- [ ] `go test ./internal/api -run TestNoReadHandlerReachesTheCollectorsYieldStatement` passes, and
`command grep -rln "PotYields" internal cmd --include='*.go'` lists, among non-test files, only
`internal/ledger/pot_yield.go`.
- [ ] No file under `internal/api`, `cmd/`, `internal/authored` or `web/` is changed, no non-test file
other than the wrapper file and `pot_yield.go` is changed, and `git diff` of `internal/ledger/queries.go`
is empty.
- [ ] `TestEveryAnswerMatchesItsGoldenFile` passes without `-update`.
- [ ] The four opt-in real-ledger tests are run once **by the review**, not by the implementer, with
`FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` set, printing counts only.
- [ ] The replacement test was seen failing once, against a view made to keep the handle of an earlier
view; and the deletion was seen to matter once: with one wrapper put back and one moved test put back
on it, the build passes, and with the wrapper removed again that test file no longer compiles. Both are
named in the final report.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, `ledger.Reader` has no query method, and the yield guard
of `internal/api` passes.

## Tests
- Unit, over the `populated` fixture of `internal/ledger/support_test.go` and the invented snapshots
  each file already builds with `ledgertest`: the existing tests of `internal/ledger`, reached through
  a view, with their expectations unchanged.
- Unit, over two invented snapshots (`ledgertest.NewAt` at a second path and `os.Rename`, as the test
  it replaces builds them): a view opened after the rename sees the new file.
- Unit, over the invented snapshot `internal/cardrules/forecast_test.go` already builds: the same test
  through a view.
- Integration, opt-in, over a real ledger: the four `realsnapshot_test.go` files, compiled in the gate
  and run by the review, counts only.
- Source test, existing and unedited: `TestNoReadHandlerReachesTheCollectorsYieldStatement`.
- Golden, existing and unedited: the answers of `internal/api` over the two invented ledgers.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/ledger/pot_yield.go`, `internal/ledger/records_test.go`,
`internal/ledger/transactions_test.go`, `internal/ledger/pot_yield_test.go`,
`internal/ledger/history_test.go`, `internal/ledger/yield_history_test.go`,
`internal/ledger/safety_test.go`, `internal/ledger/support_test.go`,
`internal/ledger/realsnapshot_test.go`, `internal/cardrules/forecast_test.go`,
`internal/cardrules/realsnapshot_test.go`, `internal/potrules/realsnapshot_test.go`,
`internal/txrules/realsnapshot_test.go`
**Reads only:** `internal/ledger/open.go`, `internal/ledger/queries.go`, `internal/ledger/export_test.go`,
`internal/ledger/schema_test.go`, `internal/ledger/ledgertest/`, `internal/api/`,
`internal/api/pots_yield_guard_test.go`, `cmd/finwise/serve.go`, `bin/ci`

Fourteen files in four packages, of which two are production code: the wrapper file, which is deleted
whole, and `pot_yield.go`, which loses one method. The other twelve are tests whose only change is to
open a view. It is labelled large for that count and mechanical for its content: there is no rule to
design and no answer to change. It stays one bead because the deletion and the tests that call the
deleted methods cannot land apart. `internal/api` and `cmd/finwise` are read to confirm that nothing
there still calls the reader's queries; if something does, that is a defect of the step before this one
and is reported, not patched here.

title: Check the write side over a real ledger with a scripted series of writes on a scratch database, saying counts and fixed sentences only
description:
## What changes for the user
Nothing on screen changes with this piece. Everything the app does when the person changes something (a
category, a split, a reimbursement, a budget, a closed month) has been proved on invented data only, and
a real history has shapes no invented one has: purchases the bank still reports as pending, purchases
abroad, taxes folded under their purchase, fifteen months of one person's habits. After this lands, one
command run on the person's own machine, against their real history and a throwaway copy of the app's
database, says whether every total still adds up after each kind of change and whether taking all of it
back leaves the database exactly as it was. It says so without ever showing an amount, a name or an id.
If this piece were wrong the person would notice in one of two ways: months later, as a total that
silently lost a split purchase or an undo that left a tag behind; or at once, as their own transactions
printed into a terminal, a log or a pull request.

## Outcome
`internal/api` has an opt-in test of the write side over a real ledger. It runs only when
`FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` names a file, opens that snapshot read-only, creates a scratch `finwise.db` in
the test's temporary directory, and checks: the two invariants of the budget's dispositions in every
month of the ledger, before and after a scripted series of writes on transactions picked by position;
what the ingest counted; that every write of the series that is a recorded change can be undone, and that
once all are undone the journaled tables are exactly as they were before the series; and, apart, that
the index of transactions only grew. Every comparison happens in memory. On success it logs counts; on
failure it says fixed sentences. The same series and the same checks run in every `go test` over the
invented ledger, where each check is also shown to fail.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is the SQLite snapshot a
separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app only reads it, and no code here ever writes
to it. *The app's database* is `finwise.db`, owned by the package `internal/authored`, where everything
the person authors is kept; the server has one only when started with `--db` ({{F1}}: the database, its
recognition and its migrations). *The manifest* is `internal/contract/contract.json`, the generated
description of the API's 82 methods; 55 are of class `write` and one, `budget.evaluateScenario`, of class
`evaluate`. *The recorder* is the layer of `internal/authored` through which every change to the app's
database is written, and *the journal* is what it writes: one row in `changes` per change (author,
method, instant, Brazil day, whether it was extended or undone) and one row in `change_effects` per
effect ({{F2}}: the recorder, the journal and undo). A *journaled table* is one the recorder knows from
its closed registry. The tables that are deliberately not journaled are `changes`, `change_effects`,
`schema_migrations`, `meta`, `tx_index`, `tx_ids`, `lines` and `pin`. *Undo* (`changes.undo(changeId)`)
is the inverse of a change's recorded effects: it restores every `before` and marks the change undone;
it is refused with the error kind `refused` and the reason `stale_change`, changing nothing, when the
change is unknown or already undone or when a later change still in force has an effect on any unit the
change touched; undo is not itself undoable. *The stand-in* is the in-memory fake backend under
`web/src/api/fake/` that the design prototype runs on; it plays no part here. *A listed transaction* is
one the API lists: the collector's clean list after the transaction rules (`internal/txrules`) folded tax
rows under their purchases and took the movements of savings pots out.

**The index.** `tx_index(tx_key, account_id, day, cents, establishment_key, bank_pending, first_run,
last_run, evaluated)` and `tx_ids(provider_id, tx_key)` are what the app's database remembers about the
transactions it has evaluated or the person has touched ({{T1}}: the transactions' tables, the index and
the dispositions). A transaction's key, `tx_key`, is minted by the app's database; `tx_ids` maps every
provider id seen to it. The two tables record observations, not decisions, so they are not journaled: a
write creates or refreshes the index row of each transaction it names, and an undo does not remove it.
No amount shown or summed ever comes from the index.

**What "pending" means.** One definition serves the queue, every count and the closing of a month: a
transaction is pending when it is pending in the app's database, the ledger lists it now, and its month's
budget has at least one line.

**What exists today (each point checked in the file named).**

- Opt-in tests over a real snapshot already exist for the read side, in `internal/ledger`,
  `internal/txrules`, `internal/cardrules`, `internal/potrules` and, in `internal/api`,
  `realsnapshot_test.go`, `realsnapshot_money_test.go`, `fresh_install_realsnapshot_test.go`,
  `pots_yield_realsnapshot_test.go` and `pots_yield_months_realsnapshot_test.go`. None of them writes
  anything.
- `internal/api/golden_test.go` holds `snapshotVariable` (`"FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT"`) and
  `goldenUpdateRefusal`, which refuses `-update` while the variable is set so that a real ledger cannot
  reach a committed file.
- `internal/api/realsnapshot_test.go` holds the helpers this test starts from. `realSnapshotPath` skips
  the test when the variable is unset. `withoutValues` fails a step with the step's name and the error's
  Go type, never its text, because the text of an error can carry a row id. `realRun.answer` calls a read
  through the router with a session open, requires 200, counts the answer, and reports a body that does
  not conform to its result schema with the words "the message is withheld", because a schema error can
  quote the value it rejected. `answerSomeDetails` picks the first, the middle and the last id of a
  month's list: that is what "picked by position" means in this repository. Its file comment states the
  rule the read side follows: no value from the snapshot, "an amount, a description, a name, a document,
  an id, a month", may reach a log or a failure message; a label this package wrote itself is not a value
  from the snapshot.
- `internal/api/realsnapshot_money_test.go` shows the house pattern for an opt-in check that CI never
  runs: the counting it relies on is exercised a second time over invented data
  (`TestTheCardCountsSeparateABillFromAPurchase`), so that it is known to be able to count and to fail.
- `internal/api/harness_test.go` builds the router for a test: `withLedger(path, now)` gives it a ledger
  reader and a fixed clock; `newTestEnv` gives it a log buffer, so the request log of a test goes to
  memory and not to the terminal. Note that `newTestEnv` fails with `t.Fatalf("NewHandler: %v", err)`,
  which prints an error's text.
- `internal/api/handler_silence_test.go`: `TestNoHandlerLogsWhatItReads` runs every read case over the
  two invented ledgers and fails if any log holds one of a list of strings only the fixtures and the
  arguments hold (`tx-`, `acc-`, `card-itau`, `LIVRARIA`, `EXEMPLO`, `Exemplo`, `2026-02`, `no-such`,
  `12345678`).

**What this test stands on, delivered by earlier work.** The write conformance harness ({{F5}}: the
harness for writes, the package `internal/authored/authoredtest` that builds invented states of the app's
database, and the canonical dump) gives three things this test reuses: a way to build a migrated
`finwise.db` in a temporary directory from a clock handed in; *the canonical dump*, a deterministic text
of the content of every journaled table, taken from the recorder's registry, equal bytes for equal
states; and its checks by mode, each a function that names what is wrong. Those checks were written for
invented data and may quote what they compared. Over a real ledger they are used for their verdict only
and their text is withheld, as `realRun.answer` withholds a conformance problem.

**The dispositions and the two invariants.** `budgetrules.Dispose` ({{T1}}) puts every listed transaction
in exactly one disposition and says what it adds to which budget line. Amounts are magnitudes in integer
cents. The first condition that matches wins:

| # | disposition | condition | counts |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | unconverted | the ledger has no value in reais for it | nothing |
| 2 | movement | a movement between own accounts or a bill payment | nothing |
| 3 | excluded | excluded with a reason | nothing |
| 4 | waiting | pending review | nothing |
| 5 | split | a debit with two or more parts | each part with a line adds its amount to that line; the rest (the amount less those parts, which is negative when they exceed it) is unassigned |
| 6 | fee | a fee row, charge or discount, that is on no line (as the existing fees rule defines it: posted) or that the person put on the fees line | a charge adds to the fees line; the credit that discounts it takes off |
| 7 | reimbursement | a credit linked to a purchase | no line; the smaller of its amount and the purchase's is applied inside the purchase, and any excess counts nowhere |
| 8 | refund | a credit that is a refund | reduces its refund line by its amount; with no refund line, nothing |
| 9 | income | a credit on a line of the income group | received on that line |
| 10 | other credit | any other credit | nothing |
| 11 | on a line | a debit with a line | its amount less the applied reimbursement |
| 12 | uncategorised | a debit with no line | nothing; its amount less the applied reimbursement is unassigned |

A row the bank still reports as pending is listed and counts like any other; the existing fees rule keeps
counting only posted fee rows. An exclusion takes effect only once it has a reason: switched on without
one, the transaction keeps counting. What a linked credit takes off its purchase is the smaller of the
two amounts, so a purchase's effective amount never changes sign.

Two invariants guard the totals, and this test checks both in every month the ledger holds, by Brazil
month:

1. For every debit of dispositions 5, 11 and 12: what it adds to lines, plus what is unassigned, plus the
   applied reimbursement, equals its amount.
2. Every listed transaction is in exactly one disposition, so the dispositions' counts add up to the
   number of transactions the API lists for the month and their amounts to the sum of the listed
   magnitudes.

Both are already a property test over generated transactions in `internal/budgetrules`. What is new here
is the real composition: the dispositions come from the same function the API uses to dispose a month
(the one that joins the ledger's rows with the authored rows and calls `Dispose`), and the number and the
sum they are held against come from another path, the answer of `transactions.list` for that month
through the router. Amounts read from an answer are turned into cents by `ParseReais` ({{F4b}}: the
parser that reads a JSON number into integer cents from its decimal text), never through a float. For
what the magnitude of an unconverted row is, follow the definition the property test of `budgetrules`
uses.

**The ingest and its counts.** `ingest.Run` ({{R2}}: the one function that brings the app's database up
to date with a snapshot) refreshes the index, pairs a vanished bank-pending row with the posted row that
replaced it, and, for every listed transaction dated on or after the *tracking start month* that was
never evaluated and whose month's budget has at least one line, indexes it, marks it evaluated and
applies the rules once: leave it, apply a line by rule, or make it pending with one of three reasons,
"Baixa confiança", "PIX para pessoa sem apelido" or "Estabelecimento novo". The tracking start month is
the Brazil month in which the app's database was created, set once from the injected clock at creation
and never again; earlier transactions are never put in the queue. A transaction whose month has no
budget stays unevaluated. A budget save calls the ingest after its own commit and before it answers. An
evaluated transaction is never evaluated again. If anything authored changed, the run records one change
whose author is `rule`; with nothing to record, no change is written. It returns counts only: indexed,
paired, unpaired, applied by rule, and pending per reason.

On a database created by this test, where nobody has yet put any transaction on a line, the rules leave
no room for some outcomes, and the test asserts exactly these consequences:

- Before any budget exists, a run evaluates nothing: applied by rule is 0 and pending is 0 for every
  reason.
- After the first budget is saved, applied by rule is 0, because a line is applied by rule only from an
  establishment's default line or from examples the person made, and there are none; "Baixa confiança"
  is 0 and no pending transaction carries a suggestion, for the same reason; paired and unpaired are 0,
  because pairing needs an index row from an earlier run.
- The pending counts of the run add up to the pending count `shell.overview` answers and to the number of
  items in the queue of `review.weekly`.
- No item of the queue is dated before the tracking start month.
- A second run right after changes nothing: no row is added to `changes`, the canonical dump is equal,
  and no index row appeared.

**The clock.** The server's clock is injected, never the host's, so that a snapshot copied days ago gives
the same run. "Today" is an instant in the Brazil month of the ledger's latest listed transaction, so the
current month has rows to act on; the scratch database is created at that same instant, so its tracking
start month is the current month, which is the state of the person's first day with the write side. The
month is taken from the ledger in memory and never printed.

**The series.** It is a fixed table of steps in the test's own file. A step names a method, how its
target is picked, and its arguments.

- *Targets are picked by position.* A step takes its transaction, pot, subscription or queue item from a
  list the API answers (the first, the middle or the last of a month's `transactions.list`, the first
  item of the queue, the first pot of the list), as `answerSomeDetails` does. No step searches for a
  name, an amount or an id, so no value of a real ledger is ever in the source.
- *Arguments are the test's own.* Line names, a tag, a note, a nickname, a reason and a scenario's name
  are invented constants of the test; amounts are constants or halves of what the answer just gave,
  computed in cents.
- *Setup, before the series.* The test saves a first budget for the current month through `budget.save`
  with invented lines in the five editable groups (income, fixed, variable, provisions, reserves), so
  that every later step has a line to name and the ingest has a budget to evaluate against. The state
  after this save and its ingest is the series' starting point.
- *Coverage.* The series performs every write whose conformance mode is a recorded change and that has a
  handler when this work is done. There are 47 such methods in the contract: the 24 writes of
  `transactions`; `budget.save`, `budget.saveScenario` and `budget.applyScenario`; `subscriptions.create`,
  `setStatus`, `setLine`, `setReviewDate` and `setNote`; `review.acceptPending`, `dismissWarning`,
  `markStepDone`, `keepSubscription`, `cancelSubscription`, `closeMonth` and `markTransferDone`; and the
  eight writes of `settings`. Among them, `transactions.applyLineToEstablishment` is the extension of an
  earlier change (it appends its effects to the `setLine` change it started from and answers the same id,
  so one undo takes back both) and `transactions.undoHistoryStep` is a recorded change that takes one
  step of a transaction's history back.
- *The other modes, once each.* A write that answers null (the same line set again on a transaction, and
  each of the six methods that answer only null until the thing they act on has a producer:
  `subscriptions.acceptSuggestion`, `subscriptions.rejectSuggestion`, `review.approve`, `review.refuse`,
  `review.propose`, `review.runWarningAction`) adds no row to the journal. The evaluation,
  `budget.evaluateScenario`, changes no table at all. `changes.undo` and `session.changePin` are not
  steps: the first is how the series is taken back, and the second is not a recorded change and has its
  own tests.
- *Three of the 47 may not exist yet.* The work this depends on guarantees handlers for 44 of them. Not
  guaranteed are `review.dismissWarning` ({{V2}}: the warnings derived from subscriptions and their
  dismissal) and `settings.setNickname` and `settings.setDefaultLine` ({{S3}}: the establishments and
  people of the settings overview and the two settings writes by key). A step exists for each of the 47;
  the three are in a named list of steps allowed to find no handler. A test that needs no snapshot holds
  the table against the registered handlers: a registered recorded-change write with no step fails it,
  and so does a name in that list whose handler exists. Its message says, in one sentence, which method
  needs a step and in which file, so that whoever adds a write later can act on it without this bead.
- *A step with no target is skipped and counted.* A real ledger may have no received PIX to link as a
  reimbursement, no pot with a stable identity, no card purchase in the current month, no warning to
  dismiss, or a single month, so that no month can be closed. Such a step is counted under a fixed label
  and is never a silent pass; a snapshot that lists no transaction at all fails the test with a fixed
  sentence. A write the server refuses with a reason (`refused`) where the step expected a change is a
  failure, reported by the method's name, the status and the reason, which are all from closed lists.

**The order of the run.**

1. Skip unless `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set. Create the scratch database. Run the ingest and assert
   the counts of a database with no budget. Check the two invariants in every month.
2. Setup: save the first budget. Assert the counts of the ingest that followed it. Take the canonical
   dump and the keys of the index: the starting point.
3. Perform the series. After each recorded change, nothing is compared yet; the change's id is kept.
4. With every change of the series in force, check the two invariants in every month again. This is the
   state that matters: splits, linked reimbursements, exclusions with and without a reason, refunds and
   a closed month are all present at once.
5. Assert that the journal gained no change authored by `rule` during the series: every tracked
   transaction was evaluated in step 2, and the rules run once per transaction.
6. Undo every change of the series, newest first. Each undo must succeed: in that order no later change
   still in force stands in the way, so a `stale_change` here is a defect.
7. Take the canonical dump again and compare it with the starting point, in memory, byte for byte.
8. Apart, check the index: every `tx_key` and every provider id present at the starting point is still
   present, and neither table lost a row. Their content may have been refreshed; their rows only grow.

**What may be printed.** The repository's rule, in full: the repository is public and a real ledger is a
person's whole financial history. A real snapshot may be opened read-only. No value from it (amount,
description, name, document, id) is ever printed, logged, copied into a file, a commit, a bead or a pull
request. A count may be shown to the person running the test and goes into no file: not the pull request
body, not a commit message, not a bead. The test runs only when `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` names a file.
Fixtures are invented. This repository also treats a month and a day as values.

For this test that means, on success and on failure alike:

- A message is built only from constants of the test (the number and the method of a step, the name of a
  check, a fixed label), counts, HTTP statuses, error kinds and refusal reasons (both closed lists), the
  names of journaled tables (they come from the recorder's registry, not from the ledger) and the Go type
  of an error. Never the text of an error, a response body, a row, a struct that holds ledger data, a
  diff, an SQL statement's parameter, a month, a day, an id, a key or a tag.
- Dumps and index keys are compared in memory. Nothing of this run is written under `testdata/` or
  anywhere else; no helper that prints a diff on mismatch, or that rewrites a golden file, is called.
- An establishment key (the identity of an establishment or a person, with the prefix `doc:`, `name:` or
  `text:`) can be a document number. It is held in memory like an id and never printed.
- The scratch database holds real values from the moment the ingest runs: the index carries account ids,
  days, amounts and establishment keys. It lives only in `t.TempDir()`, which Go removes when the test
  ends, pass or fail. If the test binary is killed, that directory survives under the system's temporary
  directory: the test's file comment says so, so the person knows what to delete.
- Helpers shared with the fixture tests may print an error's text (`newTestEnv` does). Every call that
  can fail on real data goes through a wrapper that withholds the text, as `withoutValues` does.

**What is left to the implementer, and what constrains it** (this is why the bead is `spec:open`).

- *The steps themselves*: which position each takes, in which order, and the invented arguments, under
  the rules of "The series" above. The order must let every step that can have a target have one (a
  purchase is marked reimbursable before a credit is linked to it; a purchase that will be split is not
  the one that gets a reimbursement, because a split purchase cannot have a linked reimbursement and the
  server refuses it with `split_with_reimbursement`; a subscription is created before its status is set).
- *How the index and the journal's authors are read.* Every SQL statement over the app's database is a
  registered constant of `internal/authored`, so the test carries no SQL of its own. If the functions the
  package and `authoredtest` already expose do not answer "which keys does the index hold" and "which
  authors does the journal hold since this change", the smallest addition goes in `authoredtest`.
- *How the files are divided.* The step table, the checks and the two tests may be one file or three,
  beside the existing real-snapshot tests.

**Conventions.** Work happens in a git worktree of its own and ends at local commits: atomic,
Conventional Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a plan in a commit
message. Money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path, in a test included. Every SQL
statement over the app's database is a registered constant. Interface text is Brazilian Portuguese and
everything else is English; a design value in a component comes from a token (this work touches no
component).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Without `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT`, `go test ./internal/api -run RealSnapshot -v` reports the new
opt-in test as skipped, and `bin/ci` neither runs it nor needs a snapshot.
- [ ] The same series and the same checks run in an always-on test over the full invented ledger of
`internal/api/fixtures_test.go` and a scratch database built by `authoredtest`, and pass: every step
that can have a target there has one, and the count of steps skipped for lack of a target is asserted
as an exact number.
- [ ] The series' table holds a step for each of the 47 recorded-change writes named in the Context; a
test that needs no snapshot fails when a registered recorded-change write has no step, and when a method
in the list of steps allowed to find no handler has one. The list holds at most `review.dismissWarning`,
`settings.setNickname` and `settings.setDefaultLine`.
- [ ] Each of the six null-only methods and one same-line `transactions.setLine` is called once, answers
`null`, and adds no row to `changes`; `budget.evaluateScenario` is called once and changes no table.
- [ ] The two invariants are checked in every month of the ledger at two moments: on the fresh database
and with every change of the series in force. The count and the sum of invariant 2 come from the
answer of `transactions.list`, parsed with `ParseReais`.
- [ ] The ingest's counts are asserted as the Context lists them: all zero before a budget exists; after
the first save, applied by rule 0, "Baixa confiança" 0, paired 0, unpaired 0, no suggestion on any
pending transaction; pending per reason adding up to the pending count of `shell.overview` and to the
length of the queue of `review.weekly`; no queue item before the tracking start month; a second run
adding no row to `changes` and leaving the dump and the index as they were.
- [ ] The journal gains no change authored by `rule` between the first and the last step of the series.
- [ ] Every change the series recorded is undone newest first and each undo answers 200; afterwards the
canonical dump of every journaled table equals, byte for byte, the dump taken before the first step.
- [ ] Every `tx_key` and every provider id the index held before the first step is still there after the
last undo, and neither `tx_index` nor `tx_ids` has fewer rows.
- [ ] Each check is a function that returns what is wrong, and an always-on test feeds each its own
break and requires a complaint: one change left out of the undos; one transaction dropped from a
month's dispositions; one split part left out of a debit's sum; one key removed from the index; one
pending count off by one; one change by `rule` added during the series.
- [ ] An always-on test collects every message the checks produce under those breaks over the invented
ledger and fails if any of them contains a string only the fixtures or the series' arguments hold: the
strings of `TestNoHandlerLogsWhatItReads` plus each invented argument of the series.
- [ ] `command grep -n "t.Log\|t.Error\|t.Fatal\|Sprintf\|Errorf" ` over the new files shows no format
verb fed by an error's text, a body, a row, a month, a day, an id or a key: only constants, counts,
statuses, kinds, reasons, table names and `%T`.
- [ ] The final report lists every message the new files can produce, with its format string, in one
place, and the failure path is read by the review, not only by the implementer.
- [ ] The new files write nothing to disk outside `t.TempDir()`, and `git status` after a run with the
variable set shows no new or changed file.
- [ ] The opt-in run over a real snapshot passes. It is made by whoever holds a snapshot (the review, on
the person's machine); the pull request body states that it passed and repeats none of its counts.
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, each against its own deliberate break, named in the final
report: the six breaks above for the checks; a step removed from the table for the coverage test; a
handler registered for a method of the allowed list for the same test; an invented argument printed by
a check for the no-value test.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, the always-on test passes over the invented ledger with
every check shown to fail, and the opt-in run over a real snapshot passes with its output read by the
review and found to hold counts and fixed sentences only.

## Tests
- Integration, opt-in (`FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT`), over a real snapshot opened read-only and a scratch
  `finwise.db` in the test's temporary directory: the order of the run in the Context, steps 1 to 8.
- Integration, always on, over the full invented ledger of `fixtures_test.go` and a database built by
  `authoredtest`: the same series and the same checks, with the exact number of steps skipped.
- Unit, in the pattern of `TestTheConformanceCheckRejectsAnAnswerThatDoesNotMatch`: each check fed its
  broken input (an undo left out, a disposition dropped, a split part left out, an index key removed, a
  pending count off by one, a change by `rule` added).
- Unit: the coverage of the step table against the registered recorded-change writes, with a test of the
  test, in the pattern of `TestTheCoverageCheckFailsWhenAHandlerIsMissingOrInvented`.
- Unit: no message of the checks holds a fixture's or an argument's string, over the messages produced
  under the breaks.
- Manual, by the review: the output of one opt-in run and the source of every message, read for values.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/api/realsnapshot_writes_test.go`, `internal/api/realsnapshot_writes_series_test.go`,
`internal/api/realsnapshot_writes_checks_test.go`, `internal/authored/authoredtest/`
**Reads only:** `internal/api/realsnapshot_test.go`, `internal/api/realsnapshot_money_test.go`,
`internal/api/golden_test.go`, `internal/api/harness_test.go`, `internal/api/helpers_test.go`,
`internal/api/handler_silence_test.go`, `internal/api/fixtures_test.go`, `internal/authored/`,
`internal/budgetrules/`, `internal/ingest/`, `internal/contract/contract.json`, `bin/ci`

Test code only: up to three new test files in `internal/api` (one if they read better together; the
names are the implementer's and end in `_test.go`) and, only if a read of the index or of the journal's
authors is missing, one small addition to the test-support package `internal/authored/authoredtest`. No
production file changes, no golden file is written, and the existing real-snapshot tests are read, not
edited: their helpers are in the same package and are called as they are. The collector's snapshot is
opened read-only and nothing is created beside it.

It is labelled critical although it changes no production code: it is the one place where real financial
data meets code that writes, and its mistake would be silent in both directions, a check that cannot
fail or a message that carries a value.

title: Open every screen on the backend's recorded answers
description:
## What changes for the user
The backend and the screens are written in two languages by different hands, and each is tested against its own idea of the other. A field the backend names slightly differently, or leaves out, would pass both sides' tests and show up as a blank on the person's screen. After this lands every screen is also opened, in the gate, against the exact answers the real backend gives, so that kind of mismatch is caught before anyone sees it.

## Outcome
A test in the interface's suite serves the backend's recorded answers through the API contract and mounts every screen over them, for a ledger with every shape and for an empty one.

## Context
finwise's Go backend records what each of its `read` methods answers over two invented ledgers, as golden files under `internal/api/testdata/golden/<ledger>/<domain>.<method>.json`; a Go test keeps those files equal to what the handlers return, and they are generated only from invented data. The interface (`web/`) reaches a backend through the `FinwiseApi` contract and already has a sweep test that mounts every route over two states of its in-memory stand-in and fails on a thrown error, an unhandled rejection, or `NaN`, `undefined`, `Infinity`, `null` or `Invalid Date` in the rendered text.

The two sides agree on shape through a JSON Schema generated from the contract, and the Go answers are validated against it. A schema cannot say whether a screen holds on those answers. This bead closes that gap by reusing both existing pieces: the golden files as data, the sweep as the assertion.

**The replay API.** A test helper builds a `FinwiseApi` whose `read` methods answer from the golden files of one ledger and whose other methods reject with the contract's `read_only` error, as the backend does. A method whose arguments select among answers (a month, an id) answers from the file recorded for those arguments; the helper fails loudly when asked for something that was not recorded, so a screen that requests an unexpected month is a finding and not a silent `undefined`. The session methods answer unlocked.

**Where the files are read from.** The golden directory belongs to the Go side and stays there; the test reads it by path from the repository root. It is not copied into `web/`, because a copy can go stale.

**Two implementations, one first day.** The interface's in-memory stand-in and the Go backend each say what an empty ledger looks like, and nothing keeps them saying the same thing: a group label, a default threshold or the shape of an empty budget can drift on one side and every test of both sides still passes. Over the empty ledger there is no bank data to differ, so the two must agree exactly. A test compares, for every `read` method, the backend's recorded answer over its empty ledger with the stand-in's answer over its empty-ledger state, deep-equal, apart from a short written list of fields that legitimately differ (the clock's day, the wording of the sync state) with the reason for each. A difference outside that list is fixed on the side that departed from the contract's intent, and never by adding to the list without a reason.

**What a failure means.** A screen breaking over a golden answer is a real mismatch between the two sides. It is fixed where the fault is: in the handler when the answer departs from the contract's intent, in the screen when the screen assumed more than the contract promises. It is never fixed by editing a golden file by hand.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The replay helper answers every `read` method of the manifest from a golden file, for both recorded ledgers, and a missing file for a `read` method fails the test by name.
- [ ] The sweep mounts every route of `web/src/router.ts`, plus the transaction panel, a pot's page, an account's page, the card page and a subscription's page where the ledger has one, over both ledgers, with the same assertions as the existing sweep.
- [ ] A request for arguments that were not recorded fails the test with the method and the arguments in the message.
- [ ] A write through the replay API rejects with `read_only`.
- [ ] For every `read` method, the backend's recorded answer over the empty ledger equals the stand-in's answer over its empty-ledger state, apart from a written list of excepted fields, each with its reason; changing one label in either side makes the test fail and name the method and the field.
- [ ] Renaming a field in one golden file makes the sweep fail on the screen that reads it.
- [ ] The test runs inside `npm --prefix web test`, and so inside `bin/ci`, with no browser and no running backend.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and the sweep passes over both recorded ledgers.

## Tests
- Component: the sweep over every route and both recorded ledgers.
- Unit: the replay helper's coverage of the manifest, its refusal of writes, and its failure on unrecorded arguments.
- The guard is broken once on purpose, by renaming a field in a golden file, and the failing screen named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `web/src/test/`
**Reads only:** `internal/api/testdata/golden/`, `internal/contract/contract.json`, `web/src/router.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/`, `bin/ci`

One test helper and one test file. If the sweep finds a mismatch, the fix lands in the handler or the screen at fault, in the same pull request, with a test beside it.
close_reason: A test helper serves the backend's golden files through the API contract and a sweep mounts every route, every listed pot, account and transaction over both recorded ledgers, failing on a thrown error, an unhandled rejection or broken text; a request for arguments that were not recorded fails by name. A second test requires the backend's answers over the empty ledger to equal the stand-in's, apart from a written list of excepted fields with a reason each, and fails on an excepted entry that no longer differs. The sweep found that a pot's page could not be reached from the list because its id holds a slash, fixed in the screen; the comparison found four places where the stand-in's first day departed from the backend's, fixed on the stand-in. bin/ci: CI green on the tree merged with main, 931 tests. Parity: 174 checked, 0 over 0.05%. The sweep still tolerates a read_only refusal on the scenarios route, which opens with an evaluation; a bug bead carries it.

title: Answer the frame, the accounts and the transactions from the ledger
description:
## What changes for the user
Until now every amount on screen is invented. After this lands, a person who starts the backend against their own ledger and unlocks with the PIN sees their real accounts and their real transactions: the right month, one line per purchase in reais, the tax under the purchase it belongs to, transfers between their own accounts set apart. What the app does not know yet (which budget line a purchase belongs to, tags, nicknames) shows as not filled in, never as a guess.

## Outcome
The backend answers six methods of the interface's contract from the ledger: `shell.overview`, `accounts.list`, `accounts.detail`, `transactions.list`, `transactions.filterOptions` and `transactions.detail`. Every answer is checked against the contract's schema, recorded as a golden file from invented data, and money leaves the server as an exact decimal.

## Context
finwise's interface talks to its backend through a contract described for Go by `internal/contract/contract.json`: for each method a route, a class, and schemas for its arguments and result. The HTTP layer (`internal/api`) already dispatches a `read` method to a handler registered for it, behind the PIN, and keeps a test-side list of reads still without a handler. The ledger reader (`internal/ledger`) returns typed rows in integer cents; `internal/txrules` turns a period's rows into the app's transactions (kind, signed amount, Brazil day, counterpart, establishment key, tax attached to its purchase, movements, pot movements set apart) with a tally that places every row. This bead joins them and is the first to show real data.

**What the rules expect of their caller.** `txrules.Interpret(rows, reference)` takes the reader's rows plus the accounts and the person's own documents, and returns the listed transactions, the tax rows it attached, the pot movements per account and the tally. Four things follow for this bead:
- A tax row is paired only with a purchase among the rows it was given, and a tax can fall up to 3 days from its purchase. Interpreting exactly one month would leave a tax listed on its own when the purchase is in the neighbouring month. Read the period widened by 3 days on each side, interpret, then keep the transactions whose day is inside the period. The month's tally is checked on the widened read; the cut to the period is checked by a test with a purchase on the last day of a month and its tax on the first day of the next.
- A movement (a bill payment, a transfer between own accounts) keeps one of the contract's kinds and carries a `Movement` field; it is not a separate kind.
- An attached tax is already inside its purchase's `Amount` and is also in `Tax`; it is never added a second time.
- A foreign row with no value in reais is flagged `Unconverted` and its amount is not in reais. It must not enter any sum, and the opt-in run over a real ledger reports how many there are.

**What is real and what is empty.** The backend is read-only and has no database of its own yet, so anything only the person can author comes back as on a fresh install. The contract was widened for that beforehand: a field with no honest value on a fresh install is nullable. The rule here is the same: a figure the ledger supports is real; anything else is the contract's empty value; nothing is invented.

| method | from the ledger | empty for now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `shell.overview` | today (the server's clock in America/Sao_Paulo), the first month with a transaction, the current month as the last, the sync state | pending count 0, closed months `[]` |
| `accounts.list`, `accounts.detail` | every current account with its balance, its bank, whether it has been idle for more than 30 days, and an account's transactions | the bucket an account belongs to |
| `transactions.list` | the clean list for the query's period through `internal/txrules`, newest first, filtered as the query asks | budget line, who classified it, confidence, tags, nickname, exclusion, split, reimbursement |
| `transactions.filterOptions` | the accounts | tags `[]`, lines `[]` |
| `transactions.detail` | the same base fields, the tax attached to the purchase, the original amount and currency, the instalment, the bill | history `[]`, notes, every section the person fills; `null` for an unknown id |

With an empty ledger (no account, no transaction) the first and last month are both the current month and every list is empty.

**The sync state.** `shell.overview.sync` is `ok` with the day and time of the last complete run, or a warning with a message when a connection is in trouble (a status other than `UPDATED`, an execution status other than `SUCCESS`, a last update older than 48 hours, or a consent about to expire). A message the person reads is Brazilian Portuguese and lives in one Go file with every other such string; everything else in the code is English. The stand-in's wording in `web/src/api/fake/` is the reference.

**Money on the wire.** The contract carries money as a JSON number in reais with decimals, negative meaning money out. The server holds integer cents. The conversion happens once, in a type whose JSON encoding writes the cents as a decimal literal with two places, so no float arithmetic ever touches an amount. `1999` is written `19.99` and `-6510` is written `-65.10`.

**No total of the month is computed here.** The contract's "spent" figures (the home summary's limit, the weekly review) mean what was spent on the budget's variable lines, and no transaction has a budget line yet, so those figures are 0 in later work and this bead adds no sum over the list.

**Conformance.** A test runs every handler of this bead over two ledgers built by the reader's fixture builder, one with every shape the rules know and one empty, and validates each answer against the method's result schema in the manifest with `github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6`, a test-only dependency. The same answers are stored as golden files under `internal/api/testdata/golden/<ledger>/<domain>.<method>.json`; the test fails when an answer differs from its file, and `-update` rewrites them. Because a golden file is committed to a public repository, `-update` refuses to run when `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set.

**A real ledger.** A test skipped unless `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set runs every handler over that file for every month it holds, validates every answer against its schema, checks that the tally of each month sums to its input rows, and logs counts only. No value from a real ledger is ever printed, logged or committed.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Each of the six methods answers 200 with a valid session, and its answer validates against its result schema over both fixture ledgers.
- [ ] Renaming one JSON field of any answer type makes the conformance test fail.
- [ ] `transactions.list` for February 2026 includes a fixture row dated `2026-03-01T02:30:00Z` and its list for March does not.
- [ ] A fixture purchase with its tax row appears as one line whose detail carries the tax; the tax row has no line of its own.
- [ ] A fixture pot movement is absent from `transactions.list`; a transfer between own accounts is present with the movement kind.
- [ ] Over the empty ledger, `shell.overview` gives the current month as first and last, and every list method answers `[]`.
- [ ] `transactions.detail` answers `null` for an unknown id.
- [ ] A purchase on the last day of a month whose tax row is dated the first day of the next appears in the first month as one line carrying the tax, and the tax row appears in neither month.
- [ ] A snapshot file that exists but is not a SQLite database answers 503 `ledger_unavailable`: the reader returns a typed error for a snapshot it cannot read, and the HTTP layer maps it. Today that case answers `internal`.
- [ ] `AGENTS.md` no longer says that no backend exists, and says how to see real data at the desktop.
- [ ] `1999` cents is encoded as `19.99`, `-6510` as `-65.10`, `0` as `0.00`; no handler converts cents to a float.
- [ ] A fixture connection with a status other than `UPDATED` produces a sync warning whose message is in Portuguese.
- [ ] Running the golden test with `-update` and `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` set fails without writing a file.
- [ ] The pending list of reads without a handler no longer names these six methods.
- [ ] The opt-in test over a real snapshot validates every answer of every month and logs counts only.
- [ ] `go.mod` gains `github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6` and no other direct dependency.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and the opt-in run reports every month's tally summing to its input rows with every answer valid.

## Tests
- Conformance: every answer against the manifest's schema, over both fixture ledgers.
- Golden: every answer against its file.
- Unit: the money encoding; the sync warning; the query's filters and ordering; the cut of a widened read back to its period.
- Integration with `httptest`: each method through the router with a session.
- Integration, opt-in: a real snapshot, counts only.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/api/`, `internal/ledger/open.go`, `internal/ledger/safety_test.go`, `go.mod`, `go.sum`, `AGENTS.md`
**Reads only:** `internal/contract/contract.json`, `internal/ledger/`, `internal/txrules/`, `internal/money/`, `internal/brday/`, `web/src/api/contract/`, `web/src/api/fake/`, `bin/ci`

New handler, wire-type and test files in the existing HTTP package, its golden directory, and one test dependency. If a handler needs a ledger query that does not exist, it is added to `internal/ledger` as a new file with its test.
close_reason: The backend answers shell.overview, accounts.list, accounts.detail, transactions.list, transactions.filterOptions and transactions.detail from the ledger. Money is written from integer cents as a decimal with two places and a test forbids floats in the HTTP layer. A month is read three days wider and cut back, so a tax and its purchase across a month's end are one line. Every answer validates against its schema in the manifest over two fixture ledgers and is recorded as a golden file from invented data; the golden update refuses to run with a real snapshot set. A snapshot that is not a database answers ledger_unavailable. bin/ci: CI green. Over a real snapshot every answer of every month validated, every month's tally summed to its input, and every account was placed in exactly one bank; the built server was also called end to end against it.
