One departure from the bead: a bank account's bucket is a required field of the contract and is answered as available.

title: A refused month close folds the step it was started from
description:
## What changes for the user
In the monthly closing, pressing "Fechar o mês" while the app cannot save shows the message that nothing was changed, and the month does stay open. But the step the person was looking at folds shut, as if something had happened. After this lands a refused close leaves the screen exactly as it was before the click: the step stays open.

## Outcome
A refused or failed close of a month leaves the closing tab's open step open.

## Context
finwise's interface runs against a backend that is read-only for now: every write answers with a `read_only` error, and one central function turns that into a toast ("Somente leitura por enquanto. Nada foi alterado.") and a bump of the revision counter so the screens fetch again. No write call site catches errors itself, on purpose.

The closing tab, `web/src/screens/revisao/ClosingTab.vue`, keeps which step is unfolded in its view store. Its `askToClose` sets `view.openStep = -1` before it calls the write that closes the month, so the step folds whether or not the write succeeds. Every other write on the screens changes local state only after the server answered, or not at all; this is the one place found where local state moves first.

The fix belongs in the screen: fold the step only once the close has succeeded. The central failure handling is not changed, and no error is caught here.

A test helper already exists for this kind of check: `web/src/test/readOnly.ts` wraps the stand-in so that every write is refused the way the backend refuses it, and `web/src/api/refused-writes.test.ts` already refuses a month close through a mounted screen and asserts the toast and the open month.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Mount the Revisão closing tab on the stand-in wrapped by the read-only helper, on an open month.
2. Unfold the last step, "Fechar o mês", and confirm closing the month.
3. Observed: the read-only toast appears and the month is still open, but the step is folded.
4. Expected: the read-only toast appears, the month is still open, and the step is still unfolded.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] After a refused "Fechar o mês" through the mounted closing tab, the step that was unfolded is still unfolded.
- [ ] After a successful close on the plain stand-in the step folds, as today.
- [ ] `npm --prefix web run parity` still reports every state at or under 0.05%.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and the regression test fails when the fold is moved back before the write.

## Tests
- Component, regression: a refused close through the mounted closing tab leaves the step unfolded.
- Component: a successful close folds it.
- Parity: the full run, unchanged.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `web/src/screens/revisao/ClosingTab.vue`, `web/src/api/refused-writes.test.ts`
**Reads only:** `web/src/screens/revisao/useClosingActions.ts`, `web/src/test/readOnly.ts`, `web/src/api/failures.ts`, `bin/ci`

One line moved in one screen and one regression test beside the existing refused-write tests.
close_reason: ClosingTab.vue folds the step only after closeMonth resolved; nothing is caught in the screen, so a rejected write still reaches the central failure handling. The regression test refuses the close through the mounted closing tab and asserts the step stays unfolded, and that a successful close folds it; it failed before the fix and again when the fold was moved back before the write. bin/ci: CI green, 878 tests. Parity: 174 checked, 0 over 0.05%; the template is untouched.

title: Journal every change to the app's database through one recorder and undo by inverse, refusing what was overwritten since
description:
## What changes for the user
Today nothing in the app can be changed, so nothing can be taken back. In the design the person sees
"Desfazer" in a message for eight seconds after each change, and again beside each step of a
purchase's history; in the prototype that button quietly puts the whole app back to an earlier
picture, wiping anything changed in between. This work builds what will stand behind those two
buttons: each thing the person changes is remembered as one change with who made it, taking it back
restores exactly that change and nothing else, and when what it would overwrite has been changed
again since, it refuses and says so ("Isso já foi alterado depois e não pode mais ser desfeito.")
instead of destroying the later edit. Nothing is visible yet, because no button writes until later
work. If this were wrong the person would see an undo bring back the wrong category on a purchase, or
erase a later correction without a word.

## Outcome
`internal/authored` gains the layer every later write goes through. A closed, hand-written registry
names the journaled tables in two shapes, says for a table of independent facts which of two kinds it
is, and says which table is owned by another. A recorder holds one immediate
transaction and one open change and is the only way a journaled table is written; every effect lands
in `change_effects`, and a change that records nothing and is never asked for its id leaves no trace.
Undo restores a change's effects by inverse in one transaction and refuses, changing nothing, when the
change is unknown, already undone, or followed by a later change still in force on anything it would
restore, even one that put the old value back. A change can be extended so one undo takes back both
writes. The same inverse works over a chosen part of a change,
recorded as a new change, with a read-only answer to "can this still be taken back". A canonical dump
of every registered table exists for proofs. Guards fail when a table is unclassified or is written
outside the recorder. No route and no handler is added.

## Context
finwise is a personal finance app for one person. The **ledger** is a SQLite snapshot a separate
collector fills from the banks every night; the app only reads it. The **app's own database**,
`finwise.db`, is where everything the person authors lives; `internal/authored` is the only package
that executes SQL against it. **The stand-in** is the in-memory fake backend under
`web/src/api/fake/` that the design prototype runs on; it is the only existing statement of how
writes behave, and its behaviour is the rule except where this text says otherwise. The **journal** is
the record of every change made to authored data: each write is one change with an author, made of
effects, and can be undone.

**What exists when this starts.** The work that creates the database ({{F1}}) has landed:
`internal/authored` recognises and opens `finwise.db` as a pool in which every connection has
`foreign_keys(1)`, `busy_timeout(5000)`, `synchronous(FULL)`, `journal_mode(WAL)` and immediate write
transactions; it offers a read-only transaction and an immediate write transaction; it applies
embedded migrations recorded by name and checksum; and every statement it runs is a registered
constant that a test prepares against the migrated schema, with a test that fails on a statement
outside the registry and one that forbids floats in the package. Its migration `0001_journal` created
the journal's tables:

- `changes(id, at, day, author, method, extended, undone_at)`: `id` is
  `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT`, never reused; `at` the instant and `day` its Brazil day;
  `author` one of `person`, `rule`, `model`; `method` the API method that made the change; `extended`
  whether a later write appended to it; `undone_at` null until undone.
- `change_effects(change_id, seq, tbl, key, col, before, after)`: one row per effect, ordered by `seq`
  within its change.
- `meta(key, value)`, which this bead does not use.

Read the package as it is before writing: file and function names are whatever that work chose. This
bead adds no migration and does not edit `0001_journal.sql`: every database that has started with it
holds its checksum and would be refused at the next start. If the recorder turns out to need a column
that file lacks, stop and say so in the report instead of editing the file or inventing a migration
name: migration names are assigned in advance, one owner each, and none is assigned to this work.

**The decision, and what lost.** Undo is the inverse of recorded effects, refused when what it would
overwrite has changed since; the same rule serves the undo of one history step. Why: the stand-in's
undo restores a snapshot of the whole state, which silently destroys later changes, and with money
refusing is the safe failure. What lost: snapshot restore; last writer wins; restoring a step over
later edits. This is a deliberate departure from the stand-in, where `createChangeLog`
(`web/src/api/fake/changes.ts`) clones the state with `structuredClone` when a change begins and
`undo` assigns the clone back, and where `undoHistoryStep` (`transaction-edits.ts`) assigns a step's
saved fields back whatever happened to them since. What the stand-in's tests say that stays true:
an unknown change and one already undone are refused (`writes.test.ts`, "refuses a change it does not
know, or one already undone"); one undo takes back a change together with the one that extended it
("takes back the establishment-wide change together with the one it extended"); taking a step back
does not touch what was done after it, and can itself be undone (`panel-writes.test.ts`, "taking a
step back"). The departure is named in the report together with the test that pins it.

**The registry and the two shapes.** All changes to authored tables go through the recorder. The
recorder works from a closed, hand-written registry of the journaled tables. Each entry says which of
two shapes the table has, its key columns, and how a key and a row are written as canonical JSON (keys
as an array in column order):

- an **attribute table** holds one row of independent facts per key (a transaction's state, an
  establishment, a subscription, a setting). An effect is one column changing:
  `(change, seq, table, key, column, before, after)`. The registry says which of two kinds such a
  table is.
  - In a **table of optional facts** (a transaction's state, an establishment, a pot's settings) every
    column has a default, and a row whose columns are all at their defaults is the same as no row: the
    first fact written about a transaction creates its row without owning it, so taking that fact back
    later leaves the others alone.
  - In a **table of things that are created whole** (a subscription), some columns are required, and
    creating the row is itself a unit: a later change to any column of it makes the change that
    created it stale, so undo never leaves half a row behind.

  A restore is computed for the whole row and written once, never column by column.
- a **set table** holds rows that are facts by existing (a tag on a transaction, a split part, a line
  in a budget version, a closed month, a history step). An effect is one row appearing or
  disappearing: `(change, seq, table, key, null, before, after)`.

A table that is not in the registry cannot be written through the recorder, and a test fails when any
statement that inserts, updates or deletes in an authored table is executed outside it. A **unit** is
what one effect is about: a table, a key and, for an attribute table, a column; in a table of things
created whole, the creation of a row is one more unit of the change that created it. So the registry
entry of an attribute table carries its kind, and the two kinds behave differently at exactly one
point. In a table of optional facts there is no such thing as creating a row: two changes to
different columns of one key are independent of each other and each can be undone without the other,
whichever of them came first and whether or not a row existed before. In a table of things created
whole, the same independence holds between changes to a row that already exists, but the change that
created the row cannot be undone while any later change to that row is still in force.

None of those tables exists yet; each arrives with its own migration in later work, which adds its
entries to the registry. So the registry this bead ships has no production entry, and everything here
is proved on scratch tables that the tests create and register. The recorder therefore takes its
registry as a value: the package's own in production, a test's in a test.

**A table owned by another.** Some facts belong to a row of another table without being part of it,
and the registry can say that one table is owned by another. The one the write side needs is the
reason a person gives for a correction: it belongs to its history step but is kept beside it, in a
table the step owns (`history_step_reasons(step_id, reason)`, created later with the transactions'
tables ({{T1}})). The point of keeping it beside: giving a reason does not make the line change stale,
so "apply to all purchases here" and the "Desfazer" of the message still work after it; and taking the
line change back takes its reason with it. Removing a row removes the rows it owns and records them as
effects of the same change, so they come back with it. The reason a transaction's detail answers is
the one on its latest step that has one; it is stored nowhere else. For the recorder that is three
requirements. Writing an owned row is an effect on the owned row's own unit and on no unit of the
change that made the owner, so neither undo nor extension of that change is refused because of it.
Removing the owner, by a recorded write or by an undo, removes its owned rows in the same transaction.
And when a recorded write removes an owner, the disappearance of each owned row is an effect of that
same change, so undoing it brings owner and owned rows back exactly. A foreign key with a cascading
action would delete rows the recorder never saw and never recorded.

**Tables deliberately not journaled, by name:** `changes` and `change_effects` (the journal itself),
`schema_migrations`, `meta`, `tx_index` and `tx_ids` (what the database remembers about the
transactions it has seen: observations, not decisions), `lines` (a budget line's id, once minted,
exists for good) and `pin` (changing the PIN is not a recorded change and has no undo). Most of these
do not exist yet either; the list is written now so that a table added later which is in neither list
is caught. Writes to these tables happen in the same transaction as the change they accompany and are
not effects: undoing the change leaves them.

**A change.** A write handler receives a recorder that already holds one immediate transaction and
the facts of a change: author, method, the instant and the Brazil day (`brday.DayOf` of the instant;
the package never reads the host's clock). The change's row is written with its first effect, or when
the handler asks for the id because it must answer one; a handler that does neither leaves no trace in
the journal. It performs its recorded writes and returns; the caller commits. The change id is the
handle the API returns, as a decimal string; ids are never reused and are the same for the same
sequence of writes, which the golden files of later work rely on. Any failure rolls the whole thing
back. Authors are `person` (an HTTP session), `rule` (the step that brings the database up to date
with a new snapshot and classifies new transactions by rule) and `model` (reserved for a later nightly
model call). The journal is never trimmed.

That one rule about when the row is written gives the three endings the write side needs. Where a
method's result may be null, "nothing to do" and "no such target" answer null and record nothing: the
handler writes no effect and asks for no id, so no row exists. Where the result may not be null, a
write that changes nothing records an empty change and answers its id, whose undo is a no-op: the
handler asks for the id, so the row exists with no effect, and its undo succeeds. And the step that
classifies by rule records one change for a whole run only if anything authored changed; with nothing
to record, no change is written. It follows that a recorded write whose content equals what is already
there records no effect, and so by itself writes no row.

**Undo**, in one immediate transaction with foreign keys deferred to the commit:

1. Collapse the change's effects per unit (a table, a key and, for an attribute table, a column): the
   first `before`, the last `after`.
2. If the change is unknown or already undone, or a later change that is still in force has an effect
   on any of those units, refuse (the API will answer `refused` with the reason `stale_change`) and
   change nothing. The journal's order decides, not the value: a unit set from A to B, then to C, then
   back to B by later changes is not the first change's to take back. As a guard against a write that
   escaped the journal, a unit whose current content differs from that `after` is refused the same
   way.
3. Otherwise restore every `before`, in reverse order of `seq`, and mark the change undone. Undo
   returns nothing and is not itself undoable.

A change is in force while it is not undone, so once the later changes are themselves undone, newest
first, the earlier one can be undone again. In a table of things created whole, for the change that
created a row, any later change in force to any column of that row counts as an effect on its
creation; in a table of optional facts nothing does, because no change owns a row there. In step 3
the order is the order of rows: the `before`s that fall on one attribute row are combined and that
row is written once, or removed once when the change created it whole. The reverse order matters for
what SQLite cannot defer, such as a unique value handed from one row to another inside one change,
and the criterion below about that case binds whatever the implementation does with a unit written
more than once. A restore that the database refuses, or that leaves a foreign key unsatisfied at the
commit, rolls the whole undo back.

`internal/authored` knows no HTTP. It reports a refusal as a typed error of its own. The `refused`
kind and its list of reasons are added to the API's contract by separate work ({{F4a}}); turning the
typed error into the wire answer `{"error":{"kind":"refused","reason":"stale_change"}}` (HTTP 409),
and the handler of `changes.undo` itself, belong to the write dispatch, the part of the router that
hands a write method to its handler and commits ({{F4c}}). The sentence the person reads, "Isso já foi
alterado depois e não pode mais ser desfeito.", lives in the interface.

**Extending a change.** One write of the API, "apply to all purchases here"
(`transactions.applyLineToEstablishment(changeId)` in `web/src/api/contract/transactions.ts`: "Extends
a line change to the rest of its establishment; undoing it undoes both"), adds to a change already
committed. It happens in one immediate transaction that requires the origin to be a live `setLine`
change, not yet extended, whose own effects still hold; it appends its effects to the origin, marks it
extended and returns the same id, so one undo takes back both. Anything else is `stale_change`. This
bead builds the mechanism, with the required method given by the caller: reopen a committed change as
a recorder, after checking that it exists, is not undone, was made by that method, is not yet
extended, and that its effects still hold, tested the way step 2 of undo tests them: no later change
in force on any of its units, and every unit still holding its last `after`. One case is not
staleness and is not decided here: an origin whose transaction is a person or a movement between own
accounts has no establishment to extend to and is answered `not_found`. That case and the handler are
later work ({{T2}}, the writes that put a transaction on a budget line).

**One part of a change.** A transaction's history is a table of steps, each tied to the change that
produced it and of one of two kinds: a step that records what the change did to the transaction, and
a note (such as "rule created") that records that something happened beside it. Taking one step back
(`undoHistoryStep(id, stepId)`: "Restores the state before that step alone and drops the step from
the history") opens a new change that applies steps 1 to 3 to the units of that one transaction that
the step's change touched, then deletes the step. Because effects are per column, taking back "marked
as refund" leaves a refund line chosen later untouched, as the stand-in's test expects; and a step
whose columns were changed again since is refused instead of overwriting the later edit.
`HistoryEntry.undoable` is computed with the same comparison and is always false for a note, so the
panel offers only what can be taken back. A transaction's state is a table of optional facts, so this
holds in every case, including when the refund mark was the first thing ever authored on the
transaction: that first fact made the row without owning it. Being a recorded change, a step's undo
can itself be undone with `changes.undo`. Taking a line step back always leaves the "why" question closed (after
some corrections the app asks the person why; whether it is asking is part of the transaction's
state, and closing it is one more recorded write of the same new change). The steps table arrives with the
transactions' tables ({{T1}}) and the handler with the writes that put a transaction on a budget line
and keep its history ({{T2}}); what this bead builds is the mechanism they call: the same three steps
over a subset of a change's units chosen by the caller, performed inside another open change so that
the restores are that change's effects, without marking the source change undone and with the
recorder still open for the caller's further writes; and a read-only function that says whether that
inverse would be refused, usable inside a read-only transaction.

**Canonical JSON, the dump, and floats.** `key`, `before` and `after` are canonical JSON, compared as
text. The form of a row and of a value is the implementer's, with three constraints: a key is an array
in column order; the form is deterministic (the effects of a write are later compared with golden
files, and the journal is never trimmed, so values written today are compared against content rendered
years later); and no number passes through a float. That last one has a trap the package's float guard
cannot see: decoding a stored value into `any` turns every number into a `float64` without the word
appearing in the source. Amounts are integer cents (`money.Cents`) and travel as integers. The proofs
compare a canonical dump of every registered table, in which a row of a table of optional facts at
its defaults is the same as no row. The write conformance harness that later proves every write of
the API can be undone ({{F5}}) needs that same dump for every journaled table, so it is a function of
the package, not a helper buried in a test.

**The statement discipline meets the recorder here.** Every SQL statement over the app's database is a
registered constant. A recorder that assembled SQL from table and column names at run time would run
statements no test ever prepared, so each registry entry names the registered constants that read and
write its table, and no SQL text is assembled per call. Scratch tables and their statements live in
test files, which the discipline does not cover.

**What later work will ask of it,** so the design can be checked against real use: one change that
writes many rows across several tables and is undone as one (saving a budget removes later versions
with their lines, parent and children, and clears lines from transactions' state; a bulk write over
many transactions; settling a pending transaction changes its line, its establishment's default and a
nickname at once); a set row whose other columns change while its key stays (a split part that keeps
its place and loses its line); set rows with minted ids restored under the same id (a history step);
a unique value handed from one row to another inside one change (a line name within a budget
version); and a count of the changes made by one method, not undone, on given days, read from
`method`, `undone_at` and `day`, which must therefore be written faithfully.

**Failure paths this bead owns.**

| what goes wrong | what happens |
| --- | --- |
| a write fails halfway, or waits out the lock | one transaction: nothing of it is kept; the API answers `internal` |
| an undo meets a later change | `stale_change`; nothing is restored |
| two tabs, or a tab and the rule step, write at once | writes queue; each is its own change; an undo that lost the race is refused |

**Left to the implementer** (what makes this bead `spec:open`): the canonical form of a row and of a
value, within the constraints above; how a registry entry is represented, how it says which kind an
attribute table is and how it says a table is owned; how the creation of a row in a table of things
created whole is written in `change_effects`, within the columns that table has; whether a row of a
table of optional facts is deleted or kept when it returns to its defaults, the two being the same to
every reader and to the dump; the mechanism of the guard against
writes outside the recorder (a scan of the source, or a check at run time), as long as it fails on the
break named in the criteria; and how many random sequences the property test runs and how long they
are, as long as every run reaches every operation listed under Tests, a failure prints what
reproduces it, and the default `go test` run stays fast enough for the gate.

**Privacy and conventions.** No test here touches a real ledger; the tables are scratch and the
content invented, so a failing sequence may be printed in full. Work happens in the worktree it was
given and ends at local commits: atomic, Conventional Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of
a session, a work item or a plan in a commit message. Money is integer cents and no float may appear
in the money path. Every SQL statement over the app's database is a registered constant. Interface
text is Brazilian Portuguese and everything else is English; a design value in a component comes from
a token (neither arises here). The package logs nothing and prints nothing.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A recorded write to a table that is not in the registry returns an error and writes nothing.
- [ ] On a scratch attribute table of either kind, on a row that already exists, changing one column
records exactly one effect whose `tbl`, `key` (a JSON array in column order), `col`, `before` and
`after` are that unit's; changing two columns records two; writing the content already there records
none. In a table of optional facts, the first fact written for a key that has no row records that
column's effect and nothing that makes the change the owner of the row. In a table of things created
whole, creating a row is recorded so that the change is known to have created it.
- [ ] On a scratch set table, a row appearing records one effect with `col` null, `before` null and
`after` the row; a row disappearing records `before` the row and `after` null.
- [ ] A change opened with the instant 2026-12-01T01:30:00Z, author `person` and a method name stores
that method, that author and the day `2026-11-30`; an author outside `person`, `rule`, `model` is
refused; the id returned is the row's id.
- [ ] The row of a change is written at its first effect, or when its id is first asked for, whichever
comes first, and once. A recorder that records no effect and is never asked for its id leaves no row
in `changes` or `change_effects` after its transaction commits, and the next change gets the id that
one would have had. A recorder asked for its id that records no effect leaves one `changes` row and
no effect; the undo of that change succeeds, changes nothing and sets `undone_at`; a second undo of
it is refused.
- [ ] A recorder that fails after two recorded writes leaves the dump and both journal tables exactly
as they were; a recorded write and a plain write to a non-journaled table made in the same change
commit together and roll back together.
- [ ] Undo of a change restores the dump taken before the change, for both shapes and both kinds; for
a key of a table of optional facts that had no row before, the dump is equal whether or not a row at
its defaults is left behind.
- [ ] Undo is refused, with the dump and both journal tables unchanged, for: an id that does not
exist; a change already undone; a change one of whose units a later change still in force has an
effect on; a change one of whose units holds something other than its last `after` because a write
went around the journal.
- [ ] The order decides, not the value: after a first change sets a unit from A to B, a second sets it
to C and a third sets it back to B, undoing the first is refused although the unit holds B, the first
change's own `after`. Once the third and then the second are undone, the first is undone and the unit
holds A.
- [ ] A change that wrote one unit twice (from A to B, then to C) is undone when the unit holds C,
restoring A.
- [ ] In a table of optional facts, a first change writes one column of a key that has no row, a second
change writes another column of that key, and the first is undone: the undo succeeds, the first
column is back at its default and the second keeps its value. Undoing the second as well leaves the
dump equal to the one taken before either.
- [ ] In a table of things created whole, a change creates a row, a second change changes one column of
it, and undoing the creation is refused with nothing changed. Once the second change is undone, the
creation is undone and the row is gone whole.
- [ ] In a table of either kind, for a row that existed before both, two changes to different columns
of one key are independent: either is undone while the other is in force, and the other's column
keeps its value.
- [ ] A restore writes each attribute row once: on a scratch table of optional facts with a constraint
spanning two columns, a change that sets both columns in one recorded write is undone without the
database refusing any statement on the way; on a scratch table of things created whole, undoing the
creation removes the row without any statement emptying a required column first.
- [ ] After an undo, `changes` has the same number of rows as before it, the undone row's `undone_at`
is the instant given, and its effects are still in `change_effects`.
- [ ] A change that removes or creates a parent row and its children, recorded parent first and
recorded children first, is undone to the exact previous dump in both orders, with foreign keys
enforced at the commit.
- [ ] A change that deletes a row and then inserts another row taking over a unique value of the
first is undone without a constraint failure.
- [ ] An undo whose restore the database refuses (a unique value taken since by a row the change
never touched) fails and leaves the dump and both journal tables unchanged.
- [ ] Extension: a committed change made by the required method, not undone, not extended, whose
effects still hold by the test of undo's step 2, is reopened; the effects recorded then carry the
origin's id with `seq` continuing; the origin is marked extended; the id handed back is the origin's;
one undo restores the dump from before the origin. It is refused as stale, changing nothing, for: an
unknown id; an undone change; a change made by another method; a change already extended; a change one
of whose units a later change in force has an effect on, also when that change put the value back.
- [ ] Inverse of a part: over a caller-chosen subset of a change's units, inside another open change,
the selected units return to their `before`, the unselected ones keep their content, the restores are
recorded as effects of the open change, the source change is not marked undone, and undoing the new
change puts the selected units back. It is refused, changing nothing, when a later change in force
has an effect on a selected unit, and is not refused because one has an effect on an unselected unit.
- [ ] The read-only check agrees with the inverse of a part: in the property test, for every state
reached, it says "can be taken back" exactly when the inverse then succeeds, and it runs inside a
read-only transaction.
- [ ] Owned rows: writing a row of a table owned by a set table does not make the change that created
the owner stale, for undo and for extension; undoing that change removes the owner and its owned rows;
a recorded removal of an owner that has owned rows records one effect for the owner and one for each
owned row in the same change, and its undo restores owner and owned rows to the exact previous dump.
- [ ] A column set to 9007199254740993 (2^53 + 1, which no `float64` holds), then changed, then
restored by undo, holds 9007199254740993 again, and the journal's `before` and `after` for it hold
that integer exactly.
- [ ] Every table of the migrated schema, SQLite's own `sqlite_` tables aside, is either in the
registry or in the list of tables deliberately not journaled, which names `changes`,
`change_effects`, `schema_migrations`, `meta`, `tx_index`, `tx_ids`, `lines` and `pin`; a table in
neither, or in both, fails a test.
- [ ] A statement that inserts, updates or deletes in a registered table and is executed outside the
recorder fails a test.
- [ ] With two handles on one file: after a write through one handle commits a change to a unit, an
undo through the other handle of an earlier change to that unit is refused and nothing is restored;
an undo begun while another write transaction is open waits for it and then decides on what that
write left.
- [ ] The property test passes: random sequences of recorded writes over scratch tables of both
shapes and both kinds of attribute table, in which write then undo returns the exact previous dump,
undo after an interfering write is refused and changes nothing, also when later writes put the old
value back (A to B, then C, then B), a first fact is taken back from under a second in a table of
optional facts, the creation of a whole thing is refused while a later change to its row is in force,
and a parent and its children are restored whatever their order.
- [ ] The package's existing tests still pass with the new statements: every new constant is
registered and prepares against the migrated schema, and no file of the package uses a float.
- [ ] `internal/authored/migrations/0001_journal.sql` is byte-identical to what it was, and no file
outside `internal/authored/` is changed.
- [ ] The report names the test that pins the departure from the stand-in: an undo that would
overwrite a later change is refused, where the stand-in restores its snapshot over it.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, and the report names the break used for each: step 2
removed altogether (an interfering write is then overwritten); step 2 deciding by the value alone (the
A, B, C, B case is then undone); the guard on current content removed (a write that went around the
journal is then overwritten); a later change counted although it was undone; the creation of a row
in a table of things created whole not treated as a unit (the creation is then undone under a later
change); the first fact in a table of optional facts treated as owning its row (taking it back is
then refused once a second fact exists); an attribute row restored column by column (the database
refuses a statement on the way); the change's row written when the recorder opens (a handler that
does nothing leaves a row); the restores run in forward order; the collapse keeping a unit's first
`after` instead of its last; `undone_at` not set (a second undo succeeds); foreign keys not deferred;
the "not yet extended" check removed; the owned rows left behind when their owner goes, or removed
without being recorded; a number decoded through `any`; a write to a registered table added outside
the recorder; a table left out of both lists.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, the property test passes, and an interfering write makes
undo refuse with nothing changed, also when it put the old value back.

## Tests
- Property, over scratch tables created and registered by the test in a temporary database (an
attribute table of optional facts, every column with a default and a constraint spanning two of them;
an attribute table of things created whole, with required columns; a set table; a table owned by the
set table; and a parent and child pair joined by a foreign key): random sequences that every run
takes through both kinds of attribute table. For optional facts: a first fact on a key with no row,
then a second fact on another column by another change, then the undo of the first, after which the
second survives. For things created whole: the creation of a row, then a change to one column of it,
then the undo of the creation, which is refused. And through: a write on an existing row of each
kind, a set insert, a set delete, a set row whose other columns change, an owned write, a parent with
children in both orders, a change that records nothing, an empty change, an extension, an inverse of
a part, an interfering write, a unit taken from A to B, then C, then back to B by three changes, and
an undo; after each undo the canonical dump is compared with the one taken before. A failure prints
what reproduces it.
- Table: the refusals of undo and of extension, one row per cause, the later change that put the value
back and the write that went around the journal among them; a later change that was itself undone no
longer refusing; the three endings of a change (no trace, an empty change, a change with effects); the
collapse (A to B to C); per-column independence in both kinds of attribute table, including a first
fact taken back from under a second in a table of optional facts; the creation of a whole thing
refused while a later change to its row is in force, and undone once that change is.
- Unit: the journal rows a change leaves (`changes` and `change_effects`, field by field); the
integer 9007199254740993 through write, change and undo; a unique value changing hands; a restore the
database refuses.
- Unit, two handles on one temporary file: an undo that lost the race to a write; an undo that waits
for an open write.
- Unit, guards: every table classified; no write to a registered table outside the recorder; the
package's statement and float scans over the new files.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/authored/`
**Reads only:** `internal/authored/migrations/0001_journal.sql`, `web/src/api/fake/changes.ts`,
`web/src/api/fake/history.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/transaction-edits.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/writes.test.ts`,
`web/src/api/fake/panel-writes.test.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/changes.ts`,
`web/src/api/contract/transactions.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/transaction-detail.ts`, `internal/brday/`,
`bin/ci`

One package: the registry, the recorder, the journal's statements, undo with its two variants, the
canonical form and the dump, and their tests; six or seven new code files and no edit outside
`internal/authored/`. It is one package, and `size:L` only by that count of files. The migration file
is read and not edited. `internal/api` and `cmd/finwise` are not touched: nothing calls the recorder
until the write dispatch exists.

title: Answer a pot's yield fast and open the month into its daily rows
description:
## What changes for the user
Against a real ledger the Cofrinhos screen, a pot's page and the Patrimônio screen each take about fifteen seconds to open, while every other screen opens at once. And on a pot's page the month's yield is one figure, where the person asked for it to open into the days behind it; that list is always empty. After this lands the three screens open as fast as the others, and the month's yield opens into its daily rows, with a day the bank's records cannot support shown as unknown rather than as zero.

## Outcome
Every yield figure the backend answers (the pots list, a pot's page, the net worth) comes from one fast computation over the balance history, which also gives the daily rows of a pot's month. The collector's own yield statement stays in the reader only as the reference the new computation is tested against.

## Context
finwise's read-only Go backend answers the pots and the net worth from the ledger a collector fills every night. The contract's pot detail carries the month's yield and `days`, the rows behind it; the user decided in the feature interview that yield is shown per month and opens to its daily rows.

Yield is not the change in balance: a deposit raises the balance and yields nothing. The collector's README has a statement for it, copied into the reader (`internal/ledger/pot_yield.go`) and run as three statements over the same CTEs because the single statement does not prepare in this module's SQLite. It answers **one figure per window** between two days, with a `reason` column that says when the figure cannot be computed. The balance history is one sighting per night.

**Measured over a real ledger, by the review, three runs each on the built server:** `savingsPots.list` 12.5 to 15.1 s, `savingsPots.detail` 14.7 s, `netWorth.overview` 13.7 to 15.3 s. Every other read answered in under 0.4 s, including `home.summary`, which reads the same pots and balances without asking for a yield. The handlers already ask the statement only once per account that has a pot to follow, twice in all on that ledger, so the cost is the statement itself, about seven seconds a call, not the number of calls.

That statement is also why the daily rows are empty: a row per day means a window per pair of consecutive sightings, and asking it once per pair took about 70 seconds.

The reader already has a fast read of every sighting's balances and pots (`internal/ledger/history.go`), which the net worth's chart uses. `internal/potrules` already has what turns rows into a month: `DayYield`, and `YieldOfMonth`, which sums a pot's rows, keeps them oldest first, and makes the month unknown when any row is.

What is missing is the yield of each pair of consecutive sightings computed without the collector's statement: from the sightings' balances and the transfers between them, in Go or in one set-based statement, with the same formula and the same reasons for "cannot be computed" as the collector's statement gives for that pair. The collector's statement stays as the reference: a test runs both over fixture ledgers and requires the new rows to equal the reference's answer for every pair, including the pairs with a deposit, a withdrawal, a pending transfer, a pot that appears, and a pot that closes. No handler runs the collector's statement at request time.

A wall-clock figure is not something the work can honestly produce on a shared machine; the absence of the slow statement from the request path is, and a test asserts it. The review measures the time.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `savingsPots.detail` answers one daily row per pair of consecutive sightings of the month for a pot with a stable identity, oldest first, each with its day and its yield or unknown.
- [ ] When every daily row of a month is known, their sum equals the month's yield to the cent; when any is unknown, the month's yield is unknown.
- [ ] For every pair of consecutive sightings in the fixture ledgers, the new row equals what the collector's statement answers for that pair, figure and reason.
- [ ] A day with a deposit and no yield is a row of zero, not the deposit.
- [ ] A pot without a stable identity has no daily rows and an unknown yield.
- [ ] `savingsPots.list`, `savingsPots.detail` and `netWorth.overview` take their yield figures from the new computation, and a test fails if any read handler runs the collector's yield statement.
- [ ] The golden files of the three methods are re-recorded from the fixture ledgers, and the only differences from before are the daily rows that used to be empty.
- [ ] Any new statement lives in the reader's registry and is prepared against the collector's real schema by the existing test.
- [ ] The time each of the three reads takes over a real ledger is measured **by the review**, not by the lane, three runs each on a quiet machine, against the figures above, and recorded on the pull request; each is expected under one second.
- [ ] A test skipped unless `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set compares the new rows with the collector's statement over a sample of at least 20 pairs of a real ledger and logs counts only: pairs compared, equal, unknown.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and the opt-in run reports every sampled pair equal.

## Tests
- Unit over fixture ledgers: the new rows against the collector's statement, pair by pair.
- Unit: the daily rows of a month, their order, their sum against the month's figure, unknown days.
- Golden: the answers of the three methods.
- Unit: no read handler reaches the collector's yield statement.
- Integration, opt-in: a sample of pairs of a real ledger, counts only.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/ledger/`, `internal/potrules/`, `internal/api/pots.go`, `internal/api/pots_yield.go`, `internal/api/pots_detail.go`, `internal/api/net_worth.go`, `internal/api/pots_test.go`, `internal/api/net_worth_test.go`, `internal/api/testdata/golden/`
**Reads only:** `web/src/api/contract/savings-pots.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/net-worth.ts`, `bin/ci`

The yield of a pair of sightings gets a second, fast implementation beside the reference one, and the three handlers that show a yield switch to it. The card, the home summary and every other read are not touched.
close_reason: The yield of each pair of sightings is computed by pure rules from one read of the ledger, and a test requires it to equal the collector's statement, figure and reason, for every window of the fixture ledgers, reaching every reason. savingsPots.list, savingsPots.detail and netWorth.overview take their yields from it, a pot's month opens into its daily rows, and a test fails if a read handler can reach the collector's statement. bin/ci: CI green on the tree merged with main. Over a real snapshot every sampled pair equalled the statement. Measured by the review on the built server over a real ledger, three runs each: savingsPots.list 0.34 to 0.44 s, savingsPots.detail 0.34 to 0.35 s, netWorth.overview 0.33 to 0.37 s, against 12.5 to 15.3 s before. Left open: a day that cannot be supported is left out of the rows because the contract's daily amount cannot be unknown.
